works.title: 301The Dark Side of Inclusive Leadership
works.abstract: This chapter challenges the prevailing framing of inclusive leadership as an unequivocal remedy for organisational inequities. While widely celebrated as a progressive route towards more equitable and diverse workplaces, inclusive leadership remains under-examined as a managerial practice that may reproduce the very hierarchies it seeks to dismantle. We argue that the dark side of inclusive leadership can be traced to its leader-centric focus and business-case rationalities, which depoliticise inclusion, transforming it into a commodified, performative exercise. Drawing on critical diversity and organisation studies, the chapter examines the limitations of inclusive leadership’s ontological foundations and questions the legitimacy of its emancipatory claims. Cautioning against the co-option and depoliticisation of diversity, equity, and inclusion agendas, this chapter calls for a reorientation of the ontological grounding of inclusive leadership towards a relational ontology of interdependence, which offers a more radical possibility for advancing social justice.

works.title: Strengthening Structural Baselines for Graph Classification Using Local Topological Profile
Dutch pre-service teachers’ retrospective perceptions of their own academic tracking experiences
works.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open
works.abstract: Early academic tracking, in which students are placed into different classes or tracks based on academic ability, has been shown to reproduce social inequalities and shape long-term educational opportunities. Although the effectiveness of tracking has been widely studied, less is known about how future teachers recall and interpret their own tracking experiences, who may unintentionally perpetuate inequalities they themselves have possibly experienced. This study investigated retrospective perceptions of full-curriculum tracking experiences to explore issues related to educational equity. A content analysis of 93 questionnaire responses from pre-service primary teachers enrolled in non-academic bachelor’s degree programmes in the Netherlands revealed positive socio-affective, cognitive, and relational perceptions, along with negative perceptions regarding (academic) self-concept and identity. Trends across three retrospective moments were also identified and categorised as consistently positive, consistently negative, and mixed perceptions. Most respondents reported mixed perceptions, suggesting that tracking experiences are highly individualised and shaped by a combination of interrelated factors. These findings highlight the need for teacher education programmes to encourage critical reflection on tracking and its implications for educational equity.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence in Private Markets: A Survey of Methods, Applications, and Emerging Challenges
Participatory Action Research Intervention Model to Address African American Workplace Experiences
works.abstract: This dissertation examines Participatory Action Research as a framework for advancing racial equity in organizational settings, focusing on improving workplace outcomes for African American and BIPOC employees. Grounded in lived experience and professional practice, the study addresses systemic racism, implicit bias, and disparities in hiring, advancement, workload, and recognition. Using a participatory approach, employees engaged as co-researchers in iterative cycles of data collection, reflection, and intervention within a nonprofit organization in Oregon. Guided by Harro's Cycles of Socialization and Liberation, the study connects theory to practice to analyze how inequities are reproduced and disrupted. Findings indicate modest improvements in leadership support, communication, and relational trust, while persistent inequities remained in workload distribution, recognition, and advancement opportunities for Black and BIPOC staff. The results underscore the importance of disaggregated data, leadership commitment, and centering employee voice in driving organizational change. The study shows how Participatory Action Research is both a method and an intervention, fostering collective learning, strengthening relationships, and supporting cultural transformation. It also highlights the tension of increased labor placed on BIPOC participants. Overall, the research positions Participatory Action Research as a practical, participatory, and equity-centered approach to achieving sustainable organizational change.

works.title: Towards a Model of the National Market System: Fragmented and Heterogenous Venues
Psychosocial justice:Always morethan to consider
works.abstract: Aim:Psychology can be implicated in the mitigation and exacerbation of injustice. Arguably, this results from conventional ways of knowing/being supported by long held distinctions between individual/community and psychology/sociality. The aim of this analysis is to offer a way to think about knowing, being, justice and relationships that transcend polemics to realise just practices in education. This orientation invites the pursuit of psychosocial justice. Rationale:Psychology plays a contradictory and complicated role in the pursuit of social justice. Practitioners in educational settings may claim they are challenging equity and fairness through their application of psychological frameworks and methods yet do so employing reductionist and ableist models implicated in reproducing inequality. Examples are reflected in commitments to measure and cultivate characteristics such as grit, growth mindset, lifelong learning and emotion regulation. Implications:Distinctions between research and applied psychologists are rendered redundant as historically separated actions and matters remerge. Resonant within and across all aspects of our work then is an ethic of relationality. There we recognise the consequence of theory in practice, the entangled nature of people and institutions and the continuing emergence of psychosocial life. Conclusions:Thinking about relationality in this way fundamentally challenges and changes how psychology impacts the use of certain concepts and methods, as well as the formation of assumptions and conclusions about education. If committed to just practice educational psychologists cannot be given to finding finalised outcomes because there is and always will be morethan to consider.

works.title: SECURE-NBS: A conceptual framework for integrated nature-based flood risk reduction
Beyond Principlism: A Cosmopolitan and Care Ethics Approach to One Digital Health
works.abstract: This article examines the limitations of principlism in addressing the ethical challenges posed by One Digital Health. While principlism remains influential in bioethics, digital health, and global health policy, we argue that it is insufficient to capture the relational, data infrastructural, and multispecies dynamics shaping the threats to One Health. Using antimicrobial resistance as a paradigmatic case, we show that One Digital Health governance is shaped not only by distributive ethical concerns but also by structural asymmetries in data visibility, digital infrastructure, and epistemic inclusion across human, animal, and environmental domains. These asymmetries reveal a key limitation of principlism: although it articulates abstract commitments to justice and equity, it lacks the conceptual and operational resources to explain how inequalities are produced and reproduced in digital systems. To address this gap, we propose an integrated framework that combines the ethics of care, cosmopolitanism, and a FAIRER-based account of data governance. Ethics of care foregrounds situated vulnerability and relational interdependence; cosmopolitanism extends moral responsibility across global and multispecies scales; and FAIRER operationalizes these commitments within digital infrastructures and data systems. The antimicrobial resistance case study shows that this approach provides a more comprehensive account of One Digital Health governance by linking lived practices, global responsibilities, and data infrastructures. We conclude that addressing One Health threats through digital transformation requires moving beyond principle-based reasoning toward relational frameworks that integrate global commitments with contextual sensitivity.

works.title: Social Geography, Space, and Place in Education
works.abstract: Abstract Society is constituted by both historical and spatial elements; however, education research, policy, and practice often subordinate the spatial in preference for the temporal. In what is often referred to as the “spatial turn,” education researchers have acknowledged spatial concepts to facilitate understandings and inform debates about identity, belonging, social justice, differentiation, policy, race, mobility, globalization, and even digital and new communication modes, among many others. Social geographers understand place as more than a dot on a map, instead focusing on the socio-cultural and socio-material aspects of spaces. Space and place are core elements of social geography. Schools are composed of architectural, material, performative, relational, social, or discursive spaces, all of which are, at least in some respects, socially constructed. Schools and education contexts, as social spaces and places, produce and reproduce modes of social interactions and social practices while also mediating the relational and pedagogical practices that operate within. Pedagogical spaces are also about the exercise of power—a spatial governmentality to regulate behavior. Yet pedagogy can focus on place-based and place-conscious practices that highlight the connectedness between people and the nonhuman world. A focus on the socio-spatial in education research is able to foreground inequalities, differences, and power relations that are able to speak to policies and practices. As such, in this field, there is often a focus on spatial justice, where inequalities based on location, mobility, poverty, or indigeneity are analyzed using spatial understandings of socioeconomic, political, or environmental characteristics. This brings together connections between place and space in powerful combinations around justice, equity, and critical thinking.

works.title: Considerations for making informed choices about engaging in open qualitative research
works.venue: Qualitative Research in Sport Exercise and Health
works.abstract: There is currently little guidance that exists for researchers in the sport and exercise sciences on open qualitative research practices. The purpose of paper is to provide researchers with guidance regarding the considerations necessary for making informed decisions about engaging in open research practices within qualitative inquiry. The guidance was developed through a series of four working group meetings with experts in qualitative research and meetings with key stakeholders (study participants, journal editors, and data management experts). The wider open qualitative research literature also informed the guidance. Nine core values were first identified as underpinning the considerations for engaging in open qualitative research practices: Choice (academic freedom and participant autonomy); Plurality not replication; Flexibility and emergent design; Transparency; Relational ethics; Quality; Education; Equity; and Responsibility. Considerations for researchers are then provided in the following areas as they pertain to open science practices in qualitative inquiry: Types of Data; Types of Studies; Participant Groups; Anonymity and Confidentiality; Participant Consent; Storage and Stewardship of Qualitative Data; Knowledge Dissemination and Open Access Publications; Cost, Time, and Resources; and Preregistration of Qualitative Studies. This paper provides an initial framework for identifying considerations for engaging in open qualitative research practices. These considerations will help qualitative researchers make informed decisions about and plan for implementation of open science practices, as well as assessing the risks and benefits of open science practices in qualitative inquiry.

works.title: Women First
works.abstract: In this chapter, we examine the case of the mobile dating application Bumble™ and its founder, Whitney Wolfe Herd. Bumble™ and Wolfe Herd serve as an example of an organizational context that manages and disrupts traditional forms of conflict management through promotion of relational and structural strategies. Scholarship pertaining to conflict in organizational settings has examined how individuals construct their relationships and interactions with one another through gendered power relations and structures. Gender differences often are made visible in conflict styles as scholars have demonstrated that women and men interact to reproduce and disrupt expectations and experiences that systematically disadvantage one group, typically women, over the more dominant group, men. These types of conflict style dynamics exist in both offline and online settings. Through the case of Bumble, we offer strategies aimed to address conflict at individual and organizational levels that move beyond traditional conflict management strategies and aim to promote gender equity.

works.title: From Water Networks to Wellness: Data Science–Driven Design of Human-Inhabited Spaces
works.venue: IEEE International Conference on Data Engineering Workshops (ICDEW)
works.abstract: Designing inclusive urban spaces that improve personal well-being requires decision processes that are both data-driven and socially accountable, yet current analytics remain largely expert-centric and often ignore how data are unevenly distributed across neighbourhoods and communities. This paper proposes a relational, human-centred framework and platform vision that treats data distribution as a first-class object for urban design, linking heterogeneous urban datasets to well-being objectives, constraints, and evaluation metrics. We combine data science with computational creativity by modelling creativity as a relational process involving both human and non-human agents, and by supporting co-creative scenario generation and refinement through conversational interaction. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the framework embeds provenance-aware workflows that capture data lineage, modelling assumptions, and decision rationales. Finally, we outline multi-objective assessment methods that expose trade-offs among well-being, equity, sustainability, and cost under uncertainty, enabling stakeholders to compare feasible interventions rather than rely on single-point recommendations. The result is a foundation for democratizing the design, simulation, and assessment of urban solutions across diverse city contexts, with equitable water distribution as a motivating and high-impact application domain.

works.title: Introduction to Critical Special Education
works.abstract: Special education and its landmark legislation have profoundly transformed educational access for students with disabilities in the United States. Yet, despite these achievements, the field faces a profound epistemological crisis rooted in its colonial, positivist, and deficit-based foundations. This chapter situates current tensions within a Kuhnian framework, arguing that critiques from Disability Studies, DisCrit, and decolonial scholarship represent productive anomalies driving a paradigm shift toward critical special education. We interrogate how special education’s reliance on standardized assessments, categorical classifications, and medicalized logics reproduces colonial practices of sorting and control. Drawing on Freirean, decolonial, and embodied epistemologies, we propose a transformative framework that reimagines special education as dialogic, relational, and justice-oriented. Critical special education calls for methodological pluralism, epistemic humility, and the integration of social and embodied understandings of disability to dismantle oppressive structures and rebuild education as a site of collective liberation and equity.

works.title: Afterword: Reimagining Higher Education Internationalization as a Practice of Racial Justice
works.venue: Journal of Comparative & International Higher Education
works.abstract: This afterword reflects on the two-part special issue, “Examining Race, Racism, and Racialization in the Internationalization of Higher Education from Global Perspectives,” published in the Summer 2026 edition of the Journal of Comparative and International Higher Education. Bringing together twenty-nine contributions, the issue centers race as foundational to how higher education internationalization is imagined, organized, practiced, and contested across global contexts. The afterword synthesizes key insights across both volumes, showing how internationalization is shaped by colonial histories, geopolitical inequalities, market logics, legal regimes, linguistic hierarchies, and racialized structures of belonging. Contributors challenge celebratory and neutral accounts of global engagement by examining how internationalization can reproduce exclusion, surveillance, epistemic domination, and uneven mobility while also enabling solidarity, resistance, and transformation. The afterword concludes by calling for antiracist, decolonial, and justice-oriented approaches that reimagine internationalization through relationality, accountability, equity, care, and collective liberation.

works.title: The Digital Buffalo
works.abstract: Abstract Over millennia, Indigenous Peoples in Canada have sustained an intricate and spiritual connection to the physical environment, reflected in cultural practices, songs, and storytelling. This relational worldview shapes Indigenous understandings of space, now extending beyond physical terrains to include digital and virtual environments. Access to digital space has become integral to spatial justice, raising questions of equity, participation, and governance. The chapter examines the Indigenous Friends Association’s efforts to bridge Indigeneity and digital technologies through community-led education and software development grounded in Indigenous knowledge systems. It argues for ethical and inclusive technology design centered on Indigenous epistemologies, critiquing how centralized and cloud-based infrastructures reproduce colonial power in the digital realm. In some traditional teachings, the buffalo is a strong animal that does not fear or turn away from a storm. These teachings of fortitude, even in the looming turbulence of unsafe virtual spaces, reflect the mission of the association.

works.title: Virtualization of Care: Ethics, Inequality, and the Digital Turn in India’s Health Infrastructure
Active Assembly Theory and Practice
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: Assembly traces can support explicit probabilistic inference without being treated as recovered program meaning. Active Assembly Theory and Practice makes that distinction executable: transparent x86-64 fixtures are decoded with Capstone, traced under bounded Unicorn emulation, and mapped to typed observations that distinguish missing, unseen, and unsupported evidence. Two Generalized Notation Notation (GNN) specifications define passive-phase and prospective sensor models whose tensors drive real pymdp execution. A native categorical Julia/RxInfer companion consumes the passive model's same parameters (Friedman 2026; Heins et al. 2022; Bagaev et al. 2023). The sensor Agent selects an action before fixture evidence is acquired. Independent finite calculations check beliefs and policy scores; native smoothing uses the same parameters and first-observation convention. Every inference comparator and fitted diagnostic also consumes an upstream-parsed numeric GNN specification, with source-bound runtime instances and rendered model graphs. A corpus of 10 authored fixtures supports complete-fixture exclusion diagnostics. At the fixed informative likelihood, the memoryless decoder outperforms the temporal filter; temporal advantages appear under synthetic observation ambiguity. Designed category ambiguity remains a visible failure case. The separate Gaussian and categorical Bethe free-energy diagnostics are not compared numerically with policy expected free energy. The quotient benchmark contains 64 transformation-family identifiers and 4096 rows, with 16 families held out from model fitting. The co-primary portfolio includes an interpretable classifier, a temporal probabilistic model, a fixed one-layer tanh recurrent classifier, and surface baselines; the temporal endpoint reaches balanced accuracy 0.775 and macro-F1 0.772 on this frozen bounded benchmark. Held-out identifiers share authored template lineages with the fitting data. Family-resampling intervals and conditional randomization diagnostics therefore describe this finite inventory; the retrospective protocol correction withholds superiority claims. A complementary pinned static-only corpus supplies 5 licensed source projects and 100 source-contract rows, including 40 lexical witnesses, 40 contract-directed near misses, and 20 identity controls. The corpus establishes provenance and coverage; it does not execute arbitrary external binaries or support application-effectiveness claims. Selected normalized machine-state relations are checked by Python, native execution, and a bounded Lean fragment. Exact finite sensing certificates and source-bound reader artifacts make assumptions and failures inspectable. Independent physical replication remains unearned. The contribution is a reproducible substrate for testing assembly-to-inference mechanisms, with explicit limits on semantics, statistical generalization, and external validity.

works.title: Indigenous Measures for Protecting and Addressing Critical Trauma (IMPACT) – Project protocol
works.venue: Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health
works.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The Indigenous Measures for Protecting and Addressing Critical Trauma (IMPACT) project aims to transform trauma care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples by embedding Indigenous knowledges and culturally responsive practices into trauma systems. METHODS: Using Knowledge-Interface Methodology, the IMPACT will be implemented across two South Australian trauma sites through four phases: establishing trauma profiles and lived experiences; co-designing relational clinical quality indicators and patient-reported outcome measures; piloting and evaluating the program using RE-AIM QuEST framework; and translating findings into national trauma systems. Guided by an Aboriginal Governance Council, the project ensures Indigenous Data Sovereignty and community-led decision-making. RESULTS: IMPACT will lead to the co-design of relational clinical quality indicators and patient-reported outcomes that enhance cultural safety in trauma care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. CONCLUSION: IMPACT will demonstrate improved cultural safety in trauma care, increased use of Indigenous-led quality indicators, and enhanced patient-reported outcomes. IMPACT will build capacity among Aboriginal researchers, foster clinical champions, and provide a replicable model for national reform. IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH: IMPACT lays the groundwork for developing culturally responsive quality of life tools tailored to priority populations, improving outcome measurement and advancing health equity.

works.title: INCLUSIVE EDUCATION FRAMEWORK BEING IMPLEMENTED IN SWEDEN: THE ESSUNGA MODEL
works.venue: European Journal of Special Education Research
works.abstract: This study critically examines Sweden's Essunga model as an exemplar of inclusive education implementation within a decentralised governance structure. Despite Sweden's legislative commitment to equity through the Education Act 2010 and Discrimination Act 2008, municipal autonomy has created fragmented interpretations of inclusive practice. The Essunga Municipality transformed from ranking 287th nationally in 2007 to third place by 2010, achieving 96% student goal attainment and 100% secondary education eligibility through a comprehensive inclusive framework. This two-phase methodological analysis explores the conceptual foundations of Sweden's inclusive education policy and examines the practical implementation of the Essunga model through relational pedagogy, collaborative teaching structures, and elimination of deficit-based categorisation. Key enablers included strong leadership, multi-professional collaboration, student voice integration, and evidence-based professional development. The model rejected diagnostic gatekeeping, embedded special needs educators within mainstream classrooms, and fostered community-anchored support systems. However, significant barriers to replication persist, including policy ambiguity, inadequate teacher preparation, neoliberal marketisation pressures, and the model's dependence on small-scale context. While the Essunga model demonstrates that locally driven inclusive reform can yield substantial academic and social outcomes, systemic constraints limit national and international transferability without coordinated policy frameworks linking legislative intent with relational pedagogical practice. works.title: Unlocking undergraduate access to higher education: Recognition of prior learning in South Africa
works.abstract: Abstract This research note presents the University of the Western Cape’s Portfolio Development Hybrid Programme (PDHP) as a nationally recognised, pedagogically grounded model of recognition of prior learning (RPL) for undergraduate access in South Africa. Designed to enable adult learners – many without formal qualifications or with marginalised knowledge backgrounds – to enter and succeed in higher education, PDHP combines values-based curriculum design with transformative pedagogies rooted in adult learning, epistemic justice and care. Drawing on five years of longitudinal data (2020–2024) and more than two decades of institutional implementation, the study illustrates how RPL can evolve from a once-off assessment mechanism into a sustained teaching-and-learning intervention that builds academic readiness and social mobility within the adult learning context. The findings demonstrate the programme’s success in facilitating academic access for over 400 learners in the past five years and more than 900 since inception, as well as its responsiveness to digital exclusion and institutional constraints, and its alignment with the fourth Sustainable Development Goal (SDG 4) in terms of inclusive education. By theorising RPL through the institution’s framework of innovative, digital, equitable, accessible and lifelong recognition of prior learning (IDEAL-RPL), the research note explains the underlying pedagogical mechanisms – care, scaffolding, digital empowerment and reflexivity – that enable adult learners to thrive and persist at university. It further situates PDHP within the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) discourse, offering evidence of how inclusive curriculum design and hybrid pedagogies contribute to equity, transformation and sustainability in higher education. PDHP challenges dominant, compliance-oriented RPL models by repositioning recognition as a pedagogical and relational process that fosters confidence, capability and lifelong learning. Framed within global debates on education for sustainable development, it offers a scalable and replicable approach to widening participation and transforming institutional cultures towards justice, inclusion and sustainability.

works.title: Mapping the methodological gap: an integrated framework for anti-racist research with youth in public libraries
works.abstract: Purpose This paper articulates an integrated methodological framework for conducting critical qualitative research with equity-deserving youth in public library contexts. It argues that no single existing qualitative approach adequately addresses the relational, structural and communicative demands of this work simultaneously and suggests a purposeful theoretical and methodological response. Design/methodology/approach The framework integrates narrative inquiry, critical race methodology and personal meaning mapping (PMM) as an arts-based tool. Each component is examined for its specific methodological affordances and limitations, followed by an explicit argument for their integration. The study involved semi-structured interviews with 14 youth and seven parents and PMM exercises completed by 12 youth, conducted in consultation with a Black-led community organization over 18 months. Findings The three approaches are theoretically compatible and mutually necessary. Narrative inquiry governs the relational and reflexive conditions of ethical research practice with youth. Critical race methodology provides the structural analytical lens through which individual accounts are connected to institutional conditions. PMM addresses the epistemological and practical constraints of collecting verbal data from young people and produced participant-generated data that independently confirmed the analytical themes. Research limitations/implications The framework was developed and applied by a white researcher in a specific Canadian community context. Future researchers whose positionality differs or who work in different national contexts will generate different relational conditions. Originality/value This paper presents the first known application of PMM in any public library research context. It contributes a replicable and theoretically grounded integrated framework to the repertoire of qualitative methods available to critical LIS researchers.

works.title: Volume III: Simulation Results and Predictive Efficacy of the Quantum-Geometric Monetary Policy Model -A Teaching Note
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: K SC This Volume III presents the complete empirical results from executing the Python simulation framework designed in Volume II. A lightweight but faithful agent-based and networkevolution model operationalising the five cardinal principles of quantum geometry (discreteness/quantization, emergence from entanglement, induced wealth dynamics, holographic encoding, and relational/noncommutative structure) was run across Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, the Gambia, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Indonesia. Monte Carlo simulations (5 replications) compared baseline, income/remittance shock, quantum-geometric policy, and classical aggregate policy regimes. Results demonstrate that quantum-geometric interventions produce more stable inclusion trajectories, improved post-shock resilience, and more efficient network entropy profiles than classical blunt instruments. Full summary tables, key per-country insights, embedded figures, and policy implications are provided. All raw outputs (CSVs, plots, code) are archived in the accompanying GitHub repository. Also available on Academia.edu: https://www.academia.edu/attachments/133011000/download_file?s=portfolio

works.title: Reviewing Living Math on the Instant
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: This paper provides an anatomical review of Living Math (Svancara, 2025) and situates its core claim—that computation can be reconceived as shifting algorithms embodied by coupled coherence dynamics—within thirty-two related literatures. I reproduce and expand the conceptual components introduced by Svancara: the coupled dynamics [ \frac{\partial R_c(t,x)}{\partial t}=F\bigl(R_c,\nabla R_c,R(t)\bigr),\qquad \frac{dR(t)} {dt}=G\bigl(R_c,R(t)\bigr), ] and the relational feedback (R_c(t,x)\leftrightarrow R(t)). The review contrasts this model with classical, quantum, analog, interactive, biological, and hypercomputational paradigms; constructs an epistemological core and an orientation layer mapped as a topology of concepts; evaluates theoretical plausibility and empirical testability; and issues concrete recommendations for formalization and experiment. Thirty-two references spanning logic, computability, dynamical systems, analog computation, biological computation, and field/topological methods are provided in Harvard style. Also available on Academia.edu: https://www.academia.edu/attachments/129093801/download_file?s=portfolio

works.title: From monolingual virtual exchange to AI-supported multilingualism: a critical perspective
works.abstract: Virtual Exchange (VE) has become a key approach in higher education for fostering intercultural competence through online collaboration. However, despite its inclusive framing, many VE initiatives continue to rely on English as a lingua franca or other shared-language arrangements, which may reproduce linguistic hierarchies and unequal participation. This paper examines the potential of AI-supported multilingualism to rethink predominantly monolingual approaches to VE. It argues that while generative AI and translation technologies may reduce communicative barriers and enable broader participation, they do not automatically transform underlying language ideologies or power relations. In doing so, it highlights a tension between accessibility and the interactional work through which intercultural learning occurs. Drawing on Critical Virtual Exchange, relational learning, translanguaging theory, and ethical interculturality, the paper proposes a critical perspective on AI-mediated VE. It further explores how AI may support linguistic equity, multilingual participation, and translanguaging-oriented meaning-making in Virtual Exchange. At the same time, it critically addresses risks such as technological solutionism, linguistic bias in AI systems, and the reinforcement of dominant language ideologies. It concludes that AI-supported VE should be grounded in critical pedagogy and linguistic justice. In this way, VE is reframed not as a site of frictionless communication, but as a relational and ethically accountable educational practice.

works.title: GenAI Chatbot Tutors as Agents of Inclusive Education: A Review Guided by Ethics of Care and Critical Pedagogy
Institutional Patriarchy and Pedagogical Practices: Gendered Power Relations in Contemporary Schooling
works.venue: Pakistan Journal of Social Science Review
works.abstract: This study examines the interplay between institutional patriarchy and pedagogical practices in contemporary schooling, focusing on how gendered power relations are reproduced, negotiated, and challenged. Despite formal commitments to gender equality, schools continue to privilege masculine-coded behaviors, knowledge, and authority through structural hierarchies, curricula, teacher expectations, and classroom interactions. Using a qualitative research design, data were collected from online digital databases, and purposive sampling was employed to select studies addressing gender, institutional structures, and pedagogical practices. Thematic analysis identified seven major themes: structural hierarchies in schools, gendered curriculum and knowledge production, teacher expectations and gendered pedagogy, classroom interactions and peer dynamics, symbolic and cultural capital in education, resistance and agency, and implications for policy and equity. Findings indicate that gendered norms are embedded in both formal and informal educational processes, shaping students’ participation, recognition, and academic trajectories. Simultaneously, students and educators exercise agency, employing strategies of negotiation and resistance that challenge patriarchal practices. Integrating Bourdieusian and feminist perspectives, the study highlights the relational and structural mechanisms of gendered power in schooling and emphasizes the need for inclusive pedagogies, reflective teaching, and equity-focused policy interventions. These insights contribute to understanding how schools foster more equitable educational environments whereas addressing persistent gendered disparities.

works.title: Transformative Social Work and Epistemic Justice
works.abstract: Drawing on feminist, Indigenist, post-anthropocentric, and critical posthumanist approaches, our chapter considers epistemic justice as a key outcome of foundational transformation in contemporary social work. We begin by critically examining how dominant forms of conventional Euro-Western social work have emerged from a modernist, androcentric paradigm. The constraints of this paradigm are also explored, including its embedded hierarchies, binaries, and disembodiment, which generate and reproduce a range of intersecting systems of oppression and epistemic injustices. We then demonstrate how this paradigm is inconsistent with social work's core values. We articulate a transformative social work framework underpinned by relational communitarian practices, equity, fairness, and liberation. Drawing on insights from our feminist participatory social work action research, we explore the creative possibilities for epistemic justice offered by transformative social work. Our chapter concludes that a richer, holistic, and more diverse epistemology is needed for social work to comprehensively embody epistemic justice.

works.title: Learning Effective Interfaces from Opaque Stochastic Systems: Capacity, Selection, and Validation Limits
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: When can a model learned from restricted observations reliably replace an opaque stochastic system? This paper investigates the gap between an adequate model existing, a fitting procedure producing it, and a calibration rule selecting it. The study presents a sequence of finite software investigations culminating in a comparison on 48 opaque synthetic systems. All compared methods use the same fitting and calibration records and are evaluated against complete interaction laws, including joint outputs, delayed effects and resource-sensitive behavior. A portfolio of probabilistic automata and controlled hidden-state models passes 1,063 of 1,152 registered complete-law tests at a total-variation allowance of 0.15, compared with 970 for a passive tree control and 869 for a minimax tree bank. A prespecified secondary portfolio without the bespoke group-aware candidates reproduces the broad improvement, while mechanism-specific regressions remain. A post-reveal capacity check establishes that every target fits the general 16-state instrument family. Nevertheless, under the original fitting budget, only 39 of the 48 systems receive an individually passing produced candidate, and only 37 receive one through calibration selection. Architectural capacity therefore does not guarantee successful finite-budget learning or selection. A separately reported post-hoc sensitivity analysis increases fitting effort on the 11 original failures while retaining the same public data. The expanded portfolio contains a passing model for seven of these systems and selects one for five. Conditional diagnostics identify preparation-dependent response mixing in the challenge regressions. These findings show that fitting effort materially affects candidate production while selection and residual fitting failures persist. The paper distinguishes model capacity, candidate production, calibration selection and validation coverage. It documents shared evaluation specifications, paired outcomes, source provenance and the limits of aggregate scores. The retrospective sensitivity analysis is outcome-selected and does not replace the original primary results or constitute an independent replication. This computational preprint studies finite synthetic systems. It does not establish all-context adequacy, general superiority over untested learning methods, or empirical evidence of consciousness. It forms part of the broader Shadow Theory research programme while keeping its operational findings separate from phenomenal interpretation.
