works.title: Social networks as pathways of political mobility in Portuguese governments
works.abstract: Political mobility in executive appointments is often explained through party affiliation and career trajectories, yet relational embeddedness across institutional arenas may also characterise those who reach ministerial office. We examine, retrospectively and in an exploratory manner, whether the social networks formed by co-participation in Portuguese governmental and parliamentary venues are associated with ministerial appointments. Using web-scraped data on the composition of the Constitutional Governments and the Portuguese Parliament between 2015 and 2024, complemented with the Registers of Interests of government and parliament officials, we construct an individual-venue bipartite network and its projection onto individuals. We estimate the cumulative network of Governments XXI-XXII and, within each policy-domain, retrospectively screen potential candidates for the XXIII Government by ranking actors in the top five positions of at least one centrality measure (betweenness, reach, closeness, weighted closeness, or eigenvector), computed on portfolio-specific subgraphs and restricted to nodes reachable from the Prime Minister. With the identification of 9 out of 16 in-network ministerial appointments, this procedure outperforms both a random selection baseline (mean recall 0.6%) and a career-ladder heuristic based on prior secretarial experience in the same domain (recall 12.5%), consistent with network centrality being informative about the appointment process in stable, well-populated policy-domains. We assess whether Ministers exhibit systematically higher institutional reach than non-ministerial actors using bipartite degree centrality, visualised via a log-scaled KDE, and validated with non-parametric tests (10,000-iteration permutation tests and Mann-Whitney U tests). We decompose connectivity by venue type (e.g., Government, Parliament, Political Party) using a categorical profile comparison and cosine similarity. Ministers display higher bipartite degree centrality than non-ministerial actors (mean 0.0200 vs. 0.0105; difference 0.0096; permutation p-value = 0.021; Mann-Whitney p-value < 0.001). Categorical profiles diverge substantially (cosine similarity 0.494), with significant gaps concentrated in Government and Parliament venues, while Parliamentary Bodies show no meaningful difference (p-value = 0.919). Venue-specific projected network analysis further reveals that the minister-non-minister centrality gap is largest within the political party network, where ministers score nearly double on eigenvector centrality (+96.0%; permutation p-value = 0.003), pointing to elite positioning within partisan structures.

works.title: The Schoolhouse of Modernity
works.venue: Journal of Contemporary Issues in Education
works.abstract: This paper introduces the Schoolhouse of Modernity as an architectural analytic for understanding how modern schooling reproduces defuturing logics even as it claims to advance progress, equity, and sustainability. Extending critiques of the “House of Modernity,” we show how the Schoolhouse operates as a globally circulating blueprint—materialized through policies, metrics, infrastructures, and pedagogical norms that standardize learning and foreclose alternative futures. Through a room-by-room mapping of its architecture, we demonstrate how schooling organizes knowledge, subjectivity, and time in advance, rendering modernity’s assumptions natural and benevolent. Moving beyond reformist approaches, the paper advances a transition imagination oriented toward the undoing of the Schoolhouse through a set of situated gestures—unlearning, composting, hospicing, preserving, repairing, rewilding, and walking out—that resist synthesis, move at different tempos, and demand ongoing response-ability to power, relation, and place. Rather than offering solutions or blueprints, the paper reframes educational futures as processes of restorying—collective, relational, and more-than-human practices through which learning is reimagined beyond mastery, extraction, and universality in times of planetary uncertainty.

works.title: The Contrast Between the Law of Tawhid and the Ideas of Shari’ah-Compliance and Maqasid As-Shari’ah and Its Extension: An Empirical Work
The Symplectic Computational Ontology, Vol. III: Civilizational Symbiosis, Computational Constitutions, and the Post-Unitary Human Condition
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: This third and concluding volume of the Symplectic Computational Ontology trilogy moves from the mathematical foundations (Vol. I) and engineering realization with sovereign hardware (Vol. II) to the profound civilizational consequences of a world whose dominant computational substrate is symplectic, categorical, and non-Archimedean. It examines how symbit-based continuous reasoning, Fukaya-encoded multi-ontology governance, bi-Hamiltonian constitutional negotiation, and p-adic ultrametric cognition reshape human thought, legal and political institutions, economic and ecological ordering, and long-term civilizational resilience. The volume proposes a "Symplectic Compact" — a new social contract grounded in the geometric and categorical structures developed across the trilogy — and articulates institutional mechanisms (computational constitutions, gentle multi-ontology protocols, antifragile symplectic clusters) through which humanity might navigate the transition to a genuinely pluriversal post-unitary order. It concludes by identifying the existential stakes: whether the symplectic paradigm enables a more relational, less extractive civilizational logic or merely reproduces older asymmetries in more mathematically sophisticated forms. Also available on Academia.edu: https://www.academia.edu/attachments/133170279/download_file?s=portfolio

works.title: The evolution of AI-driven sustainable finance: A bibliometric and systematic review of ESG performance and investment strategies
works.abstract: The exponential growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionized sustainable finance, transforming how investors evaluate Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria. However, a significant gap persists regarding the practical integration and transparency of these complex algorithmic models into reliable investment signals, as traditional approaches are often hindered by data lags and greenwashing risks. To address this evolving challenge and bridge the divide between technical innovation and portfolio application, this study employs a rigorous hybrid research design. The proposed study integrates a bibliometric mapping of 388 Scopus-indexed documents published between 2020 and February 2026 alongside an in-depth systematic thematic review of 39 high-impact, implementation-focused studies. The analysis identifies a transformative shift in model dominance driven by data structure: tree-based ensemble models currently dominate structured corporate sustainability assessment (observed in 8 key studies), while Transformer and Large Language Model (LLM) architectures are emerging to extract narrative signals from unstructured text. Additionally, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are increasingly adopted to map hidden, non-linear dependencies in credit risk and complex supply chains. Furthermore, the evaluation highlights a critical need for model interpretability; while Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks like SHAP and LIME are increasingly utilized to meet strict regulatory transparency requirements and clarify ESG predictions, many existing models still fail to provide actionable validation for investors. From a practical perspective, this synthesis offers a strategic roadmap for fund managers. By translating raw ESG signals into decision-grade intelligence, it facilitates the integration of transparent, XAI-verified outputs into active portfolio optimization, risk management, and the mitigation of greenwashing risks, directly supporting strategies like best-in-class screening and thematic tilting. Finally, the integrity and scholarly reliability of these insights are reinforced by the strict adherence to the PRISMA protocol, ensuring the reproducibility and long-term validity of the synthesized evidence.

works.title: The color of friendship: Examining barriers and bridges of disclosure and responsiveness in cross-race friendship
works.abstract: Self-disclosure and responsiveness are foundational processes within friendship. However, in cross-race friendships—where race-based experiences differ—disclosing race-related experiences can threaten the relationship by triggering identity-threat (i.e., concerns of being devalued) for racially minoritized individuals. This pre-registered research examined the relational outcomes that racially minoritized individuals feel during race-related disclosures to White friends (Study 1) and investigated White individuals’ responsiveness, relational outcomes, and racial advocacy intentions following a cross-race friend’s race-related disclosure (Study 2). In Study 1, Black (N = 203) and Latine (N = 227) Americans imagined disclosing a negative race-related (e.g., discrimination), positive race-related (e.g., beliefs in equity growing up), or neutral (e.g., ideal dinner guest) experience to a close White friend. Relational outcomes (i.e., identity-safety, disclosure willingness, perceived understanding, and relational intimacy) were assessed. In Study 2, White Americans (N = 238) listened to a pilot tested audio clip in which they imagined a close Black friend disclose a negative race-related, positive race-related, or neutral experience. White participants’ comfort, conversation outcomes, relational intimacy, and racial advocacy intentions were assessed along with qualitative responsiveness. Across both studies, exploratory mediators included meta-stereotyping concern (Studies 1-2), intergroup anxiety (Studies 1-2), and intergroup empathy (Study 2). Black and Latine participants imagined relational barriers, including increased intergroup anxiety and less perceived understanding when disclosing a negative race-related experience to a White friend. Nuanced mediation patterns emerged among Black participants, demonstrating that sharing race-related experiences, regardless of valence, increases meta-stereotyping concern and intergroup anxiety, ultimately undermining relational outcomes. Unexpectedly, mediation patterns did not replicate for Latine participants. In Study 2, White participants who listened to a close cross-race friend share a negative race-related (vs. neutral) or positive race-related (vs. neutral) experience reported greater intergroup anxiety, negative conversation outcomes and less comfort, as well as increased relational intimacy. Nuanced mediation results underscored the role of meta-stereotyping concern and intergroup anxiety in undermining outcomes during a negative race-related disclosure, while intergroup empathy fostered more relational intimacy and racial advocacy intentions. Analyses of responsiveness revealed that White friends responded with distinct listening patterns when responding to a negative race-related versus positive race-related or neutral disclosure. This research adds to our understanding of close cross-race relationships and illuminates a pathway towards strengthening cross-race friendship and improving interracial interactions broadly.

works.title: The GTUD Riemann-Sphere Experiment II: From Selection to Matter-Like Identity, Binding, Composition and Internal Laws - A Proof of Concept for the Grand Theory of Universal Dynamics (GTUD)
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: Can selection generate its own matter-like structures, distinct families, interactions and internal laws without being told what matter or known physics should look like? GTUD/Riemann Experiment II tests this question in a discrete Riemann-sphere world governed by fixed Selection and retention rules. Known particles, masses, charges, spins, quantum numbers, gravitational equations and Standard-Model identities are excluded as generative targets. Matter-like structure, family identity, abundance, interaction and law must therefore emerge from the model itself before any comparison with established physics is made.The experiment identifies an operational matter-like onset at six-node recurrent structures. This threshold is not defined by size alone: it is the first supported level at which otherwise similar structures acquire different future-law behavior, recur independently across carriers and grow directly into higher recurrent identities. One such structure is embedded in 102 of 135 higher recurrent identities and produces recurrent descendants through direct Native transitions. Continued testing establishes a branching multi-level genealogy rather than a single predetermined growth path. The resulting spectrum contains 135 recurrent exact identities with distinct structural and dynamical roles.The model also develops unequal abundance and interaction laws without fitting them to physical targets. A parent-conditioned transition law predicts which recurrent identities become common: on fresh data, the frozen model improves predictive log score over a parent-blind baseline in every independent run and reproduces the observed abundance ranking with Spearman correlation above 0.99. A separate relational variable, K, measures compatible realization along the corridor between bounded structures. Surgical interventions that change K while leaving the surrounding world fixed causally increase locking, merger and recurrent higher-product formation. Independent carrier tests reproduce the effect across all tested pair classes. Multi-lineage structures form sustained material-like episodes, while the stronger claim of indefinitely stable bulk matter is not supported.Beyond individual structures, Experiment II discovers a hierarchy of internal laws. These include formation and branching laws, family-conditioned response laws, geometric lifetime distributions, non-uniform product spectra, rank-frequency and structural-information relations, approximate detailed balance and stationarity, size-dependent drift and fluctuation laws, carrier-scaling relations, exact recruitment rules and exact predictive-state quotients. By C455, forty-three internal law families are supported or exactly audited. Attraction-like source behavior also decreases systematically with separation and increases with aggregate bounded organization, but the measured microscopic profile is not an exact universal inverse-square law. Discrete relational state cells provide a limited structural comparison with approaches such as loop quantum gravity, without identifying them with spin networks, Planck-scale geometry or spacetime quanta.The later C456-C2700 programme asks a stronger question: are these results tied uniquely to the original microscopic Selection and memory rules? Exhaustive rule-space, null-model and retention-architecture tests show that they are not. The exact Native truth table and hard-reset memory rule are therefore not uniquely required. At the same time, alternative retention architectures preserve major parts of the emergent portfolio, including abundance prediction, material-like episodes, statistical law forms and predictive compression. Exact memory-depth results further identify a broader class of retention systems sharing the same higher-level predictive organization.Together, these findings establish the defined proof of concept of Experiment II: a physics-blind Selection-conditioned world can autonomously develop a matter-like onset, recurrent identities, unequal populations, relational binding and reaction, higher composition and a substantial internal law architecture without known physical objects or laws being inserted as targets. The subsequent robustness programme narrows the claim by showing that the successful organization is more general than one exact microscopic implementation. The results do not identify the generated structures with known particles or establish GTUD as a description of the physical universe. They provide a reproducible mathematical and computational basis for testing whether the same generative architecture has physical counterparts, with positive results, failed hypotheses, null tests and provenance preserved in the accompanying record.

works.title: Financial Fraud Detection via the Integration of Regulatory Inquiry Semantics and Graph-Enhanced Stacking Ensemble Learning
works.abstract: With the continuous strengthening of regulatory oversight in capital markets, reliance on a single financial indicator often exhibits clear limitations when addressing complex financial fraud scenarios, making it difficult to fully capture the multidimensional characteristics of corporate behavior. To this end, this study proposes a financial fraud detection framework that integrates regulatory inquiry semantics with a graph-enhanced stacking ensemble approach, from the perspective of textual analysis of stock exchange regulatory inquiry letters. First, GLM-4-Flash is employed to perform topic extraction and semantic parsing of regulatory inquiry letters, and temporal alignment is incorporated to synchronize textual information with financial features. Second, key features are selected based on Permutation Importance, while the Node2Vec graph embedding method is introduced to model the latent relational structure among firms. Finally, using LightGBM and XGBoost as base learners, an ensemble framework is constructed by incorporating TabNet and multiple gradient boosting tree models, forming a heterogeneous stacking system. Furthermore, an adversarial training mechanism, namely the Fast Gradient Method (FGM), is integrated to enhance the model’s robustness and generalization capability. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms traditional single-model approaches in terms of predictive performance and generalization ability, while also exhibiting strong stability and interpretability in imbalanced classification scenarios.

works.title: Compassion by Design
works.abstract: This OSF repository will host applied tools, templates, methods, measures, and open prototypes to enable transparent replication and context-sensitive adaptation of Compassion by Design across diverse settings. Grounded in compassion science, contemplative traditions, and trauma-informed co-production, Compassion by Design is a transdisciplinary, equity-centred framework that uses enacted co-design (relational praxis) to develop, test, and implement digital and non-digital interventions that activate and sustain compassionate, relational capacities across people, teams, and systems. The approach combines brief embodied practices and narrative engagement with iterative prototyping, mechanism testing (e.g., affiliative-soothing activation), and reflexive process evaluation so that design and practice generate evidence in tandem. By embedding governance and policy guardrails, the framework supports compassion as a system-level commitment rather than solely an individual obligation. Intended outcomes include improved wellbeing, strengthened social connection, epistemic justice, fairer research partnerships, and organisational change that sustain compassionate practice over time. Compassion by Design was developed through Denise Quesnel’s transdisciplinary PhD research at Simon Fraser University from 2017-2025, with pragmatic–realist co-production involving people with lived experience, community organizations, academic and health-system partners, and researchers + practitioners across health, social, spiritual, educational, and creative domains. We acknowledge the contributions and support from all involved in shaping Compassion by Design into its present-day iteration.

works.title: Clan Structures as Catalysts for Educational Leadership in Northern Uganda
works.abstract: Clan structures in Northern Uganda remain enduring systems of social organisation, shaping authority, identity, and community decision making across Acholi and Lango societies. Drawing on ethnographic studies, academic research, policy reports, and historical scholarship, this chapter examines how clan authority intersects with educational leadership in rural and post-conflict settings. It argues that clan institutions function as sources of legitimacy, informal accountability, custodians of land, and mediators of conflict, while also reproducing inequalities linked to patriarchy, lineage hierarchy, and generational exclusion. Using an integrated framework combining culturally responsive leadership, hybrid governance, and Indigenous knowledge systems, the chapter shows that educational leadership in Northern Uganda is relational, negotiated, and culturally embedded. At the same time, a critical perspective reveals both enabling and constraining aspects of clan authority, particularly regarding gender and equity. The chapter advances a model of hybrid governance, demonstrating how customary and statutory systems can coexist through safeguards, participatory mechanisms, and culturally responsive leadership, contributing to debates on decolonial educational reform in post-conflict contexts.

works.title: Towards a paradigm shift for decolonizing international development projects
works.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how power and knowledge operate in international development projects (IDPs) and how epistemic injustice is produced through their structural and relational configurations. It advances a decolonial perspective by integrating power-as-process with the colonial matrix of power (CMP). Design/methodology/approach The paper adopts a conceptual and critical reflexive approach, drawing on international business (IB), critical management studies and decolonial scholarship. It develops an analytical framework to examine how epistemic injustice is enacted across multiple levels of IDPs. Findings The paper shows that epistemic injustice is structurally embedded in IDPs and enacted across institutional, political, organisational and individual levels. Dominant power-as-resource perspectives obscure the relational nature of power and contribute to the marginalisation of local knowledge. By contrast, a power-as-process perspective reveals how epistemic hierarchies are reproduced and contested through everyday practices. Research limitations/implications The study calls for empirical research to examine how epistemic justice can be operationalised in diverse development contexts. Practical implications The paper highlights the need for decolonial reflexivity and for recognising local actors as legitimate epistemic agents to foster more inclusive practices. Social implications This perspective allows for developing strategies that address historical injustices and promote social equity, further contributing to global efforts to tackle grand challenges. Originality/value This paper contributes to IB and project management by repositioning IDPs as key sites of analysis and by linking power-as-process with the CMP to address epistemic injustice.

works.title: Beyond Authorship: Co-designing Inclusive Contribution Infrastructures
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: Who receives credit in science influences not only individual careers but also who participates, leads, and shapes the future of research. Yet traditional authorship practices often privilege a narrow range of intellectual contributions while overlooking the relational, organizational, and infrastructural labour essential to successful collaboration. As Big Team Social Science becomes increasingly common, there is a growing need to rethink contributor recognition to promote transparency, accountability, and justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion. This presentation reports on the initial outcomes of five Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training (FORRT) Team Credit hackathons, where researchers, educators, and open science practitioners collaboratively explored ways to improve contributorship practices. Participants identified limitations of the CRediT taxonomy, particularly its inability to recognize relational, organizational, mentoring, community-building, and other forms of infrastructural labour that underpin successful collaboration. Discussions also highlighted how existing contribution frameworks can reinforce hierarchies by privileging researchers with institutional prestige, seniority, or leadership roles while limiting recognition for early-career researchers, contributors from underrepresented regions, and those performing less visible work. We argue that contributorship infrastructures do more than document contributions—they shape collaboration, governance, accountability, and participation. By sharing these community-driven findings, we demonstrate how participatory approaches to developing contribution infrastructures can help move beyond authorship toward more transparent, inclusive, and responsible models of collaboration in BTSS, while identifying priorities for the future development of contributor recognition systems.

works.title: The Impact of Fintech on Islamic Finance and Capital Markets in Qatar Using Network Analysis
ADVANCING ETHICAL INNOVATION IN HUMAN-AI COLLABORATION: TRUST AND LEGITIMACY IN TECHNOLOGY-MEDIATED TEAMS MEDIATED TEAMS
works.venue: Scholar Works at UT Tyler (The University of Texas at Tyler)
works.abstract: Human Resource Development (HRD) confronts a central paradox in the digital age. The technologies designed to broaden access to learning and collaboration often reproduce the same social hierarchies that HRD seeks to challenge. Artificial intelligence (AI), digital collaboration platforms, and algorithmic management are widespread features of organizational life. Yet these systems do not generate inclusive outcomes for all workers. Women of Color (WoC), situated at the intersection of racialized, gendered, and technological structures, experience digital transformation as both possibility and constraint. They encounter opaque decision systems, diminished authority in virtual teams, and digitally-mediated microaggressions, while also developing new capacities for digital resilience and leadership. This dissertation addresses that paradox by advancing a multilevel theory of Socially Legitimized Trust in technology, built across three interconnected layers of trust formation: technical trust, social/relational trust, and relational trust. The inquiry asks how trust forms at the system level through consistent and transparent technical functioning, who gains meaningful access and capability within digital environments, and whose experiences are 11 marginalized or affirmed through daily interactions in technology-mediated teams. These layers create the developmental pathway through which organizations either legitimize or delegitimize trust. The manuscripts follow this scaffold. Chapter II examines technical trust by identifying the mechanisms that support reliable and explainable AI teammates. Chapter III advances social/relational trust by analyzing the capability, access, and institutional conditions that enable or constrain digital inclusion. Chapter IV further investigates social/relational trust by exploring how WoC experience, negotiate, and repair trust within digital team interactions. Chapter V synthesizes these insights to articulate a multilevel theory of Socially Legitimized Trust that positions trust not only as a psychological state, but as a developmental mechanism linking technical reliability, institutional legitimacy, and equitable participation. The contribution is both theoretical and practical. The study offers HRD a coherent framework for building trustworthy and socially legitimate AI systems and a roadmap for designing technology-mediated work that supports ethical performance and intersectional equity.

works.title: Inventory Scale - An Enterprise-Grade Multi-Branch Inventory Management Platform with AWS-Based CI/CD and Blue-Green Deployment Strategy
works.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
works.abstract: Modern retail and distribution enterprises face persistent challenges in coordinating real-time stock visibility, order lifecycle management, and inter-branch inventory transfers across geographically dispersed locations. Conventional inventory systems often suffer from monolithic architectures that hinder continuous delivery, limit horizontal scalability, and introduce prolonged downtime during deployments. This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of a cloud-native, multi-branch inventory management platform that addresses these limitations through an asynchronous RESTful API backend built with Fast API and SQL Alchemy on Python 3.12, a reactive single-page application frontend developed with React and TypeScript, and a PostgreSQL relational database managed via Alembic schema migrations. The proposed system incorporates a role-based access control model distinguishing ADMIN, MANAGER, and STAFF privileges, real-time inventory notifications delivered over WebSocket connections, automated low-stock alerting, and cross-branch stock-transfer workflows with full audit trail persistence. Deployment reliability is achieved through an AWS-integrated CI/CD pipeline comprising AWS Code Commit, Code Build, and Code Pipeline, culminating in a zero-downtime blue-green deployment strategy on AWS Elastic Beanstalk. Experimental results demonstrate sub-100ms median API latency under simulated concurrent loads, a deployment rollout time of under three minutes, and zero production downtime during environment switchovers. The system's modular architecture and serverless-adjacent hosting model provide a reproducible, cost-effective blueprint for scalable inventory management in cloudfirst organizations.

works.title: Acquiring Supplier Networks: Domestic Mergers for International Supply Chain Resilience
A Global Core Patient-Reported Outcome Set for Menopause: Development and Validation of the cPRO-MARiE Framework Across Thirteen Countries (MARIE WP2a)
works.abstract: Background: Menopause affects more than one billion individuals worldwide, yet outcome measurement in research remains narrow, inconsistent, and largely focused on vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms. Existing frameworks do not adequately capture the broader functional and psychosocial impacts reported by patients. We aimed to develop and validate a global Core Patient-Reported Outcome Set for Menopause (cPRO-MARiE) using prospective mixed-methods data from thirteen countries. Methods: We analysed quantitative data from 5,228 participants and qualitative interviews from 302 individuals across thirteen countries spanning diverse socio-cultural and health-system contexts. Validated instruments assessed symptom severity, psychological wellbeing, cognitive function, sleep disturbance, pain and somatic symptoms, and functional outcomes. Qualitative data underwent reflexive thematic analysis guided by the Delanerolle–Phiri framework. A COMET-aligned process integrating quantitative severity patterns, qualitative thematic convergence, cross-country reproducibility, psychometric validation and equity considerations was applied to derive the core outcome set. Findings: Seven domains were consistently identified across all settings: sleep disturbance; psychological wellbeing; cognitive function; pain and somatic symptoms; vasomotor symptoms; genitourinary and sexual health; and social, relational and occupational functioning. These domains demonstrated conceptual stability, cross-country reproducibility and psychometric coherence and were strongly linked to functional impact. The resulting cPRO-MARiE specifies mandatory Tier 1 patient-reported outcomes within each domain, with Tier 2 outcomes retained for context-specific and equity-focused research. Interpretation: cPRO-MARiE is the first empirically derived, globally validated core outcome set for menopause. By capturing symptom domains and functional impacts prioritised by patients across diverse settings, it provides a robust and clinically meaningful framework for outcome measurement in research, routine care, and health-system evaluation.

works.title: Tech for Social Impact: Measuring and scaling the outcomes of digital transformation in communities
works.venue: International Journal of Computing and Artificial Intelligence
works.abstract: Digital technologies are transforming how communities obtain their services, mobilize, and respond towards shocks. However, the social impacts of those changes, in particular, their role in community resiliency, are not yet well-measured and poorly scaled. This essay creates an interdisciplinary, context-based model and a convenient tool of measurement (the Social Resilience Impact Index, SRII) to evaluate digital transformation projects at the community scale. The study presents a multi-dimensional indicator architecture (access, inclusion, capabilities, relational outcomes, and adaptive capacity), measures based on a socio-technical systems theory, resilience scholarship, and offers methods to construct composite indexes, as well as methods of validation, participatory and longitudinal evaluation. The paper also looks into scaling pathways (horizontal replication, vertical policy integration, and systemic ecosystem transformation) and comes up with tangible tools, such as a scaling-readiness checklist and a participatory dashboard template, that can be used by practitioners and policymakers. Its contribution is conceptual (filling measurement gaps in the digital social impact literature) and practical (something with testable hypotheses, empirical designs, and policy recommendations). The framework considers equity, local co-production, and adaptive metrics, which change according to the changing context.

works.title: Reframing mentoring in initial teacher education: a Bourdieusian analysis of pre-service teachers’ experiences amidst policy reform in England
works.venue: Higher Education Skills and Work-based Learning
works.abstract: Purpose This study investigates mentoring practices within Initial Teacher Education in England during a period of significant policy reform. Informed by Bourdieu’s theory of capital and habitus, the research explores how pre-service teachers (PSTs) experience mentoring relationships and how these experiences shape their professional identity and development. Design/methodology/approach Through focus group interviews, the study examines the distribution of economic, cultural, social and symbolic capital within school placements and the power dynamics inherent in mentor-mentee relationships. Findings reveal considerable variability in the quality and inclusivity of mentoring, with unequal access to support, feedback and professional opportunities impacting PSTs’ confidence, sense of belonging and agency. Findings The study highlights how one-size-fits-all mentoring frameworks risk reproducing inequalities, particularly for PSTs from marginalised backgrounds. It calls for mentor training that moves beyond procedural compliance to incorporate equity-focused, individualised support strategies. Originality/value The paper concludes by advocating for mentoring models that explicitly address social justice, professional inclusivity and the complex relational dynamics that shape teacher development in a highly regulated education system.

works.title: Reading with all our senses: EDI picturebooks, inclusion and critical sensory multimodal literacy in early childhood
works.venue: European Early Childhood Education Research Journal
works.abstract: The article explores how equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) are woven into literacy practices in early childhood education and care (ECEC). Drawing on an interpretive, conceptual–empirical synthesis of four case studies, it examines how young children engage with EDI-oriented picturebooks in kindergarten settings and how these encounters shape participation and belonging. Critical sensory multimodal literacy provides the analytical frame, in dialogue with queer theory, childhood studies, and postcolonial perspectives. The analysis suggests that EDI literacy involves more than diversifying book selections. It is realised in the interactional conditions of shared reading: who is encouraged to speak, which languages and communicative modes are recognised, and how children's bodily and emotional engagements are supported. Across the cases, children demonstrate nuanced understandings of race, gender, rights, and participation when guided by sustained, dialogic mediation. At the same time, these spaces can reproduce discriminatory talk, gender policing, and racial hierarchies, highlighting the complexity of EDI work in ECEC. The article concludes by outlining implications for educators and policymakers, arguing that inclusion is enacted through the sensory, multimodal, and relational dynamics of shared reading.

works.title: Unapologetically Claiming the Significance of Joy in Higher Education
works.abstract: This article advances a Chicana Feminist, constructivist, and intersectional account of joy as a critical—yet persistently underrecognized—pathway for transforming U.S. higher education. We situate contemporary racialized faculty labor within colonial and neoliberal university regimes that privilege Eurocentric epistemologies, intensify surveillance and standardization, and reproduce racialized organizational logics that constrain legitimacy, belonging, and advancement for racialized scholars. Drawing on scholarship on racialized organizations, racialized emotions, and Chicana Feminist epistemologies—as well as our positionalities as Latinas in the academy—we argue that joy functions as both an epistemic refusal and a decolonial method. We theorize and propose the significance of joy as a mechanism of rejecting fragmented and disembodied rationality so as to reorient knowledge production toward humanistic, embodied, and community-rooted inquiry. It has, we argue, the potential to open pathways for institutional transformation. Accordingly, we theorize joy not as an apolitical affect or a private emotional state, but as an embodied and relational praxis. We conclude by proposing a reimagined academic culture that centers joy as a shared, structural commitment—one that affirms the dignity and agency of racialized faculty and enables universities to pursue their humanistic missions with rigor, equity, and care.

works.title: Graph Transformers and Vision Models for Intelligent Urban Mobility and Smart City Governance
works.abstract: lligent urban mobility and smart city governance. It situates advanced urban artificial intelligence within a broader methodological architecture that begins with uncertainty, measurement validity, and research design, then proceeds through statistical explanation, causal inference, predictive machine learning, scalable engineering, and applied governance. The argument throughout is that urban analytics becomes publicly valuable only when relational modeling, visual evidence, and large-scale computation are joined to defensible assumptions, explicit evaluation logic, and accountable institutional practice. Graph transformers are treated as powerful tools for representing networked dependencies across roads, transit systems, freight corridors, and governance jurisdictions, while vision models are positioned as mechanisms for converting complex street-level conditions into analyzable evidence about safety, accessibility, compliance, and service performance. Across chapters, the manuscript develops frameworks, protocols, scorecards, and governance artefacts that support research reproducibility, operational deployment, and policy interpretation. Particular attention is given to global applicability across South Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas, where infrastructure maturity, sensing capacity, and regulatory expectations vary significantly. The book is designed for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking an academically grounded yet implementation-aware foundation for trustworthy urban AI. Keywords graph transformers, vision models, urban mobility, smart city governance, causal inference, statistical modeling, trustworthy AI, multimodal transport analytics, computer vision, reproducibility, MLOps, urban data engineering, mobility equity, policy analytics, network intelligence, resilience governanc

works.title: Representations of Finland in contemporary Finnish popular music
works.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to study representations of Finland in contemporary Finnish popular music. Finland’s self-image and concerns are reflected in the popular music of the time and it is important to take stock and self-evaluate as Finland turns 100. Theoretically, this study relies on Cultural Studies in the sense that it views nations as being continuously reproduced through texts and other discursive actions. The data consists of 21 songs of different genres of popular music and released between 1999 and 2016. The method combines qualitative Relational Content Analysis and Critical Discourse Analysis. I identify and exemplify commonly occurring themes with extracts from the songs. The themes are then analysed with regard to their cultural, historical and economic context. I relate the recurring representations to the themes identified by Malmberg’s (1999) journalistic analysis of the content of pop song lyrics. I also comment on the intertextual connections between the Finland and Finnishness presented in the songs. My study shows that Finland is represented in Finnish popular music through the following themes: an ironic take on depression and alcohol, marginalisation, patriotic landscapes, glorified countryside, materialistic and meaningless lives of millennials, Finns and the world, gothic dystopia, political protest, and everything is okay.

works.title: Architecture Science: A Research Program for Architecture Formation and Transformation
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: AS-02 converts the bounded foundations of Architecture Science into an externally actionable research program for architecture formation and transformation. It specifies research workstreams, major research questions, empirical hypothesis families, minimum experimental units, comparative-study requirements, negative controls, simulation roles, dataset and benchmark architectures, counterexample programs, replication levels, maturity criteria, and explicit program-level strengthening, narrowing, absorption, restructuring, partial-rejection, and reconstruction/discontinuation dispositions. The paper is deliberately evidence-bounded. Architecture Science-specific empirical propositions remain at CS-2 — Research Hypothesis or lower. The release does not claim that Architecture Science is an established independent discipline, that universal architecture laws have been demonstrated, that generalized architecture reconstruction has been validated, that transferable identity criteria or the transformation taxonomy are established, that hostile-domain transfer or independent generativity has been demonstrated, or that architecture-level analysis has shown added value over the strongest appropriate native methods. The initial research portfolio prioritizes architecture-versus-aggregate discrimination through unstructured and randomized-relational negative controls, generalized reconstruction against strong native inverse methods, identity and transformation classification, hostile-domain transfer, comparative added-value testing, independent unassisted use, and benchmark/data specification. The program is designed so that negative results, counterexamples, predecessor-discipline capture, specialization collapse, native-method superiority, and replication failure can narrow, restructure, absorb, or reject Architecture Science propositions. This Zenodo record is designed as a single co-release object containing the AS-02 manuscript and its Supporting Constitutional & Scientific Record. The Supporting Record provides bounded traceability for claim states, literature and comparator burdens, falsification conditions, cross-domain limitations, adversarial objections, anti-immunization rules, evidence and replication state, maturity constraints, and research provenance. The Canonical Release Baseline Manifest records the Stage-0/Stage-1 lineage used for release preparation.

works.title: SQL for Data Analysis
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: SQL for Data Analysis is a visual and practical guide to using Structured Query Language for real-world analytical work. The book is designed for data analysts, data scientists, data engineers, BI developers, students, and professionals who want to transform raw data into reliable, decision-ready insights. The book develops SQL knowledge progressively, beginning with relational databases, tables, schemas, data types, keys, constraints, data integrity, and safe data-management practices. It then covers essential analytical techniques, including SELECT queries, filtering, sorting, aggregation, GROUP BY, HAVING, joins, set operations, subqueries, Common Table Expressions (CTEs), views, temporary tables, CASE expressions, data cleaning, date analysis, and window functions. In addition to SQL syntax, the book emphasizes analytical thinking: defining business questions, understanding data grain, validating results, reproducing KPIs, detecting data-quality problems, building reusable reports, and communicating findings to stakeholders. Realistic datasets, annotated SQL queries, diagrams, query outputs, common mistakes, interview questions, practical exercises, and portfolio-oriented projects are used throughout the book. The visual structure connects each business problem to its underlying schema, SQL logic, expected output, validation process, business interpretation, and practical application. The book therefore serves both as a structured learning resource and as a professional reference for solving analytical problems with SQL. Topics include: • Relational databases and database thinking • Data modeling, schemas, keys, and constraints • SQL data types and table creation • CRUD operations and transaction safety • Data importing, cleaning, and validation • Filtering, sorting, and date-based analysis • Aggregation, GROUP BY, and HAVING • Joins, set operations, and multi-table analysis • Functions, CASE expressions, and data transformation • Subqueries, CTEs, views, and temporary tables • Window functions and advanced analytics • KPI validation and data-quality checks • Reusable reporting and analytical workflows • SQL interview questions and problem-solving patterns • Query optimization and performance awareness • Real-world projects, dashboards, and portfolio development The central objective of this book is to help readers move beyond memorizing individual SQL commands and develop a repeatable method for turning business questions into accurate, validated, and actionable data insights.

works.title: Livelihood vulnerability of urban waste pickers in Indonesia: Insights for inclusive circular economy transitions
works.abstract: Rapid transitions toward circular economy and waste-to-energy (WtE) systems in Indonesia are reshaping urban waste economies, creating new risks for informal workers who rely on recyclables for their livelihoods. This study assesses the livelihood vulnerability of waste-picker households in Surakarta using the Livelihood Vulnerability Index (LVI), grounded in the IPCC’s exposure–sensitivity–adaptive capacity framework. Using cross-sectional data from 85 households complemented by qualitative interviews and participatory assessments, the analysis employs entropy-weighted indicators and regression models to identify the main determinants of vulnerability. Independent and seasonal waste pickers emerge as the most vulnerable, driven by high exposure, income dependence, and limited adaptive capacity. At the same time, aggregator-affiliated workers are relatively protected through informal institutional linkages—though such arrangements can reproduce dependency and unequal power relations. Education exerts only a modest effect, reflecting structural barriers that constrain mobility within informal labour markets. By extending the LVI to an urban context and embedding it within a just transition lens, the study advances theoretical understanding of vulnerability as a dynamic, relational process shaped by governance and technological change. Policy implications highlight the need for inclusive transition mechanisms—formal recognition, cooperative integration, and expanded social protection—to align environmental modernization with social equity and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 11 and SDG 12).

works.title: The Role of Art Activism in the Prefigurative Politics of Food System Transformation
works.venue: Palgrave studies in environmental transformation, transition and accountability
works.abstract: Using food system transformation as a lens, this chapter explores the common ground between art activism and prefigurative politics. Art activists that engage with food production embrace it as a tool for both aesthetic expression and political critique, by deconstructing the inequality of food systems and proposing alternative models of human interaction with the land that emphasise care, diversity, equity, justice, relationality, and sovereignty. By creating living examples of sustainable alternatives, fostering experimentation, challenging dominant systems, cultivating hope and agency, and integrating social and ecological concerns, prefigurative politics and art activism are therefore closely intertwined, influencing and complementing each other in the pursuit of social transformation. Artists can make grassroots projects visible and tangible, possible and probable, effective and meaningful, replicable and connected, local and open, while the creative process itself can be considered as a method of prefiguration, by making speculation easier to experience, to experiment with, and ultimately to enact, assembling matter into form as a capacitor of a prefigurative imaginary at work. Art activism has unique potential to engage with deep leverage points in sustainability transformations by focusing on fundamental myths, paradigms, and systems of meaning-making, and to link to structural and institutional change through chains of leverage.

works.title: Enunciative Practices and Dataset Curation: Toward a Decolonial Semiotics of AI-Generated Imagery
Mapping the Green Economy in India: A Multi-Sectoral Conceptual Framework Integrating Technology, Sustainability, and Inclusive Growth
works.venue: International Journal of Latest Technology in Engineering Management & Applied Science
works.abstract: The green economy has emerged as a transformative paradigm that reconciles environmental sustainability with economic growth and social equity. Despite India's ambitious commitments to net-zero emissions by 2070 and its rapidly expanding renewable energy sector, existing literature remains fragmented across individual industries, offering little integrative conceptual guidance. This article addresses that gap by developing a multi-sectoral conceptual framework that maps the architecture of India's green economy across twelve interrelated industry clusters. Drawing on conceptual synthesis and a systematic review of secondary literature, the study integrates Green Economy Theory, the Sustainable Development Framework, Circular Economy principles, Innovation Systems Theory, and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria into a unified analytical model. The framework identifies four functional layers—core productive sectors, enabling technology and finance sectors, circular and resource management systems, and social and inclusive drivers—and theorises the relational logic connecting them. The paper further discusses India-specific drivers, structural challenges, and policy implications. The findings contribute a replicable conceptual architecture applicable to large emerging economies navigating the sustainability transition, while providing a foundation for empirical validation and sector-specific research.

works.venue: Palgrave studies in race, inequality and social justice in education

works.title: Individualized Consideration as a Multilevel Justice Mechanism in Educational Leadership: A Structured Review of 2024–2026 Evidence
works.abstract: Educational institutions continue to reproduce inequities in access, recognition, participation, professional development, and decision-making despite increasingly explicit commitments to inclusion. This structured review examines individualized consideration, a dimension of transformational leadership, as a relational mechanism through which educational leaders may advance—or inadvertently weaken—social justice. Peer-reviewed literature published from January 2024 through July 20, 2026 was identified through transparent searches of Google Scholar-indexed records and publisher platforms. Twelve eligible reviews and empirical studies were analysed using thematic narrative synthesis. The synthesis generated a multilevel model comprising five interdependent mechanisms: recognition of differentiated needs and identities; relational trust and dialogic communication; equitable mentoring and capability development; participation and shared influence; and leader reflexivity linked to institutional accountability. Across the evidence base, transformational and supportive leadership were associated with teacher efficacy, collaboration, resilience, performance, job satisfaction, and reduced strain. However, recent social justice and inclusive leadership research demonstrates that interpersonal support is insufficient where institutional rules, informal networks, resource allocation, and governance arrangements continue to distribute opportunity unevenly. Individualized consideration contributes to social justice only when differentiated responses are need-sensitive, accessible through formal routes, transparent, reviewable, and converted into organizational learning and structural reform. The review advances leadership scholarship by distinguishing equitable responsiveness from selective benevolence and by specifying testable pathways through which individualized consideration may influence distribution-sensitive educational outcomes. Keywords: individualized consideration, social justice leadership, transformational leadership, educational leadership, equity, inclusion.

works.title: Reliable Machine Learning for Molecules and Materials: From Actionable Uncertainty to High-Throughput Data
works.abstract: Scientific machine learning (ML) has substantial potential to accelerate discovery across chemistry, materials science, and biomedicine. However, this potential remains largely unrealized in practice because the field has focused almost exclusively on model architecture while neglecting the surrounding engineering systems. These systems determine how data is stored and accessed at scale, how molecular structure is encoded so that task-relevant information is faithfully exposed to learners, and how prediction uncertainty is quantified in a manner that supports safe and actionable decision-making. This dissertation argues that reliability is an emergent property of the end-to-end scientific ML system, not the model alone, and that progress requires treating data infrastructure and uncertainty quantification as engineering problems on equal footing with model architecture. Three contributions are presented, organized around two engineering pillars: reliable, actionable uncertainty quantification and standardized high-throughput data access. First, distribution-specific uncertainty quantification is systematically studied for heterogeneous catalyst property prediction using k-fold ensembling, Monte Carlo dropout, and deep evidential regression applied to crystal graph convolutional neural networks on the Open Catalyst 2020 dataset. A five-metric evaluation portfolio spanning accuracy, sharpness, dispersion, calibration, and tightness reveals that no single method dominates before recalibration, while evidential regression emerges as the most accurate, disperse, and tight method after scalar recalibration. A hydrogen-adsorbate enumeration case study demonstrates that recalibration is essential for translating uncertainty estimates into reliable high-throughput screening decisions. Second, this trustworthy uncertainty is made actionable through test-time neighbor fusion, which adapts evidential neural networks to refine molecular property predictions at inference time, without retraining, by treating structurally and property-relevant training neighbors as noisy observations. Across 16 molecular datasets, the property-guided variant (PG-EviKal) reduces RMSE by a median of 19.4% relative to the evidential baseline on 14 of 16 datasets while improving calibration. Third, underpinning both, PubChemQC-PM6-GM is introduced, a curated derivative dataset comprising approximately 146 million molecules with PM6-level frontier orbital energies, canonicalized atomic coordinates, and InChI-derived permutation-consistent atom orderings. A high-throughput data access pipeline built on the WebDataset framework achieves sustained ingest rates averaging approximately 54,000 molecules per second and peaking near 65,000 on commodity HPC hardware, enabling scale-matched training for the first time on this corpus. A controlled benchmark further establishes where this data-layer canonicalization matters. It is decisive for generative coordinate modeling and for atom-row consistency, yet neutral for rigid-motion-invariant structure–property prediction, an honest delineation of when standardization is worthwhile. Taken together, these contributions constitute a blueprint for engineering reliable scientific ML systems. Calibrated uncertainty quantification, first measured and then acted upon, converts model predictions into actionable, trustworthy outputs, and standardized, high- throughput data access establishes the foundation for reproducible learning at scale. The dissertation concludes with a forward-looking roadmap that includes extending the test-time neighbor-fusion framework from molecules to adsorption energies on catalytic alloy surfaces, distribution-specific uncertainty quantification for molecular property models, and the coupling of uncertainty estimates with generative workflows.

works.title: Prevention Fit as Calibrated Processual Alignment
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: Prevention fit is often treated as an intuitive judgement that an intervention suits a recognised problem. Such judgements remain analytically weak when the crime phenomenon, the intervention, the prevention claim, and the relevant contextual conditions have not first been independently specified. This paper defines prevention fit as a claim-relative and calibrated relation between a frozen Crime-Process Profile and a frozen Prevention-Mechanism Profile under declared contextual conditions. Prevention fit is assessed through exactly eight dimensions: process-level fit; mechanism fit; target-bearer fit; temporal fit; scale fit; intensity fit; feasibility and reproducibility fit; and evaluative fit. The paper distinguishes potential and realised fit, direct fit and complementary relevance, local and system fit, fit and sufficiency, and fit and empirical effectiveness. It develops a multidimensional fit vector, non-compensatory threshold rules, necessary and supporting correspondence, the fit-claim authority declaration, bounded claim ceilings, short-form non-substitution, mandatory escalation, and high-judgement adjudication using stable, sensitive, and indeterminate classifications. This is Paper 3 of 6 and the central relational paper in the Prevention Fit Programme. Its output is a frozen claim-relative prevention-fit record. It does not diagnose the full structure of misalignment, construct portfolios, or establish effectiveness.

works.title: Enacting Multiple Childhoods: Micro‐Politics of Individualization and Collectivity in Norwegian Classrooms
works.abstract: Abstract Childhood in Norwegian schools is increasingly shaped by digitalization, framed in public discourse as both a risk and a necessity. Policy promotes digital competence as a basic skill, and digital technologies in classrooms form part of socio‐material practices that negotiate tensions between neoliberal individualization and Nordic welfare ideals of equity and collectivity. This study examines how learner positions in everyday classroom practices participate in the enactment of multiple childhoods, and how such enactments materialize broader societal struggles over autonomy, responsibility, and collectivity in Norwegian education. Using a relational ontological approach, we conducted a focused ethnography in a 5th‐grade Norwegian classroom. Data included two days of video‐recorded lessons and four semi‐structured focus group interviews with teachers and students. Analysis traced how assemblages of students, teachers, curriculum, digital technologies, and spatial arrangements participate in enacting learner positions and multiple childhoods. We found that learners were enacted in two dominant but intertwined ways: as autonomous individuals responsible for self‐regulated progress and as collaborative participants in collective practices. Digital technologies, work plans, and seating arrangements often scripted individualized learning, yet peer interactions and spatial configurations enabled moments of shared engagement. These enactments reflect contested ideals of childhood and education, revealing how neoliberal logics and welfare‐state values coexist and collide in everyday schooling. Childhoods in digitalized classrooms emerge as relational and fluid, enacted through socio‐material practices that negotiate competing norms of individualization and collectivity. Attending to the micro‐politics of the classroom challenges binary debates on technology and learning and illuminates how educational practices reproduce societal hierarchies of autonomy, accountability, and collectivity.

works.title: Volume II: Design of a Python Simulation Framework for Testing the Predictive Efficacy of the Quantum-Geometric Monetary Policy Model
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: This second volume presents the complete design of a modular Python simulation framework to empirically test the predictive efficacy of the quantum-geometric monetary policy model introduced in Volume I. The framework employs agent-based modelling (ABM) augmented with network science to operationalise the cardinal principles of discreteness, emergence from entanglement, induced wealth dynamics, holographic encoding, and relational structure. Simulations are parameterised for nine capital-starved Global South economies: Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, the Gambia, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Indonesia. The programme generates comparative forecasts against classical aggregate monetary models (inflation targeting, broad money growth rules) across scenarios of income shocks, remittance volatility, and policy interventions (quantized micro-credit, holographic feedback loops). Predictive efficacy is evaluated via metrics including out-of-sample inclusion growth accuracy, wealth distribution resilience (entanglement-entropy analogs), and network connectivity emergence. The design supports reproducibility, extensibility, and integration with real-world datasets (GSMA, World Bank Findex, central bank transaction logs). This volume serves as both a technical blueprint and pedagogical resource for computational economists, central banks, and development practitioners. Also available on Academia.edu: https://www.academia.edu/attachments/133009149/download_file?s=portfolio

works.title: Evolving culturally competent veterinary care: a community-based partnership with the Santee Nation
works.abstract: Access to veterinary care remains a profound equity issue across the United States, particularly in Indigenous communities where animals hold vital cultural and spiritual significance. This case study examines a longitudinal, community-based partnership between Kansas State University's College of Veterinary Medicine and the Santee Nation, offering a model of culturally competent veterinary outreach grounded in the principles of One Health, cultural humility, and decolonizing education. Over 7 years, the program has evolved from a small animal service-learning initiative into a multifaceted, community-guided collaboration that integrates student learning, tribal leadership, and interprofessional engagement. Key programmatic components include structured cultural preparation, provision of mobile veterinary care-including equine services prioritized by the community-relationship-centered practices, and ongoing feedback loops. Students engage in implicit bias assessments, autoethnographic reflection, and historical learning about land-grant institutions and tribal sovereignty. Clinical interactions emphasize relational accountability, transparency, and the centering of Indigenous knowledge. Community members, in turn, act as co-educators and co-designers, reshaping what competent veterinary care looks like within a tribal context. Findings illustrate how veterinary outreach, when framed through reciprocal partnership rather than charity, can build trust, improve access, and foster professional identity formation rooted in equity. This model aligns with national calls for culturally responsive care and offers a replicable framework for institutions seeking to reimagine their role in tribal health and veterinary education. The program advances the scholarship of engagement by demonstrating how veterinary institutions can co-create just and sustainable systems of care alongside historically excluded communities.

works.title: UNVEILING GENDER BIAS THROUGH CRITICAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS: REPRESENTATION IN ENGLISH FOR NUSANTARA MERDEKA CURRICULUM TEXTBOOK
works.venue: GLOBAL Education Language and Humanity Journal
works.abstract: This study critically examines gender representation in the English for Nusantara Grade VII textbook, the flagship English Language Teaching (ELT) material for Indonesia’s Merdeka Curriculum. Using a qualitative design and Fairclough’s three-dimensional Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA), twelve multimodal extracts from Chapter 1 were analyzed to uncover how male and female identities are portrayed through text and visuals. The findings reveal a clear imbalance in both frequency and agency: male characters appear nearly three times more often than female characters and are consistently depicted as active protagonists with hobbies and social interactions, while female figures are limited to passive or relational roles, such as sisters or unnamed peers. Despite the curriculum’s stated goal of inclusivity and gender equity, the textbook subtly reproduces patriarchal ideologies and hegemonic masculinity through muted female voices and restricted social positioning. These results echo global patterns of gender bias in ELT materials and highlight a critical gap between policy aspirations and classroom realities. The study concludes by offering practical implications for teachers, textbook authors, and policymakers, emphasizing the need for gender-sensitive material development and critical literacy approaches in ELT classrooms

works.title: Topological Data Analysis for Climate Risk, Urban Resilience, and Smart-City Sustainability
works.abstract: Abstract: This manuscript develops a doctoral-level framework for applying topological data analysis to climate risk, urban resilience, and smart-city sustainability. It argues that cities should be modeled as high-dimensional relational systems in which heat, flooding, infrastructure fragility, service access, demographic vulnerability, and adaptive capacity interact across spatial and temporal scales. Persistent homology, Mapper graphs, geospatial data engineering, causal inference, and trustworthy machine learning are combined to produce analytical tools that can identify durable exposure clusters, fragile infrastructure pathways, and policy-relevant discontinuities in complex urban evidence. The book progresses from foundational theory and uncertainty-aware research design to causal evaluation, predictive modeling, reproducible MLOps, and sectoral governance applications. It emphasizes global applicability for South Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas, while cautioning that models must be recalibrated to local data quality, institutional capacity, and equity conditions. The practical outputs include research protocols, causal diagrams, topological feature libraries, resilience scorecards, deployment checklists, governance artifacts, and future research roadmaps. Written for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers, the manuscript offers a coherent reference architecture for transforming complex climate and smart-city data into auditable, participatory, and policy-actionable intelligence. Keywords topological data analysis, persistent homology, climate risk, urban resilience, smart-city sustainability, urban heat islands, flood risk, geospatial analytics, environmetrics, causal inference, machine learning, graph intelligence, MLOps, climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction, equity analytics, digital twins, urban governance, remote sensing, sensor data, policy evaluation, infrastructure resilience, sustainability indicators

works.title: Barriers Within: Gender Disparities in Public Sector Academia in Pakistan
Using Wikidata’s Ontology in Practice: A Neuro-Symbolic, Community-Centred Workflow for Integrating and Reusing Humanities Datasets
works.abstract: This article presents an ontology-centric workflow for adding, curating, analysing, and reusing humanities datasets with Wikidata. Anchored in a digital-humanities project that confronts data silos and gendered inequities—especially related to the Francoist repression and censorship—it combines a neuro-symbolic AI stack with a co-creative, community-driven methodology. We first operationalize “the ontology of Wikidata,” clarifying how classes, properties, and constraints behave in practice; how reified statements, qualifiers, and references guide modelling choices; and how Entity Schemas encode formal, testable expectations. We then detail an ontology-first pipeline aligning local humanities databases to Wikidata via reconciliation (OpenRefine), controlled property usage (constraints and ShEx), and scaled editing (QuickStatements, Mix’n’match). The paper contributes reusable modelling patterns for persons, works, events, censorship decisions, and provenance, adaptable across humanities domains. Using SPARQL in the Wikidata Query Service (WDQS), we demonstrate discovery and analysis alongside metrics for coverage, data quality, and equity—focusing on the visibility of women and other gender identities—while situating results within prior scholarship on gender gaps and the ways Wikidata mitigates and mirrors societal bias. Finally, we show how an ontology-backed knowledge graph (KG) underpins retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to reduce large-language-model hallucination and bias, detailing how the HerStory NeSyAI project embeds Wikidata structures within an explainable neuro-symbolic architecture. Our contribution is case study and template: a step-by-step, reproducible method for humanities teams to use Wikidata’s ontology not merely to retrieve data but to publish, govern, and reuse datasets with verifiable, community-aligned semantics.

works.title: Five Misconceptions About Interview Modes or: How to Improve Our Thinking About Face-to-Face Versus Remote Interviewing
works.abstract: New technology brings new methodological opportunities. While long limited to face-to-face interviewing, today’s interview researchers can choose from a plethora of options, including email, instant messaging, telephone, and video interviews. Consequently, the issue of interview modes and their relative strengths and weaknesses has received increased attention. In this article, we take stock of existing writings on interview modes in qualitative interview research. Drawing on key insights from more general theorizing about face-to-face and remote interaction, we identify and challenge five key assumptions in writings about interview modes: (1) that physical copresence ensures more and better data; (2) that interview modes have determinate effects on interaction; (3) that remote interviewing should seek to replicate face-to-face interviewing; (4) that interviews modes should be held constant within each study; and (5) that face-to-face interviewing is unmediated. We counter each assumption with a series of more productive methodological principles and advance instead a view we call interview mode pluralism, which offers a more nuanced and relational understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different interview modes. The article thus helps increase the methodological literacy of those conducting and evaluating qualitative interview research, enhancing the likelihood that researchers select those tools best suited for their tasks, and reducing the chance that evaluators dismiss research based on their methodological prejudice.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: A Sociological Study
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education systems has generated profound structural, relational and ideological consequences that remain underexplored from a sociological standpoint. While much of the existing discourse gravitates toward the technical dimensions of AI its algorithmic efficiencies, adaptive learning capabilities, and automation potentials relatively little attention has been paid to how these technologies reproduce, challenge, or reconfigure the social hierarchies and institutional arrangements that define contemporary universities. Drawing on sociological frameworks including Bourdieusian field theory, critical pedagogy and social stratification theory this paper examines the ways in which AI technologies are transforming teaching, learning, and institutional governance in higher education. The study employs a qualitative meta-analysis methodology, synthesizing findings from peer-reviewed literature published between 2014 and 2024 across disciplinary fields including educational technology, sociology of education, and science and technology studies. Three central objectives guide the inquiry: first, to critically examine the sociological dimensions of AI adoption in universities; second, to assess how AI-mediated learning environments interact with pre- existing social inequalities; and third, to explore the implications of AI-driven governance on academic culture and faculty autonomy. Findings indicate that while AI holds transformative potential for democratizing access and personalizing pedagogy, it simultaneously risks reinforcing algorithmic bias, deepening the digital divide, and displacing the humanistic core of higher education. The paper concludes by advocating for a critically informed, equity- centered framework for AI integration one that places social justice at the center of technological design and institutional policy. Sociology of education, Digital equity,

works.title: A Hybrid Agentic RAG Architecture for Legal Decision Support: Integrating Utility-Based Reasoning with LLM-Orchestrated Retrieval
works.venue: International Conference on Trends in Quantum Computing and Emerging Business Technologies (TQCEBT)
works.abstract: The present paper explains a hybrid variety of an Agentic Retrieval- Augmented Generation (RAG) model, the model that results in goal-oriented and utility-oriented agentic reasoning in legal guidance. It purports to seek to study family law cases with large-scale language models (e.g. GPT-4, Claude 3, Gemini 1.5, DeepSeek-R1) on the basis of modular retrieval systems (vector stores, graph databases, relational DBs) and post-hoc bias and factuality. This agent is dynamically deciding what to do which can be retrieval, critique, reformulation etc but this choice depends on a parametrized utility that considers the accuracy, neutrality and latency of responding. The qualitative research is simulated legal consultation to which we apply simulated grounded Maharashtra based case law and thematic biases. The results show that the verifiability of the responses (through citation) and hallucinations are greater and lesser respectively in the two sexes and also that there exists no difference in how law is framed. This schema is biased to multistage reasoning and self-correction which has become the default of agentic AI and constitutional alignment. The journal is institutionalizing a field-specific reproducible architecture that entails the introduction of ideals of equity throughout AI decision pipelines into sensitive areas such as justice systems.

works.title: The Socioeconomic Disease in Canada: A Métis Nation Case Study on How Colonial Governance Models and Patriarchal Leadership Cultures Produced the Symptoms of Housing, Homelessness, and Mental Health Wounds that Festered into National Emergencies
works.abstract: Building on author’s Wounded Leadership Theory, this thesis examines ethical public sector leadership within hierarchical Canadian governance systems through a critical, genealogical, and multidisciplinary lens. It analyzes how colonial governance structures, patriarchal leadership cultures, identity authorizing practices, and administrative power imbalances reproduce systemic harm that disproportionately affects Indigenous peoples, youth, and neurodivergent individuals, especially women within these groups. As the document notes, “Harm emerges not only through overt policy decisions but also through imposed colonial governance structures,” revealing how invisible harms persist beneath narratives of reconciliation, diversity, equity, and inclusion. A case study of Métis Nation–Saskatchewan (2014–2026) demonstrates how federal intervention, administrative restructuring, and political fragmentation destabilized Indigenous governance, weakened community autonomy, and intensified housing, homelessness, and mental health vulnerabilities. These outcomes reflect long standing governance architectures rather than isolated failures. Collectively, the thesis concludes by identifying leadership knowledge gaps and proposing relational, non-hierarchical, and community-centered governance practices capable of disrupting systemic cycles of harm and strengthening ethical leadership and positive role modeling within Canada’s public and nonprofit sectors.

works.title: Performing the Way to Positive and Developmental Relationships in Outside-of-School Programs
works.abstract: Relationships come first is a widely recognized pillar of outside-of-school time (OST) youth development programs and often held up as an important way to distinguish OST from in-school settings.
