For many, this relational focus positions OST programs as spaces for advancing social justice and equity for marginalized youth. Bulanda and McCrea (2013) highlighted constructive relatedness—“feeling connected to others, to caring for and being cared for by those others”—as an important feature of OST programs that strengthens youth’s wherewithal to move forward despite challenges of poverty, community violence, educational disadvantage, social exclusion, and racial discrimination (p. 103). While programs and people can be celebrated for the support they bring to youth, researchers have also pointed out that they can function as sites of containment that reify deficit perspectives and racist discourses (Baldridge, 2019). Guiding Black youth in urban settings is often contradictory; youth workers and supportive adults are often tasked with simultaneously introducing youth to mainstream standards and striving to encourage personal, cultural, and creative expression. This speaks to the importance of attending to the “how” of relationship building: employing processes that can maximize support and the sharing of social capital in ways that reorganize rather than reproduce social inequalities.

works.title: Mapeo global del conocimiento científico sobre las Enfermedades Tropicales Desatendidas de la piel (Skin-NTDs): Un análisis bibliométrico
works.abstract: Here is a professional English description of your protocol, structured as a project summary or abstract. The language is tailored for an academic or scientific audience: Project Summary Title: Global mapping of scientific knowledge on Skin Neglected Tropical Diseases (Skin-NTDs): A bibliometric analysis Description:This project proposes a comprehensive, analytical, and relational bibliometric study to map the global scientific landscape of Skin Neglected Tropical Diseases (Skin-NTDs). By employing a rigorous and reproducible methodology, the study will extract literature spanning a 20-year period from the Scopus database. The retrieval process utilizes a highly sensitive and specific search strategy that combines controlled vocabulary (MeSH/Emtree) with free-text keywords covering general Skin-NTD concepts, specific pathologies, and programmatic contexts.Following standardized deduplication and manual screening processes to ensure clinical relevance, the data will undergo advanced bibliometric and network analyses. Utilizing tools such as R (bibliometrix), VOSviewer, Gephi, and SciVal, the study will evaluate temporal publication trends, institutional and country-level productivity, and funding landscapes. Furthermore, topological evaluation of scientific networks and text-mining techniques will be applied to trace the conceptual evolution of the field, with a strong emphasis on assessing geographical equity and identifying asymmetries in global research collaboration.

works.title: Decolonizing Engineering Education: A Cross-Institutional Approach Using Participatory Action Learning and Action Research (PALAR)
works.abstract: PURPOSE OR GOALThis paper presents findings from the Building a Legacy in Engineering (BLE) project, a crossinstitutional collaboration between a Predominantly White Institution (PWI) and a Historically Black College and University (HBCU) aimed at transforming engineering education through a decolonizing lens.We define decolonizing as the disruption of dominant Eurocentric and technocratic paradigms and the elevation of community-rooted knowledge, historical accountability, and relational approaches to both pedagogy and design.PROPOSED METHODOLOGY Grounded in Participatory Action Learning and Action Research (PALAR), BLE engages students, faculty, and community members as co-researchers in iterative cycles of inquiry, design, reflection, and implementation of sustainable infrastructure solutions in historically marginalized communities.Drawing on qualitative data collected in Year 2, including structured student reflections, semi-structured interviews, field observations, and community partner feedback, this study identifies key outcomes such as the development of critical consciousness, enhanced cross-cultural collaboration, and the emergence of anti-racist, community-centered engineering practices.Students transitioned from deficit-based assumptions to asset-based engagement, and from top-down design thinking to collaborative problem-solving rooted in community knowledge and priorities.The program also catalyzed institutional shifts in how faculty engaged with engineering ethics, co-leadership, and interdisciplinary learning.One notable example includes student teams redesigning irrigation systems based on feedback from local elders, demonstrating adaptive design and cultural humility. CONCLUSIONAlthough BLE is grounded in the U.S. South, its flexible model, emphasizing long-term relationships, place-based learning, and critical reflection, offers a framework for adaptation in national and international contexts seeking to transform engineering education through justicecentered practices.Potential for replication lies in its integration of culturally responsive pedagogy with rigorous design instruction, though such implementation requires strong institutional commitment, faculty training, and sustainable community partnerships.Limitations of the study include the challenges of coordinating across academic calendars and institutions, uneven student participation, and the resource demands of maintaining community engagement beyond the academic year.Nonetheless, BLE offers a replicable and transformative approach to reimagining engineering education as a relational, reflective, and justice-oriented practice that centers equity, historical context, and community voice.

works.title: Development of an AI-Assisted Mobile Point of Sales and E-Commerce System with Real-Time Inventory Synchronization
works.abstract: Indonesian micro, small, and medium enterprises (UMKMs) face significant operational bottlenecks due to their reliance on manual and fragmented sales and inventory management systems. To address these challenges, this research designs, develops, and evaluates PasPOS, an integrated mobile Point of Sales (POS) and E-Commerce system tailored for Indonesian micro-retailers, utilizing Toko Mpok Nani as an implementation case study. Developed chronologically using the Agile Scrum framework across eight sprints, the platform implements a decoupled microservices architecture. This infrastructure consists of a centralized Laravel 12 backend API and Flutter-based Admin and Member applications, all synchronized through an 11-table relational database. Furthermore, the Admin App integrates an edge computer vision-based barcode scanning feature to accelerate cashier transactions using standard smartphone cameras. System validation via User Acceptance Testing (UAT) using a structured Likert-scale questionnaire yielded an overall average score of 4.44 out of 5.00 for the Admin App and 4.43 for the Member App, classifying both as "Very Good". These empirical findings demonstrate that PasPOS successfully eliminates cross-channel stock inconsistencies while offering a replicable architectural blueprint for broader UMKM digitalization initiatives.

works.title: Entity Conditioned Opportunity Intelligence through an Evolving Knowledge Manifold
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: This preprint introduces an entity-conditioned framework for opportunity intelligence: identifying and evaluating actionable opportunities in relation to the capabilities, resources, objectives and constraints of a particular individual, organisation or consortium. The framework connects heterogeneous observations, behavioural interpretations, temporal relationships and feasible action paths within an evolving knowledge manifold. This manifold is operationally defined as a provenance-linked relational state with semantic representations and domain-specific views. Opportunities may originate from explicit announcements or emerge through the interpretation of observed changes and their plausible consequences. The central contribution is a structured decision record connecting evidence, interpretation, entity capability, feasibility, uncertainty and subsequent outcomes. A versioned decision policy supports reproducible recommendations from frozen inputs, while feedback informs later revisions and model development. The theoretical foundations draw on KAI Spaces, Midpoint Projection Theory (MPT), its variational-autoencoder application, Symmetry-Aware Sequential Flow and the Midpoint-Compatibility Principle (SASF/MCP), Entity Portfolio Optimization (EPO), and the Sampokilis System foundations. Their proposed roles concern knowledge representation, projection, sequential validation and evolving entity memory. Version 0.1 presents the conceptual framework, mathematical notation, reference architecture, operating cycle and evaluation protocol. It establishes a basis for implementation and comparative testing; empirical performance and practical effectiveness remain research questions.

works.title: An ethics of care and Ubuntu reimagination in academic development
works.venue: South African Journal of Higher Education
works.abstract: Academic induction programmes are often designed to professionalise new academics within the normative expectations of the university. Yet, in many Global South contexts, these programmes remain tethered to Eurocentric frameworks that privilege compliance, productivity, and individual achievement over relational and ethical forms of becoming. This article explores how an Ethics of Care and Ubuntu reimagination can offer decolonial alternatives for academic development praxis, re-centring human connection, reciprocity, and collective flourishing as foundational to professional learning. Decolonisation, understood as more than a metaphor, is a political, ethical, and epistemic project aimed at dismantling the colonial matrix of power that continues to define whose knowledge counts and whose humanity is recognised (Ndlovu-Gatsheni 2015). Coloniality persists as a system of domination that positions the Global North as the arbiter of knowledge and truth, while rendering African epistemologies peripheral. Within higher education, these hierarchies manifest in institutional cultures, pedagogical practices, and induction programmes that implicitly reproduce colonial logics of being and knowing. A decolonial turn in academic development therefore demands a shift from technocratic notions of induction to relational, dialogical, and care-centred engagement where professional learning becomes a shared, humanising process rather than an administrative requirement. This article draws on my reflective praxis as a facilitator on an academic induction course at a South African university. A critical incident forms the anchor: a participant’s remark, “Noooo… I don’t want to see you. Every time I see you, my stress levels go up because I know I owe you something!”, expressed in reference to the e-portfolio submission required for course completion. Using Rolfe, Freshwater and Jasper’s (2001) reflective framework ‒ “What?” “So what?” “Now what?” ‒ this moment becomes a lens through which to interrogate how institutionalised expectations of compliance can erode trust, induce emotional fatigue, and reproduce hierarchical power relations within academic induction. The article’s theoretical framing draws on Ethics of Care (Tronto 1993; Noddings 2012) and Ubuntu philosophy (Waghid and Smeyers 2012; Hlatshwayo, Shawa and Nxumalo 2020) to propose an alternative approach to academic development: one that recognises interdependence, compassion, and mutual accountability as essential dimensions of scholarly growth. Ethics of Care foregrounds attentiveness and responsiveness to others’ needs, while Ubuntu articulates a relational ontology encapsulated in the phrase “I am because we are.” When interwoven, these frameworks invite a re-humanisation of academic induction, transforming it into a praxis of care, humility, and shared responsibility. By positioning this reflection within the broader decolonial discourse, the article argues that Ethics of Care and Ubuntu provide generative pathways to disrupt deficit narratives of ‘development’ and to re-imagine induction as a collaborative and affirming process. The study offers a situated, practice-based contribution to ongoing conversations about decolonising higher education in the Global South. It envisions academic induction as a site of ethical relation and collective becoming where care is not peripheral, but central to the pursuit of decolonial futures.

works.title: Delivering Walkable Neighbourhoods? A Critical Examination of Five New Urban Extensions/Emerging New Towns in England
works.abstract: Walkability has reemerged as a central interest within planning, public health, and built environment research, yet evidence demonstrates that new urban extensions or emerging New Towns across England continue to reproduce conditions of car dependency and limited active travel options. This paper examines the structural, spatial, and sociocultural factors shaping walkability through an in-depth analysis of five residential case studies. It draws on spatial analysis and assessment of resident behaviour using sociodemographic data. Findings indicate significant disparities in walkability outcomes, with some developments characterised by fragmented layouts, weak public transport integration, and environments that make walking impractical or undesirable. The paper argues that walkability must be understood as a multidimensional, relational property of place, rather than a static design feature. The current dominant planning practices continue to prioritise vehicular access and associated infrastructure, undermining national goals for decarbonisation, health equity, and sustainable mobility. Thus, this study identifies the spatial, governance, and policy conditions necessary to deliver genuinely walkable neighbourhoods and highlights the systemic barriers that continue to constrain progress. The findings offer critical insights for planners, policymakers, and developers seeking to create environments that support healthier, more equitable, and less car dependent futures.

works.title: Methodological Sovereignty in Community-driven Language Research:
works.venue: International Journal of Indigenous Language Media and Discourse
works.abstract: This paper advances a framework of methodological sovereignty in community-driven language research by detailing a Decolonial mixed-methods study on Tonga language revitalization in Zimbabwe. Despite constitutional recognition of Tonga among Zimbabwe’s sixteen official languages, its marginalization persists in education, governance, and public domains. Conventional research approaches often reproduce these exclusions through extractivist methods and Eurocentric paradigms. In response, this study employs a convergent parallel mixed-methods design grounded in Indigenous epistemologies particularly Ubuntu and Sankofa and aligned with principles of relational accountability and epistemic justice. The methodology integrates qualitative tools such as focus groups and auto-ethnographic journaling with quantitative surveys, ensuring both cultural responsiveness and analytical rigor. Data collection and analysis were carried out in four Tonga-speaking districts using participatory strategies to foreground community voices and counter hierarchies in knowledge production. The study demonstrates how embedding Indigenous worldviews in all phases of the research process supports linguistic revitalization, disrupts epistemic dominance, and reclaims agency in how Indigenous languages are studied and sustained. Through dialogic co-production, contextualized sampling, and ethical reciprocity, the research illustrates how methodological sovereignty is essential to achieving genuine sociolinguistic equity in postcolonial contexts.

works.title: Making Wellington (Earthqueake) Resilient: Creating Building Inventory Dataset for Seismic Risk Assessment and Management
works.abstract: Wellington City Council earthquake resilience strategy began addressing the city’s building stock as early as 1970’s. Major events that shook our country during this decade (in particular the Kaikoura earthquake) highlighted information gaps in the form of scarce of detailed and up-to-date information about the existing stock of buildings in a high earthquake risk city like Wellington. Our project has assembled an inventory of mid- to high-rise buildings in the Central Business District to facilitate multidisciplinary research within Flagship 3’s Coordinated Project. Crossing over the engineering and social sciences, the ongoing projects supported by the building inventory are: (1) providing best scientific knowledge about the expected seismic performance of concrete buildings; (2) assessing the impact of multiple building failures including the downstream consequences of associated cordoning; (3) developing a path for seismic retrofitting that includes prioritization of retrofits and (4) informing the design of a regulatory structure that can facilitate the reduction of risk associated with earthquake vulnerable buildings. The inventory dataset is hosted online in a MapViewer where researchers can visualise, filter and download spatial and attribute data of either the entire inventory, or buildings that satisfy specific criteria. Researchers can access the data in GIS conventional formats (as a file relational geodatabase or a Web Feature Service) or non-GIS file formats (e.g. csv files). Further developments include the addition of geophysical information (e.g. hazard information) and socioeconomic data (e.g. Land values). Ultimately, the inventory is intended to be a core input for seismic risk assessment and management, as well as a methodology that can be replicated in the greater Wellington and other parts of NZ.

works.title: Transcending boundaries: enacting social justice through practices of freedom in health and physical education curricula
works.venue: Curriculum Studies in Health and Physical Education
works.abstract: In this paper, we explore how the enactment of Health and Physical Education (HPE) curricula can transcend national boundaries. Based on data from Aotearoa New Zealand, Norway, Spain and Sweden, the paper examines how teachers’ enactment of HPE curricula reflects, reproduces and resists social justice goals. Utilizing Foucault’s concept of ‘practices of freedom’, we explore how teachers navigate power-laden curricular and institutional discourses to foster inclusion, equity and social cohesion. Using data generated from curriculum documents, school-based field visits, classroom observations and interviews with HPE teachers, we draw on thematic analysis to identify how teachers adapt content, build relational pedagogical spaces and exercise critical judgement to resist exclusionary norms. Our analysis emphasizes the role of teachers as agents who negotiate curricular frameworks in ways that respond to students’ lived realities and transcend traditional disciplinary and national boundaries. By conceptualising HPE curricula as both regulatory structures and sites of possibility, the paper argues for an approach to HPE that recognises teachers’ capacity for ethical reflection, local adaptation and transformation. Such an approach is central to disrupting inequitable power relations and enabling both students and educators to contribute to a more just and inclusive world.

works.title: Whose nature, whose city? : environmental justice and the governance of urban biodiversity in cities around the world
works.abstract: Urban biodiversity planning is increasingly positioned as a vehicle for both ecological conservation and social equity, yet whether it delivers on either commitment remains poorly understood. This dissertation evaluates whether and how 98 Local Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (LBSAPs) from 26 countries engage with environmental justice, asking how plans frame values, who is included in decision-making, how disparities in benefits and burdens are addressed, and whether the three dimensions operate interdependently in practice. Drawing on Schlosberg's tripartite framework, it employs mixed methods combining AI-enabled data extraction, manual coding, and qualitative discourse analysis. Across all three dimensions, urban biodiversity planning more often reproduces than challenges existing inequalities. Instrumental and regulatory values dominate recognition, while justice- oriented relational values appear in fewer than one in five plans, and the dissertation introduces false recognition to explain how symbolic inclusion of alternative worldviews neutralises their transformative potential. Procedurally, 72% of plans employ participatory mechanisms but only 18% redistribute decision-making authority; marginalised groups record the lowest inclusion scores of any actor type and zero authorship credit across the corpus. Distributively, half are silent on how benefits and burdens are shared, and marginalised communities, when recognised as harmed, rarely receive comparable programmatic response. Across the corpus, justice engagement on any dimension occurs only under three conditions: integration of non-hegemonic discourses such as relational values, social equity, and Indigenous knowledge; targeted inclusion of marginalised populations; and presence of justice-mandating legal frameworks. The actor-specificity thesis further establishes that it is not participation in general but the inclusion of particular actors that predicts just outcomes. These findings produce the structural Catch-22 of marginalised group inclusion: the actors whose inclusion most powerfully transforms distributive and cross-dimensional planning outcomes are those most systematically excluded from governance. Together, the results yield a fragmented justice thesis that empirically qualifies Schlosberg's mutual constitution hypothesis. Plans from Mexico City, Medellín, Fort Collins, Melbourne, and three South African cities show transformation is achievable through structural commitment: legal mandates binding distributional analysis, institutional designs placing affected populations in governance authority, and frameworks treating inequality as a produced condition requiring remedy.

works.title: How Female Leaders Perceive the Influence of Gender on Career Advancement in the Indonesian Construction Industry
works.abstract: Women who work in leadership positions in the construction industry in Indonesia face gender related challenges. Grounded in Acker’s theory of gendered organizations, this qualitative hermeneutic phenomenological study examined how women leaders experience and interpret gender-related workplace challenges. I collected data through semistructured interviews with nine women leaders in the Greater Jakarta Metropolitan Area and analyzed the data using the modified van Kaam method. Manual coding produced seven emergent themes. Key findings showed that gender inequality is embedded in organizational culture, policies, and everyday practices rather than occurring as isolated incidents. Women leaders reported heightened scrutiny, the need to continually demonstrate competence, and structural expectations intersecting with socioreligious norms. Gendered organizational processes reproduce barriers through routine workplace interactions and cultural symbols. Women leaders navigate these barriers using strategies such as continuous learning, relational leadership, and family and collegial support. This dissertation contributes to positive social change by providing empirical insights that inform organizational policies, including flexible work arrangements, transparent promotion processes, and leadership development programs tailored to women’s experiences, thereby promoting gender equity, increasing women’s participation in construction, and supporting broader workforce inclusion.

works.title: Beyond neurodiversity and diagnostic capital: a biopsychosocial manifesto and ‘grammar’ for inclusion
works.abstract: This paper argues that inclusive education requires a coherent conceptual and operational framework capable of aligning identification, provision, and outcomes across systems. Drawing on analysis of contemporary SEND theory and policy, it identifies persistent fragmentation arising from reliance on diagnostic categorisation and inconsistent definitions of inclusion. While the neurodiversity movement has contributed significantly to reframing difference as a natural and valuable aspect of human variation, it does not, in isolation, provide a sufficiently specified framework for system design, resource allocation, or equitable access to support.In response, the paper advances the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and its underpinning biopsychosocial model as a ‘grammar for inclusion’. The ICF offers a standardised and relational framework for describing functioning, capturing the dynamic interaction between biological, psychological, and environmental factors. It enables a shift from categorical identification towards contextually grounded functioning profiles, supporting more equitable, needs-led systems.The paper further examines the socio-political dynamics of the English SEND system, highlighting how diagnostic capital and quasi-market forces reproduce inequalities. It concludes by proposing that an ICF-informed approach can integrate neurodiversity-affirmative perspectives within a broader, system-oriented framework, operationalised by the ICF, to enhance coherence, equity, and participation.

works.title: The Significance of Emmanuel Mounier's Communitarian Personalism in Promoting Just and Equal Education
works.venue: Proceeding International Conference on Religion Science and Education
works.abstract: This article explores the relevance of Emmanuel Mounier’s communitarian personalism for advancing a vision of education that is both just and equal. Mounier’s personalism places the human person at the center of social and cultural life, affirming dignity, freedom, and responsibility while rejecting individualism and collectivism alike. By situating personal development within the context of community, Mounier emphasizes that education must nurture not only intellectual abilities but also the relational and ethical dimensions of personhood. Through qualitative method, this paper underlines Mounier’s ideas by criticizing how such a modern framework of education is shaped primarily by competition, technocracy, and utilitarian values, which often reproduce social inequalities. Instead, communitarian personalism calls for pedagogical approaches that cultivate solidarity, participation, and mutual recognition, ensuring that education serves the flourishing of all rather than the privileges of a few. This article argues that Mounier’s vision provides valuable resources for addressing contemporary debates on inclusion, equity, and justice in education. By integrating personal dignity with communal responsibility, his thought fosters a model of education that promotes human development in its fullness, encourages democratic engagement, and resists structures of exclusion. In conclusion, Mounier’s communitarian personalism offers a philosophical foundation for reimagining education as a transformative practice of justice, equality, and shared human growth.

works.title: Network and Topological Models of Social Polarization, Collective Behaviour and Information Diffusion
works.abstract: Abstract Social polarization, collective action and information diffusion arise through interacting social ties, institutional settings and changing media environments. This monograph develops a network and topological research framework using the directly relevant and transferable methods in the supplied source corpus. Ten themes connect multiplex graph measurement, multidimensional polarization, heterogeneous coordination, exposure pathways, causal influence, persistent topology, graph learning, simulation, equity and longitudinal evidence. Five chapters move from concepts and ethics through causal identification and topological modelling to data systems, validation and governance applications. The framework distinguishes observed sharing from persuasion, network homophily from social influence, and stable topological signatures from social meaning. It proposes time-stamped event schemas, graph filtrations, pre-registered counterfactuals, simulated challenge sets and disclosure-aware audit packets. Such artifacts allow researchers to compare explanations without asserting that a predictive association is a causal mechanism. Suggested evaluations address structural missingness, spillovers, platform changes and unequal opportunities to participate or seek remedy. Public discourse, mobilization and content interventions supply illustrative research settings, not empirical findings. The book closes with an evidence program that combines privacy-preserving longitudinal data, independent replication and institutional review. Its practical contribution is a falsifiable way to study how relational structure and information flows shape group boundaries and collective behaviour under uncertainty. Keywords social polarization, collective behaviour, information diffusion, social networks, topological data analysis, persistent homology, graph neural networks, homophily, social influence, multiplex graphs, causal inference, interference, cascades, coordination thresholds, conversational entropy, agent-based simulation, misinformation, temporal networks, algorithmic governance, privacy, equity

works.title: Integrated data platform: Backbone of cancer research office.
works.abstract: e13653 Background: The management of research portfolio and workflow is crucial for every research entity in a cancer center. It ensures efficiency and quality of study startup (SSU), subject accrual, regulatory compliance, quality assurance, etc. A Clinical Trial Management System (CTMS) would help with research administration. However, for research with resource constraints, it can be difficult and expensive. In this poster, we present a budget-friendly, in-house integrated data platform to improve data integrity, centralize data storage, and automate performance tracking that has been applied in our center. Methods: We built the platform using Microsoft (MS) SQL Server, MS Access and Tableau through the following steps. First, we discussed with team leaders to determine data elements required for research portfolio tracking. Second, we designed and built a relational database in MS SQL server, including entity tables and reference tables. Third, we cleaned up historical data that was previously stored in various Excel files and transferred them into the newly built database. Fourth, based on fields in entity tables, we created different forms in MS Access as data entry interface. Lastly, we developed SQL queries to extract data, and visualized results in Tableau dashboard suite to address distinct needs. Results: Database and data entry interface were built in 2021. First set of dashboards were launched in 2022, including accruals and studies overview, active studies list, SSU timeline, iRIS directory and Protocol Evaluation and Monitoring Committee (PEMC) Review. In the following years, we kept adding new functions to the existing tools. In 2024, Quality Assurance (QA) tracker was implemented. At the end of 2025, this platform had managed 324 studies (69% therapeutic), 4097 accruals (9% therapeutic), 378 QA records (29% reviews have findings), 56 PEMC meetings (167 protocols reviewed), and 150 Institutional Review Board (IRB) continuing reviews. This platform received positive feedback across teams and leadership regarding improved efficiency and quality of research administration. Conclusions: For a research office with limited resources and lacking CTMS, this platform is a cost-effective, sustainable and replicable solution. Due to flexibility of the system, different modules can be added on as our demands expand. Centralized data storage and performance tracking improves transparency and provides a more comprehensive insight into research portfolio.

works.title: Exploring practitioner values in Inclusive Science Communication: An Australian perspective
works.abstract: Even as the values of inclusive practice gain recognition in some contexts, they are contested and unevenly supported in others. Inclusive Science Communication (ISC) has developed in response to calls for increased diversity, equity, reflexivity and ethicality in research and practice. In Australia, the centring of First Nations knowledge systems in government policy affirms the worth of Indigenous perspectives but risks assimilationism or tokenism. We explored the values of Australia-based ISC practitioners to reflect on existing and emerging traditions of science communication and to consider how science communicators can engage with new traditions of authentic inclusion. Values influence motivations, methodologies and outcomes, yet the values of ISC practitioners are under-studied, particularly in Australia. We conducted a thematic review of values embedded in the work of Australian-based ISC practitioners via 15 peer-reviewed articles. Asking how inclusion is positioned in Australian science communication traditions, we inductively analysed statements of motivation, practice and positionality to identify practitioner values and their potential to shape traditions. ISC is not uniformly defined, yet its practitioners share common values: cultural sensitivity, collaboration, environmental concern, empowerment, advocacy, reflexivity, equity and the centring of marginalized, Indigenous and non-Western knowledge systems. Those values perform multiple functions, reflecting a reconfiguration of existing traditions, challenging epistemic and structural assumptions or inspiring emergent traditions grounded in relationality, social justice, care and reciprocity. ISC disrupts traditional boundaries. Our findings suggest that Australian ISC practitioners are co-creating new traditions across disciplinary boundaries and institutional constraints, embodying pluralism, justice and cultural transformation. Their values invite critical reflection on which traditions we inherit, reproduce or reimagine, and how science communication traditions can become more authentically inclusive through intentional, values-driven practice, rather than uncontested ‘tradition’.

works.title: Colonial Financial Architecture: Hierarchy, Drain, and Discipline
works.abstract: The systemic dynamics of three features of the international financial architecture, that of the international currency hierarchy, sovereign indebtedness, and economic austerity, are examined through the conceptual frameworks of international financial subordination, decoloniality, and feminist political economy. Dependency and world-systems theorists assert that unequal exchange, facilitated through an unequal currency hierarchy marked by the U.S. dollar at the apex, enacts flows of value and resources from the South, or periphery, to the North, or core. When nations borrow in a currency they do not control, they are exposed to devastating exchange rate shocks, resulting in economic crises and intensification of indebtedness generating gendered inequalities, expressed through the erosion of livelihoods, well-being, and public provisioning. Contemporary sovereign debt crises enact a continuity of “drain of wealth” from colonial past, reflecting the largesse of finance and international loan and bond contracts in classical theories of imperialism. In the absence of a statutory regime for restructurings, market access to international money is contingent on austerity-financed repayment, which reproduces and maintains the unequal hierarchy of humanity, as gendered and racialized bodies become involuntarily shock absorbers. A triangular lens employing international financial subordination, decoloniality, and feminist political economy situates gendered and racial inequalities as the primary mechanism through which economic shocks are carried out. The overarching intention that intertwines the structural with the intersectional and decolonial is to enact a process of transformation toward reparative equity that is historical, intersectional, relational, and material. Dismantling and repairing the unequal hierarchy of humanity requires the active countering of dehumanization as a precondition of decoloniality. In parallel, policy space and corrections such as regulation and social provisioning alone are necessary and yet inadequate to systemically overhaul the monetary and debt architecture. It is, to a great extent, the unequal relations between nations, institutions, and actors that must be balanced as a precondition for emancipation through equity, agency, and dignity.

works.title: Reframing Educational Leadership as Experiential Ecology: An Integrated Model for Artificial Intelligence, Embodiment, Well-Being, and Inclusion
works.venue: Advances in Social Science, Education and Humanities Research/Advances in social science, education and humanities research
works.abstract: Contemporary educational leadership is increasingly mobilized to address digital transformation, student and teacher well-being, and inclusive education.Yet, these domains are predominantly operationalized as parallel and additive agendas, resulting in fragmented interventions that fail to reconfigure learning environments at a systemic level.A critical gap emerges in leadership studies: the absence of integrative models capable of accounting for the coconstitutive nature of cognitive, technological, and socio-emotional processes in contemporary education.Grounded in Embodied Cognition (Varela et al., 1991;Shapiro, 2019) and ecological approaches to learning, the paper proposes the Embodied Ecological Leadership Model (EELM).The model conceptualizes leadership as a designoriented function that operates through the orchestration of four interdependent dimensions: embodied experience, artificial intelligence as adaptive mediation, systemic well-being, and ecological inclusion.Within this model, artificial intelligence is reframed as a relational and adaptive infrastructure shaping learning processes (Holmes et al., 2022), while well-being is treated as a structural indicator of system sustainability rather than an ancillary outcome (OECD, 2021).Inclusion is conceptualized as an emergent property of responsive and accessible environments, in alignment with European policy priorities on equity and participation (European Commission, 2020, 2022).By shifting leadership from managerial coordination to ecological design, the EELM offers a theoretically grounded and operationalizable model for reconfiguring educational systems.The paper contributes to international debates by advancing a systemic perspective that enables replicable analysis and intervention across micro, meso, and macro levels of educational practice.

works.title: Modeling Data Resource Allocation Networks: Valuation and Policy in the Digital Economy
Introduction to Open Intervention “Relating to Role Models” Assignment
works.venue: Journal of Open Educational Resources in Higher Education
works.abstract: This article introduces a novel assignment designed to foster inclusive, student-centered learning in a first-year general chemistry course at a Canadian university. Developed as part of a United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Fellowship, the assignment invites students to explore and present chemistry role models with whom they personally identify, culminating in the creation of artifacts that highlight diverse contributors to the field. Grounded in Goal 4: Ensuring Inclusive and Equitable Quality Education, the assignment integrates principles of universal design for learning, relational pedagogy, and open educational practices. Students engage in reflective and creative processes that support professional identity development, disciplinary belonging, and agency. The assignment is scaffolded across three parts, guiding students to investigate role models and share their findings, engage with their peers’ artifacts, and present themselves as future contributors to the discipline. Rubrics are intentionally designed to be inclusive and non-judgmental, aiming to reduce some forms of instructor bias. This work contributes to the growing body of literature on representation in STEM education and offers a replicable model for embedding equity-focused pedagogy into gateway science courses. By centering student voice and choice, the assignment aims to transform the chemistry classroom into a space of belonging, relevance, and possibility. The intervention may be particularly transferable to introductory STEM disciplines, such as biology, physics, engineering, and health sciences, where professional identity development and belonging are similarly important. Future dissemination will support adaptation across disciplines and institutions.

works.title: The CORE Framework: A Process-Oriented Approach to Boosting Survey Response Rates in Grant-Funded Program Evaluation
works.abstract: Low survey response rates remain a persistent challenge in evaluation, undermining validity, credibility, and the usefulness of findings for stakeholders and funders. The problem is especially acute in grant-funded projects, where evaluators inherit, adapt, or design survey instruments under varying degrees of control, navigate access to respondents through program staff, and work under tight grant-driven timelines. While decades of methodological research suggest strategies to boost participation, few frameworks integrate these insights into a process tailored to evaluators' constraints. This paper introduces the CORE framework—Cultivate Engagement, Optimize Instruments, Remind Strategically, and Evaluate & Feedback—as a sequenced, practice-oriented conceptual model grounded in existing survey methodology literature. CORE is not presented as an empirically validated intervention; rather, it organizes evidence-based strategies into a replicable process and illustrates its application through composite examples drawn from grant-funded evaluation practice. The paper situates CORE within existing approaches, such as Dillman's Tailored Design Method and the meta-analytic strategy literature, to highlight its unique role as an evaluator-centered, cyclical process crafted to overcome the challenges of grant-funded projects. CORE combines technical rigor with relational strategies such as trust-building and transparent communication. The author concludes with implications for evaluators and funders, highlighting CORE's potential to enhance methodological credibility, equity, and grant competitiveness.

works.title: Intersectionality Reinforcing Gender Inequality Across Higher Education Institutions in Contemporary Societies
works.abstract: This study explores how intersectional dynamics reinforce gender inequality within higher education institutions in contemporary societies. Using a qualitative research design, data were collected through purposive sampling of published research documents, including peer-reviewed articles, ethnographies, and theoretical analyses, and analyzed through thematic analysis. Eight major themes were identified: 1) the intersection of gender, class, and socioeconomic background; 2) cultural norms, ethnicity, and gendered educational experiences; 3) institutional structures and gendered power relations; 4) curriculum, knowledge production, and epistemic marginalization; 5) classroom interaction and pedagogical practices; 6) academic networks, mentorship, and professional opportunities; 7) intersectional barriers in leadership and decision-making; and 8) policy implications and pathways toward inclusive higher education. Findings reveal that women, particularly those from marginalized social groups, experience compounded barriers that affect access to resources, academic participation, leadership opportunities, and career advancement. Intersectionality, coupled with Bourdieuian concepts of cultural and social capital, elucidates how structural, cultural, and relational mechanisms reproduce gendered hierarchies within universities. The study emphasizes the need for policies and practices that address overlapping forms of disadvantage, promote inclusive pedagogy, diversify curricula, and provide equitable mentorship and networking opportunities. By applying an intersectional lens, this research highlights pathways for achieving greater equity, representation, and empowerment for women in higher education.

works.title: Trauma-Informed and Healing-Centered Public Service
works.abstract: In this chapter, we uplift the need to recognize emotional labor and neurobiologically challenging nature of public service and diversity, equity, inclusion, and liberatory justice (DEILJ) work. We affirm consistent calls to cultivate an ethics of care, relationality, and interdependence in public service contexts to serve both the public and the public servants. Building on existing interdisciplinary literature we extend a call for trauma-informed and healing centered (TIHC) public service organizations. This chapter seeks to offer an expansive and nuanced understanding of trauma. We offer an understanding of trauma from both neurobiological perspectives as well as socio-psychological perspectives. Collectively, these perspectives inform us about historical, inter-generational, persistent institutional, and personal trauma of oppression, and hence, the need to center repair and healing as a core approach for LPS. We discuss the need to foster TIHC approaches in public service to avoid harm and re-traumatization for populations we serve and to engage in the challenging and necessary work of repair to address historical and systemic oppression. We envision TIHC public service to acknowledge and address historical, inter-generational, and persistent institutional trauma from oppression. TIHC public service framework seeks to examine the ways trauma from oppression is reproduced in public service contexts. It seeks to cultivate supportive and life-affirming organizational systems and cultures where individuals and collectives can engage in the process of repairing and healing from trauma of oppression.

works.title: Indigenous Environmental Justice in Global Seascapes: Sovereignty, Knowledge, and Multispecies Relations
The Ethno-Sexual Hyphen: Communicating Gay-Mizrahi Subjectivity in Israeli Workplaces
works.abstract: This study examines how gay-Mizrahi men in Israel navigate the communicative processes through which workplace subjectivities are constructed, negotiated, and legitimized. Mizrahiness refers to a Jewish ethno-cultural position associated with Middle Eastern and North African ancestry, historically shaped by unequal relations with Ashkenazi hegemony and intersecting class, geographic, cultural, and gendered hierarchies. Based on semi-structured interviews with self-identified gay-Mizrahi men across diverse occupational sectors, this study examines how sexuality, ethnicity and professionalism are read together in everyday organizational interactions. The findings reveal three strategic mechanisms: identity calibration, hyphenated subjectivity, and compensatory professionalism. Identity calibration refers to the ongoing tuning of identity visibility, timing, intensity, and communication. Hyphenated subjectivity captures the relational process through which gayness and Mizrahiness are not simply combined but continuously negotiated in relation to social expectations and organizational norms. Compensatory professionalism describes intensified investment in excellence, credentials and self-control to counter anticipated devaluation. These mechanisms show that organizational belonging is not a static outcome of diversity or inclusion but an advanced communicative achievement. Thus, this study contributes to workplace communication and Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) scholarship by illustrating how marked workers achieve professional legibility. We argue that DEI practice must move beyond visible categories of diversity towards affective and communicative dimensions through which inequality is reproduced.

works.title: Editorial Introduction: Gradient Voices in Education (Volume II)
works.abstract: This editorial introduction to the second volume of Gradient Voices in Education returns to the concept of gradient voices as a way of understanding identities, experiences, and expressions shaped through movement, contradiction, relationality, and uneven recognition. Rather than treating marginalized voices as simply additive to existing conversations about diversity, this volume positions them as central to understanding how education organizes, naturalizes, and sustains inequality. Situated within a political moment marked by intensified attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion, antiracist teaching, queer and trans life, and historical truth-telling, the special issue examines how educational institutions continue to operate through racialized, gendered, colonial, and linguistic regimes of recognition. The stories in this volume refuse to separate educational critique from lived complexity. Across critical autoethnography, collaborative autoethnography, oral history, case study, testimonio, phenomenological reflection, poetry, playlist, and Indigenous storywork, contributors show how students, educators, and scholars navigate harm, build relation, reclaim voice, and imagine otherwise within and against institutional constraints. As editors, we argue that these manuscripts are not supplemental conversations about diversity, but indispensable analyses of education itself. Together, they expose the fault lines of schooling and affirm that gradient voices are central to understanding what education has been, what it continues to reproduce, and what it might yet become.

works.title: Internationalization of Graduate Education from the Periphery
works.abstract: Internationalization has become both an organizing ideal and an evaluative metric in graduate education, yet its dominant forms remain shaped by competition, rankings, and asymmetries between academic centers and peripheries. This essay offers a conceptual and reflective contribution to that debate from an underrepresented standpoint: a graduate nursing program located in the Brazilian Amazon. Drawing on critical reflection and a purposive reading of the higher education and nursing literature, it examines how internationalization is conceptualized, how it has unfolded in Brazil, and what structural barriers and pathways shape its trajectory in regions distant from the country’s academic core. We argue that prevailing models, organized around mobility and productivity, tend to reproduce center–periphery hierarchies and to frame internationalization as an external imperative rather than a situated, relational, and ethical process. The Brazilian case shows uneven advancement, with opportunities concentrated in consolidated institutions of the South and Southeast and persistent barriers of funding instability, linguistic inequity, bureaucracy, and fragile institutional policies. Read from the Amazon, these dynamics point toward a situated internationalization grounded in equity, reciprocity, South–South cooperation, internationalization at home, and the social mission of public universities. The contribution lies in showing how a peripheral, discipline-specific standpoint can sharpen critical internationalization debates and widen the range of voices that shape the field of higher education.

works.title: GTIM A Route-Scoped Evidence Operations and Discovery Governance Framework
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: GTIM A Route-Scoped Evidence Operations andDiscovery Governance Framework Technical Report and Worked Case Study Case study: KRAS G12D-mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomaMRTX1133-induced autophagy-glutathione escape Bouchelit Mohammed El AminGTIM - Independent Open-Science ProjectVersion 1.0 | 10 July 2026Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21288009 Publication classificationMethodology paper / technical report / preprint. This document is not peer reviewed and does not claim a new biological discovery for the KRAS route. The original scientific contribution is the GTIM evidence-operations, novelty-governance, and research-portfolio framework. Abstract AI-assisted biomedical research can generate hypotheses faster than experimental programs can evaluate them. The resulting bottleneck is not idea production but evidence operations: defining the exact claim, locating route-matched data, separating direct functional evidence from proxies, preserving negative results, assessing novelty without confusing search failure with novelty, and selecting the next experiment under constrained resources. This report presents GTIM (Genome/Target Intake Machine), a deterministic, route-scoped framework for pre-wet-lab hypothesis readiness and discovery governance. GTIM combines exact-route intake, evidence-class controls, a GO / NO-GO / DATA-NEEDED decision triad, provenance receipts, a Novelty Gate, a Diamond Knowledge Network, a White Space Engine, a replication acceptance contract, and a Hypothesis Economy for portfolio prioritization. The framework is demonstrated using a known preclinical route in KRAS G12D-mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: MRTX1133-induced autophagy-dependent glutathione survival adaptation. GTIM correctly treats this route as a known control mine with bounded functional support from one published source, authorizes a replication scout, and blocks Green, Gold, or public Diamond promotion until independent route-exact evidence is receipted. The case illustrates the framework’s intended contribution: not to replace experimental science or rebrand published findings as discoveries, but to reduce avoidable wet-lab expenditure, prevent evidence leakage across contexts, and convert open evidentiary gaps into explicit acquisition targets. Keywords hypothesis triage; evidence governance; pre-wet-lab decision support; provenance; replication; novelty assessment; KRAS G12D; pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma; autophagy; glutathione; research portfolio optimization Plain-language summary GTIM is designed to answer four questions before a laboratory commits resources: What exactly is being claimed? What evidence directly matches that claim? Is the claim already known, partially explored, or genuinely untested? What is the smallest next evidence object that would most improve the decision? The system does not certify therapies. It produces bounded research decisions and preserves the reasons for those decisions. Table of contents 1. 1. Problem definition 2. 2. Design principles 3. 3. GTIM system architecture 4. 4. Evidence model and decision semantics 5. 5. Novelty, discovery, and white-space governance 6. 6. Diamond Knowledge Network 7. 7. Hypothesis Economy and portfolio optimization 8. 8. Worked case study: KRAS G12D PDAC 9. 9. Secondary calibration cases 10. 10. Reproducibility and software release model 11. 11. Limitations and threat model 12. 12. Discussion and conclusion 13. References 14. Appendices 1. Problem definition The practical research problem addressed by GTIM is the growth of hypotheses without a corresponding growth in disciplined evidence processing. A plausible biological narrative is not equivalent to an executable claim. A literature citation is not equivalent to a route-exact evidence object. A high novelty score is not equivalent to truth, and a strong known result is not a new discovery. These distinctions are often collapsed in informal AI-assisted workflows. 1.1 The operational bottleneck · Claims are frequently underspecified with respect to disease, biomarker, intervention, comparator, endpoint, model, and time window. · Expression or survival associations are incorrectly promoted to protein activity, functional dependency, treatment response, or clinical actionability. · Evidence from neighbouring routes is transferred across diseases, drugs, endpoints, or mechanisms without an explicit transfer gate. · Negative and null results are lost, causing repeated expenditure on already failed designs. · Novelty is inferred from incomplete searching rather than recorded as a confidence-bounded search result. · Research portfolios are ranked by narrative excitement rather than information gain, execution risk, cost, and opportunity cost. 1.2 Intended use GTIM is a pre-wet-lab evidence operations desk. It is intended to support research prioritization, evidence acquisition, replication planning, and auditability. It is not a clinical decision-support system, diagnostic tool, medical device, or substitute for laboratory validation. Core positioningGTIM does not prove a therapy and does not perform the experiment. It identifies where not to drill, where one more sample could be decisive, and what receipt is required before a claim may be promoted. 2. Design principles Principle Operational meaning Route exactness Every executable claim is scoped to a disease/model, biomarker or state, intervention, comparator, endpoint, and evidence modality. Evidence-class integrity Direct perturbation, longitudinal observation, cross-sectional proxy, prediction, and missing data are not interchangeable. No silent fallback A missing functional tile cannot be replaced by TCGA expression, survival association, or a neighbouring disease. Append-only provenance New evidence appends to prior receipts; it does not overwrite historical results. Negative-route preservation Executed negative or no-support routes remain locked and visible unless stronger route-exact evidence justifies formal review. Novelty-evidence separation A route can be strong but known, or novel but unsupported. Steering is not promotion Memory, white-space, and portfolio outputs can change priorities but cannot change scientific decisions or evidence tiers. Human governance Material promotion remains subject to explicit review even after an automated gate is passed. 3. GTIM system architecture The framework is organized as a sequence of bounded transformations. The generic core contains evidence and governance semantics. Disease-specific heads define vocabularies, route schemas, and admissible evidence objects without modifying the core decision logic. Problem Space -> Prior Knowledge Graph -> Coverage Map / White Space Engine -> Mechanism Composer -> Candidate Route Generator -> Novelty & Discovery Gate -> Route-Exact Evidence Engine -> Scientific Decision -> Diamond Knowledge Network -> Hypothesis Economy / Portfolio Optimizer 3.1 Major components Component Function Hard boundary Exact Route Intake Normalizes the claim and required evidence schema. Unclassified or empty claims do not receive scientific verdicts. Evidence Engine Searches, builds, and executes route-matched tiles. Proxy evidence cannot close a functional-response gate. Novelty Gate Classifies known, partially explored, and untested exact routes. Not a patent novelty opinion or proof of worldwide first disclosure. White Space Engine Maps sparse mechanistic edges and evidence debt. Steering-only; no evidence transfer. Diamond Knowledge Network Stores evidence atoms, failures, control mines, and frozen route results. Memory cannot change decisions or tiers. Replication Contract Defines the minimum independent evidence package. Passing produces review eligibility, not automatic promotion. Hypothesis Economy Ranks investments by information gain, cost, risk, impact radius, and overlap. No auto-funding or scientific promotion. 4. Evidence model and decision semantics 4.1 Evidence classes Evidence class Example Permitted inference DIRECT_MATCHED_PERTURBATION Drug or genetic perturbation with matched comparator and functional endpoint. Route-scoped functional response. DIRECT_CONTEXT_MISMATCHED_PERTURBATION Same mechanism, different disease, allele, drug, or endpoint. Analogy or transfer hypothesis only. LONGITUDINAL_OBSERVATIONAL Before/after or time-series measurements without matched causal intervention. State transition or temporal association. NATURAL_EXPERIMENT Quasi-experimental biological or clinical contrast. Bounded causal support where assumptions hold. CROSS_SECTIONAL_PROXY Expression, survival, or cohort association. Association only. PREDICTED_IN_SILICO Model-generated interaction or dependency. Candidate prioritization only. NO_RELEVANT_DATA No executable object found. DATA-NEEDED, not negative evidence. 4.2 Decision triad Decision Meaning Typical next action GO Required route-scoped gate is closed at the specified evidence level. Advance within the explicit scope and governance limits. GO_BOUNDED Evidence supports a limited action, such as replication or further acquisition, but promotion is blocked. Execute the named next evidence object. NO-GO Route-exact negative evidence or a decisive failure rule is present. Stop, redesign, or preserve as a negative calibration route. DATA-NEEDED The claim is coherent but no admissible executable evidence object closes the gate. Acquire or construct the specified tile. NOT-EXECUTED Input

works.title: SEDOS — A FAIR dataset for technologically-detailed modeling of Germany´s energy transition
works.abstract: State-of-the-art modeling approaches for energy system planning reflect the interdependencies across demand sectors such as buildings, transport, and industry, the supply sector, and the transformation sector. However, modeling continues to be hindered by the fragmentation of data sources, inconsistent formats, and the extensive effort required for data acquisition and harmonization. To address these challenges, this paper presents the open dataset SEDOS, tailored for technologically-detailed modeling of the German energy system. SEDOS offers a comprehensive, structured, and up-to-date collection of data across all energy sectors, supporting cross-sectoral analyses. The dataset is based on a relational model structure that ensures consistency between technologies, commodities, and sectors, and is accessible through an interactive online dashboard. SEDOS includes scenario data up to the year 2070, hourly time series, and a detailed representation of more than 2000 technologies. On the demand side, the dataset records the development of energy services and products for the supply of which a broad technology portfolio is characterized in terms of its technical and economic parameters. While focused on Germany, the dataset incorporates a European perspective for the power sector to enable cross-border market assessments. A key novelty of SEDOS is its alignment with the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable), supporting transparency, reusability, and integration into diverse modeling frameworks, which lowers the entry barrier for modelers and facilitates consistent and reproducible energy system analyses. This paper outlines the methodology behind the dataset, presents its structure and contents, and describes instructions for use in long-term energy system planning and sector integration studies.

works.title: Reframing inclusive governance through equitable leadership in child sexual violence policy: Evidence from Surakarta City, Indonesia
works.abstract: This article investigates inclusive governance through equitable leadership in local child sexual violence policy in Surakarta City, Indonesia. This study argues that without equitable leadership, namely relational, distributed, and pro-vulnerable group leadership, inclusive governance tends to be procedural and ineffective. This study differs from previous studies that emphasize the importance of participation, collaboration, and accountability, but have not yet placed leadership as a key element. This research uses a multi-method design, combining a systematic literature review (SLR) and Focus Group Discussion (FGD) with 10 local stakeholders in Surakarta City. Surakarta City was selected purposively because it is quite progressive in addressing children's rights issues, having received an award as a child-friendly city at the national level, yet an increase in cases of sexual violence still occurs. The findings were synthesized into eight principles of equitable leadership: justice-oriented leadership, equitable institutional reform, disrupting the status quo, moral courage, community-oriented leadership, gender-diverse strategic leadership, recognition of indigenous leadership, and equity-minded leadership training. The proposed leadership model provides a conceptual framework for interpreting leadership dynamics within local child protection governance. This study can positioning leadership as a key enabling dimension in the functioning of local child protection governance in regions to be free from sexual violence, and contributes to the achievement of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 16.2, which aims to end abuse, exploitation, trafficking, and all forms of violence against children through a local approach that can be replicated in the context of developing countries. • Introduces equitable leadership as a missing dimension in inclusive governance. • Employs a multi-method design combining SLR and FGD with multi-stakeholders. • Identifies six dimensions of just leadership bridging theory and practice in policy. • Demonstrates how leadership drives institutional coherence in child protection systems. • Offers a replicable framework contributing to SDG 16.2 through local policy reform.

works.title: Understanding the resilience of children living on an American Indian reservation: A mixed methods participatory study
works.abstract: AIM: To explore the resilience of children, six to thirteen years old, living on a Northern Plains American Indian Reservation using a situation specific nursing theory. BACKGROUND: American Indian and Alaska Native children experience mental health inequities compared to their white peers, including substance use, suicide, depression, and anxiety. Resilience is a strength of children that can be leveraged to improve their mental health. DESIGN: A parallel convergent mixed methods design. METHODS: A community advisory board culturally adapted resilience instruments. During two weeks in summer 2022, forty-seven children/caregiver dyads completed surveys about the child's resilience. Descriptive statistics gave the scores of each child's personal, relational, and total resilience. A subset of 20 children participated in a semi-structured interview. RESULTS: Children scored high on overall resilience, and higher on the relational subscale than the personal subscale. Caregiver survey scores were not significantly correlated with their child's scores and were higher than the children's scores. Qualitative coding revealed six themes of resilience. Integration of data showed a concordance and expansion of the quantitative data across themes. CONCLUSION: The children reported high resilience supported by a strong ecosystem of relationships. Resilience, as explained through children's voices, corroborated with findings from the surveys. IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING: Findings will help nurses across sectors of primary, secondary, and tertiary care create resilience-enhancing interventions and prevent mental health crises in this community. IMPACT STATEMENT: This findings from this study will inform local mental health interventions on the Reservation. The study provides a reproducible design to adapt to other Indigenous communities. PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: A community advisory board was a partner in every stage of the study. Children and caregivers participated in data collection. CONTRIBUTION TO THE WIDER CLINICAL COMMUNITY: This research provides knowledge that will further social justice efforts within nursing to promote health equity across diverse populations.
