works.title: Visibility Bias in Learning Analytics: Coded Dashboard Indicator Corpus
works.abstract: Purpose. This project investigates whether learning-analytics dashboards systematically misrepresent educational contribution. Dashboards increasingly mediate consequential judgments about students and teachers, surfacing risk flags, prompting interventions, and shaping how engagement and effectiveness are understood. Because they operationalize a construct of educational contribution through the behavioral traces available to them, the indicators they make visible come to define what counts as contribution. This study asks whether that operationalization is not merely incomplete but directionally skewed, and whether such a skew constitutes a construct-validity problem. Approach. The project introduces and tests the concept of visibility bias: a directional form of construct underrepresentation in which dashboards privilege outcome-proximal, trace-legible contributions while underrepresenting preventative, relational, contextual, and system-stabilizing forms of educational work. Drawing on validity theory (Messick), trace-data validity (Winne), and invisible-labor scholarship (Star & Strauss; Daniels), the study develops a six-category contribution-visibility typology and applies it in a structured content analysis of 100 documented dashboard indicators drawn from major learning-management platforms and peer-reviewed dashboard systems. Two coders independently coded the corpus; inter-rater reliability was substantial (Cohen's κ = 0.79), and disagreements were adjudicated against the codebook. Findings. The coded distribution shows a pronounced and directional skew: roughly three-quarters of codable indicators are outcome-proximal, relational contribution appears only as thin interaction traces, system-stabilizing contribution is marginal, and contextual and thick relational contribution are absent from the sampled dashboard surface entirely. The skew is strongest in the vendor-documented platforms most educators actually use, making the estimate conservative with respect to deployed analytics. These findings are scoped as a claim about the teacher- and learner-facing dashboard surface, not about all data a platform captures. Significance and expected outcomes. The project contributes a named, theoretically specified, and empirically demonstrable construct that gives designers and researchers a way to detect and partially correct construct underrepresentation in analytics systems. It carries implications for dashboard design, for the validity of inferences drawn from learning analytics, and for equity in how less-visible forms of learning support are recognized. This repository archives the materials supporting the study and enables independent verification: the full coded corpus, both coders' raw passes (from which the reliability statistic can be reproduced), the codebook, and the adjudication record.

works.title: Financial Literacy as Provident Infrastructure Savings Capacity, Monetary Agency, and the Reproduction of Development
Whose voice is heard? Mental health professionals’ involvement, epistemic injustice, and the ethics of psychiatric advance directives
works.abstract: Women living with mental health conditions, neurodevelopmental disorders, or other forms of psychosocial disabilities are disproportionately exposed to coercive practices, structural stigma, and epistemic marginalization. Psychiatric advance directives (PADs) have been proposed as tools to promote autonomy and reduce coercion, yet their implementation in practice remains complex. When a mental health professional is designated to support the person in drafting the directive, they may face specific ethical challenges, including the risk of exerting undue influence on the person's choices. This mini review offers a critical synthesis of theoretical and ethical frameworks to clarify mental health professionals' roles in facilitating PADs. Drawing on the four models of the clinician-patient relationship developed by Emanuel and Emanuel, and Fricker's concept of epistemic injustice, we analyze how relational dynamics influence the drafting process. These models provide a useful framework to conceptualize the mental health professional's role within an alliance aimed at support in restoring agency, trust, and recognition. This analysis highlights how ethically sensitive facilitation may transform PADs into spaces of epistemic repair, ensuring that mental health professionals' involvement respects women's autonomy and lived experiences instead of inadvertently reproducing existing power imbalances. This synthesis contributes to socio-political and clinical debates on PADs, care ethics, and health equity, emphasizing the need to recognize and value experiential knowledge. It also underscores the importance of training and having institutional frameworks that empower mental health professionals, particularly nurses, to act as agents of ethical and epistemic justice in supporting the drafting of PADs.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence-driven Optimization of Nature-based Carbon Sequestration: A Scalable Architecture for Urban Climate Resilience
works.venue: International Journal of Environment and Climate Change
works.abstract: As the climate crisis intensifies and urban populations swell, megacities face compounding threats from carbon emissions, urban heat islands (UHIs), and ecosystem degradation. While nature-based solutions (NbS) offer a promising response through ecological restoration and carbon sequestration, current NbS deployments are often fragmented, non-adaptive, and lack quantitative optimization. This research presents a cutting-edge, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven architecture that operationalizes NbS through a scalable, data-intensive framework. It integrates deep learning (DL) for satellite-derived land classification, graph neural networks (GNNs) for spatial co-benefit mapping, and reinforcement learning (RL) with dynamic reward weighting to optimize intervention strategies in real time. Life cycle assessment (LCA) and ecosystem service valuation modules are embedded to ensure holistic, cross-sectoral impacts. The architecture is deployed in a high-resolution case study of Dhaka, Bangladesh, a climate-vulnerable megacity, achieving over 8,500 metric tons of modeled annual carbon sequestration, 2.1°C reduction in UHI intensity, and quantifiable gains in urban biodiversity and flood mitigation. The system ingests multi-source data, including Sentinel-2, LiDAR, and CMIP6 climate projections, while leveraging federated learning to ensure decentralized, privacy-preserving optimization across municipal zones. A carbon market compatibility layer, aligned with Verra, UN-REDD+, and Article 6 frameworks, enables eligibility for climate finance and offsets. The approach also integrates social equity metrics and indigenous ecological knowledge to prioritize interventions in marginalized zones. This work delivers a first-of-its-kind decision-support platform for AI-optimized NbS that is globally scalable, policy-aligned, and climate-finance ready. It represents a paradigm shift from heuristic-based planning to algorithmically adaptive ecosystem engineering, accelerating progress toward net-zero emissions, SDG convergence, and resilient urban futures. The framework is poised to inform urban sustainability strategies worldwide, offering a replicable model for AI-governed environmental transformation in the age of planetary emergency.

works.title: Expanding the Horizon: A Strategic Framework for Institution-Wide Simulation-Based Learning
works.abstract: This Dissertation-in-Practice addresses the absence of an institutional strategy for simulation-based learning at Mohkinstsis Community College (MCC; a pseudonym). Simulation-based learning is structured, experiential learning activities that replicate real or potential scenarios, allowing students to develop skills and confidence in a low-risk, simulated environment. Although this type of learning has been widely researched and implemented in various disciplines for its effectiveness in enhancing student outcomes, MCC lacks a coordinated, institution-wide approach to its integration. The intent of this dissertation is to cocreate a sustainable and realistic strategy that can be implemented with broad-based support. Central to this work is the commitment to cultural safety and ensuring that both Indigenous and Western knowledge systems are recognized, respected, and valued equally. The strategy is grounded in a two-eyed seeing approach, with particular attention to dismantling systemic barriers that silence equity-deserving voices. The proposed change process is guided by Kotter’s eight-stage change model, supported by the principles of relational work of systems change, and framed through a transformational and shared leadership lens. Three potential solutions are explored and critically evaluated, with the chosen approach demonstrating the strongest alignment with institutional priorities, while also maximizing the use of existing resources and expertise to enable timely and effective implementation. Appreciative inquiry and the plan-do-study-act cycle provide the foundation for continuous improvement, monitoring, and evaluation. The dissertation concludes with a knowledge mobilization plan aimed at sharing lessons learned and inspiring change across the institution in support of inclusive, high-quality experiential learning.

works.title: The ways communication ease knowledge sharing: an examination of three organizations with knowledge intensive services
works.abstract: Over the decades, practitioners and researchers alike have increasingly focused on how organization members can effectively share knowledge in an effort to create and maintain knowledge-intensive services. The growing interest in knowledge sharing is due in part to the increased digitalization and specialization of work practices. For example, the advance of computer-aided design, 3D printing, programming languages, financial regulation, and algorithmic stock trading places an increasing requirement on organization members to keep up with changes in their environment. Rapid technological and regulatory changes drastically impact and change how knowledge-intensive services must be approached. Organization members are unable to independently develop the expertise needed to create, maintain, and deliver complex services on their own. Knowledge sharing allows organization members to rely on others to provide services. Effective knowledge sharing increases organizational member’s performance, and in turn benefits organizations. However, organization members are faced with challenges that hinder knowledge sharing. Organization members become experts by repeatedly engaging in their area of expertise. Repeated engagement in an area limits the ability to generate expertise in other areas. The way organization members approach problems, the solutions they see, and the way they communicate is impacted and grounded by their repeated engagement. Organization members with different expertise have unique vocabulary, interpretations, and work practices. This dissertation examines how awareness of differences and the development of common ground between organization members can ease knowledge sharing. In doing so it is tested whether awareness of difference is sufficient for knowledge sharing compared to the existence of common ground between organization members. A mixed methods approach, blending social network analysis with observations and interviews, is used to answer the primary research question and hypotheses. Observations, interviews, and social network data is used to map the communicative relationships between organization members and identify the statistical likelihood of their co-occurrence in three organizations. The observations and interviews are analyzed using a grounded theory approach and content analysis, while the social network survey data is analyzed using descriptive statistics, quadratic assignment procedures, and exponential random graph modeling. In aggregate, this dissertation examines the type of communication and relational mechanisms that ease knowledge sharing between organization members.

works.title: Clouded vision: Reframing multi-marginal landscapes through a lens-based practice
works.abstract: This practice-based doctoral submission presents a decade of lens-based inquiry into the visual representation of multi-marginal landscapes, examined through the interrelated conceptual frameworks of “’hin places’, partial opacity, and more-than-human relationality. The portfolio of published works spans five bodies of practice — Maunga (2014–2017), Tongariro Power (2015–2017), An Age of Iron (2017–2020), Clouded Vision (2024-5), and 1000 Years Per Inch (2024–2025) — and moves between the colonised and contested landscapes of Aotearoa New Zealand and the post-industrial multi-marginal landscapes of the English Midlands and Northwest. The research is driven by two interrelated questions: how can a lens-based practitioner represent colonised, and exhausted landscapes without reinscribing extractive practices upon them; and how can lens-based practice reposition marginal landscapes as protagonists rather than backdrops or resources. The thesis argues that prevailing documentary conventions of landscape photography — characterised by the fixed viewpoint, optical clarity, and the dispassionate aesthetic of large-format practice — reproduce the anthropocentric and colonising logics they may nominally oppose, rendering landscapes as image-resources available for contemplation and consumption. In response, the research develops an alternative methodology grounded in three interconnected propositions. The first is the theorisation and practice of partial opacity as a constitutive ethics of lens-based image-making. Drawing on Édouard Glissant’s concept of the right to opacity — understood, following Drabinski, as an anticolonial resistance to modes of knowing that seek to absorb, possess, or render the Other fully legible — the research advances opacity not as an aesthetic preference but as a structural condition of ethical relations. This proposition is extended beyond the human subject to encompass more-than-human protagonists and is enacted through a set of disruptive production and post-production methods: speculative fieldworking; and the strategies of selection, occlusion, appropriation, and re-assemblage that together produce what the research terms ‘the enigmatic image’. The second proposition concerns the theorisation of fieldwork as a relational-ethical practice rather than a neutral method of visual data gathering. Drawing on situated feminist epistemology, the kaupapa Māori protocols developed through sustained engagement with Ngāti Rangi, and Polly Stanton’s conception of fieldworking as a process of making-with, the research positions the practitioner’s embodied, porous, and situated arrival at a site as a pre-productive ethical orientation. The practitioner is understood as a participant in a more-than-human encounter rather than a surveyor of it. The third proposition advances the productive interval — drawn from Trinh T. Minh-Ha’s critique of naturalism in documentary practice and Lyotard’s theorisation of the fissure between discours and figure — as the site at which relational ethics and aesthetic innovation converge. Post-production strategies are reoriented away from their conventional function of resolving and polishing the image, and toward the generation of disruptive, affective, and partially opaque image-forms that act upon the viewer at the level of the unconscious, resisting assimilation into the extractive visual regimes of contemporary landscape photography. A significant strand of the research reﬂects critically on the particular obligations and risks of working as a tau iwi, or non-Māori, practitioner within the post-colonial context of Aotearoa. The thesis demonstrates how an ethic of care developed through engagement with Indigenous cosmologies, kaupapa Māori research protocols, and the counsel of Ngāti Rangi knowledge-holders can be carried forward, with appropriate reﬂexivity, into subsequent practice in the landscapes of England. The most recent work, which introduces chromatography — a pseudo-scientific process of soil portraiture — and a critically interrogated collaboration with generative artificial intelligence, extends the research’s ethical and methodological concerns into the ecological and technological conditions of the present moment. Taken together, the portfolio and accompanying critical writing propose a photo-filmic practice that operates as a form of planetary alliance. Through the integration of speculative fieldworking, surrealist-inﬂected post-production, and an ethics of partial opacity, this research advances new methodological and conceptual pathways for engaging with thin places in lens-based practice. The clouded vision articulated across the submission does not seek clarity or resolution; it aﬃrms affect, uncertainty, and more-than-human relationality as the conditions through which responsible and responsive visual knowledge can emerge.
