works.title: "How are you?" Listening as Political Communication: Affective Infrastructure, Trust, and Democratic Renewal in Italy's Centre-Left"
works.venue: IRIS Research product catalog (Sapienza University of Rome)
works.abstract: In an era of post-political trends and the rise of prominent leaders, the notion that engaging with a party's supporters could stimulate political participation, particularly in marginalised urban areas and social peripheries, might appear unconventional. However, the research project commissioned by the Italian Democratic Party and conducted by our research unit focused precisely on this combination. This paper presents the findings of a two-tier research project conducted as part of a nationwide, grassroots listening campaign carried out between February and June 2026. Situated within critical political communication scholarship, the study posits that listening can be considered a form of communication infrastructure with the potential to reshape relationships between political parties and their social constituencies particularly in contexts of declining institutional trust (Rosanvallon, 2008; Wilson & Swyngedouw, 2016). This occurs despite challenges such as affective polarisation (Iyengar & Krupenkin, 2018), deep mediatisation (Hepp, 2020), and participatory exhaustion. The research design articulates a dual-layered empirical architecture that foregrounds the dialectical relationship between grassroots political subjectivities and institutional communication strategies. Conceptually grounded in critical theories of communication, media, democracy studies, and mediated political participation, this framework interrogates listening as a contested field where power relations, affective economies, and democratic legitimacy are negotiated and reproduced, rather than merely as a tactical instrument. The first analytical strand examines the listening phase oriented towards party members, supporters and peripheral publics situated at the margins of formal political participation. Methodologically, this investigation uses a triangulated approach, combining qualitative depth with mixed-method breadth. Face-to-face encounters, semi-structured interviews and survey instruments generate a multidimensional empirical corpus capable of capturing both individual narratives and collective patterns of political engagement and disengagement. This strand interrogates four interconnected communicative dimensions that, together, illuminate the texture of contemporary democratic disaffection: 1) affective politics and everyday vulnerability. The research foregrounds the affective dimensions of political subjectivity by posing the seemingly simple question, 'How are you?'. This methodological entry point enables the analysis of how personal anxieties, experiences of precarity and structures of vulnerability are articulated, mediated and potentially politicised within everyday discourse. The investigation reveals how neoliberal individualisation processes fragment collective experience while simultaneously creating latent grounds for solidarity through shared precarity. 2) Future-Oriented Imaginaries and the Politics of Hope. Beyond immediate concerns, the research explores participants' future-oriented imaginaries by examining articulated hopes and the conditions that might restore collective political possibility. Aspirations relating to social justice, ecological transition, workplace dignity and intergenerational equity are analysed as communicatively constructed horizons that illuminate the material and symbolic conditions through which hope acquires political traction, rather than as abstract ideals. 3) Relational positionality towards institutional politics. The third analytical focus examines how participants articulate their relationship with politics in general, political parties as organisational forms, the centre-left political formation and the Democratic Party specifically. Attention is paid to the communicative strategies through which political distance, disillusionment or tentative affiliation are expressed. 4) Media ecologies. Media ecologies and communicative infrastructures are examined. Underpinning these dimensions is an examination of the mediated nature of political listening itself. The second empirical strand shifts the analytical focus from the subjectivities of citizens to the listening campaign itself, examining it as a political communication strategy embedded within institutional power relations. Through qualitative content analysis of campaign materials, discourse analysis of official messaging, organisational ethnography and in-depth interviews with PD leaders and campaign coordinators, this phase will investigate how listening is strategically framed, operationally implemented and institutionalised within party communication structures. This strand foregrounds several critical tensions: A) The dialectic of openness and control. The research examines the structural contradictions between bottom-up democratic openness and top down strategic management. How are grassroots contributions filtered, translated, and incorporated into programmatic priorities? What selection, interpretive, and codification mechanisms determine which voices are amplified and which remain inaudible? These questions shed light on the power dynamics that govern the transformation of participatory input into political narratives and policy positions. B) Institutional translation and domestication. The analysis focuses on the processes through which diverse citizen expressions are translated into coherent party discourse. This 'communicative labour' of institutional appropriation reveals how listening campaigns risk reproducing the very hierarchies they ostensibly challenge, transforming genuine dialogue into extractive data collection and authentic participation into managed consultation. C) Negotiating party power structures. Finally, the research investigates how listening is negotiated within existing intra party power configurations. This dimension foregrounds listening not as a neutral democratic practice, but as an area of contention where competing visions of party identity and political strategy clash. By combining audience-centred research with an analysis of party-level communicative practices, the paper advances a relational understanding of listening as a form of political communication. The main hypothesis is that listening-based strategies can potentially disrupt top-down agenda-setting logics, thereby fostering the co-production of political meaning and policy legitimacy. However, it also highlights the structural and organisational constraints that shape the transformative capacity of listening within contemporary party politics. By framing listening as core infrastructure for rebuilding trust and re-embedding political parties within the lived experiences of their constituencies, particularly in contemporary democratic peripheries, the paper contributes to debates on participation, representation, and democratic renewal.

works.title: Race, Property, and Population Health: Examining Policy-Driven Patterns of Whiteness, Anti-Blackness and Health Inequity in Metropolitan Detroit
works.abstract: Trenchant health inequities between Black and White Americans persist in metropolitan areas in the Midwest and Northeast characterized by high levels of residential segregation and municipal fragmentation. The recalcitrance of these racial and spatial relations more than a half-century after the 1968 Fair Housing Act underscores the need to investigate the contemporary institutions and laws that reproduce White supremacy and its embodied consequences in US metropolitan areas. This three-paper quantitative dissertation draws on critical race theory and methods from the fields of demography, social geography, and legal epidemiology to examine policy-driven patterns of Whiteness, anti-Blackness, and health inequity in metropolitan Detroit. This project seeks to better understand how structural racialization operates through municipal institutions, fiscal inequities, and property tax foreclosure law to uphold a racialized metropolitan hierarchy of population health. Chapter 2 (paper 1) examines the relationship between geographical Whiteness and excess mortality across municipalities (cities and townships) in the tri-county Detroit Metropolitan Area (DMA) in 2010 using data from the Michigan Department of Community Health and the US Census. This study found that stark inter-municipal disparities in excess death between White and Black populations in the DMA could be partly attributed to a protective relationship between suburban Whiteness and mortality that preponderantly benefitted White residents. Conceptualized within a relational framework of spatial White supremacy, this study problematizes the undue health benefits of suburban Whiteness within a racialized metropolitan health hierarchy where Black populations suffer disproportionately from excess death. Integrating data from the Michigan Department of Treasury and the American Community Survey (ACS), Chapter 3 (paper 2) builds on Chapter 2 by exploring whether the protective health status of suburban Whiteness could be explained by systemic fiscal advantages that benefit the health of predominantly White suburbs at the expense of Black populations. Findings revealed steep fiscal gradients in mortality among White and Black municipal populations; while the most staggering rates of excess death were documented among a cluster of fiscally poor majority-Black cities, the largest health benefits accrued to a minority of affluent and overwhelmingly White suburbs that held a disproportionate share of the region’s fiscal resources. This study is the first to employ a measure of municipal fiscal health to examine intra-metropolitan health inequities, shedding new light on how racialized patterns of fiscal accumulation and deprivation may structure persistent disparities in health. Chapter 4 (paper 3) assessed evidence for structural racialization in the spatial distribution of occupied property tax foreclosures and urban health equity across census tracts in Wayne county using the ACS, foreclosure records from the Wayne County Treasurer, and data from several public sources. The findings show that tax foreclosure law perpetuated racialized spatial patterns of housing dispossession that intersected with preexisting inequities in health; between 2014 and 2015, tax foreclosures dispossessed about 50,000 Wayne county residents, and occupied foreclosure burdens were principally concentrated in Black neighborhoods characterized by shorter life expectancies and higher rates of disability. As the first study to operationalize disparate impact for housing and health research, this research generates knowledge on how structural racialization works through colorblind laws and policies to reify racialized hierarchies of housing and health in segregated areas.

works.title: NATURE, MAGNITUDE, AND EXPLANATION OF THE EFFECTS OF EDUCATIONAL STRATEGIES AIMED AT REDUCING GENDER BIASES IN CISGENDER WOMEN PARTICIPATING IN MEDICO-SURGICAL TRAINING PROCESSES: A MIXED METHODS SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
works.abstract: Gender equity has become a contemporary challenge of structural transformation for the training of human resources and health systems globally (Cawich et al., 2026; Onyiego & Davids, 2023). Although there has been an increase in women's enrollment in health sciences faculties over recent decades, this has not translated into equal opportunities within training and professional development contexts (Cawich et al., 2026; Lim et al., 2021). This is secondary to structural, cultural, and organizational barriers—constituting sticky floors and glass ceilings—that curtail access to leadership positions, as well as academic and professional recognition. These processes are more frequent and socially validated in medico-surgical specialty settings, which are framed by androcentric and Westernized models that govern and align bodies and the relational structures of medical training and practice (Lim et al., 2021). In particular, medico-surgical specialties perpetuate substantial gender gaps. Evidence of this is that while 41.3% of general surgery residents are women, they constitute only 24.8% of the faculty, 20% of program directorships, and a mere 3% of department chairs. The aforementioned figures reflect a marked vertical segregation within the discipline that impacts women’s attainment of leadership and decision-making positions (Pickel & Sivachandran, 2024; Rakestraw et al., 2022; Riner et al., 2021). This reflects the persistence of implicit and explicit frameworks of discrimination resulting from asymmetrical and historical gender-based power relations within the training of human resources in health (Salles et al., 2019). In other words, these frameworks constitute gender biases, which have been defined as explicit or implicit beliefs, attitudes, practices, and/or stereotypes that reproduce hierarchies and inequities (Bem, 1981; Liben & Bigler, 2017; Risberg et al., 2009). Implicit gender biases structure operations and relationships for individuals, communities, and institutions without their influence being recognized. In the medico-surgical setting, leadership characteristics and superior surgical skills are attributed to men, in contrast to women, who are relegated to caregiving roles (Giles & Hill, 2015). This phenomenon impacts the academic and professional trajectories of women, whose narratives have revealed microaggressions, fewer opportunities to participate in surgical procedures, and constant questioning of their case-resolution skills. The synergy of these manifestations of gender bias deteriorates psychological well-being and job satisfaction; it also exerts cumulative effects on specialty selection, retention, research participation, funding, mentorship, and institutional promotion (Cawich et al., 2026). In response to this issue, various multi-level strategies have been developed in recent years to transform training dynamics, understanding that these traits are not immutable but rather sociocultural constructs susceptible to modification through systematic processes that permeate the education of healthcare human resources. However, the effectiveness of these strategies remains uncertain due to the heterogeneity of methodological designs, intervention durations, participant populations, and evaluated outcomes. Following the recommendations of the Joanna Briggs Institute (2024), a preliminary search was conducted in JBI Evidence Synthesis, the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, PROSPERO, MEDLINE/PubMed, Epistemonikos, DARE, and ACCESSSS. No systematic reviews were identified that synthesize and explore strategies for gender bias reduction, which constitutes an information gap for decision-making aimed at guiding the implementation of interventions that impact the well-being of women within the healthcare workforce. The objective of this study is to synthesize and integrate the available quantitative and qualitative evidence regarding the nature, magnitude, and explanation of the effects of educational strategies aimed at reducing gender biases in cisgender women participating in medico-surgical training processes, in order to understand their influence on academic, educational, and professional trajectories.

works.title: An Integrated Coordination Framework for Construction Procurement: Examining Early Supplier Involvement through Agent-Based Modeling
works.venue: ResearchWorks at the University of Washington (University of Washington)
works.abstract: Construction projects rely on complex stakeholder networks, where coordination across design and construction phases is critical to performance. Despite decades of collaborative procurement frameworks, supplier expertise is integrated late in the design process, and the behavioral mechanisms linking procurement conditions to project outcomes remain poorly understood. This fragmentation generates coordination failures that manifest as rework, RFIs, constrained innovation, and declining workflow continuity. Existing literature examines procurement structures, stakeholder behavior, and project outcomes largely in isolation. Key drivers such as risk perception, supplier participation, and collaboration intensity are rarely formalized as measurable, dynamic variables throughout the project lifecycle. As a result, the mechanisms through which governance conditions and coordination timing jointly influence performance and innovation adoption remain unclear. This study examines how procurement structure, governance conditions, and stakeholder behavior interact within a dynamic system that shapes project performance. It develops and evaluates an Integrated Coordination Framework (ICF), centered on a Central Coordination Agent (CCA), to structure early supplier engagement, compensation conditions, and coordination across the design lifecycle. A mixed-methods design integrates industry interviews with an agent-based simulation model in AnyLogic. Interview data were thematically coded and translated into agent decision rules through structured coding-to-model mapping. The model was evaluated using a four-stage validation framework: internal verification, expert-based mechanism validation, pattern validation, and quantitative benchmarking using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Four key findings emerge. First, procurement structure creates the conditions for improved performance, but governance influences whether those conditions translate into improved outcomes. Under ICF, projects achieved 75% innovation adoption, 80% fewer Requests for Information (RFIs), and stable capacity utilization (~88%), compared to 25% innovation adoption, full RFI accumulation, and declining capacity utilization (~75%) under fragmented procurement. Second, the Central Coordination Agent improves performance by shifting coordination and issue resolution upstream into the design phase, where conflicts can be addressed while decisions remain flexible. Under ICF, this earlier resolution process reduced RFI generation and stabilized construction workflow conditions. In contrast, low early redesign activity and limited RFI volume under typical procurement can create a false sense of effective coordination, as unresolved issues are deferred to later construction stages, where resolution becomes more disruptive, increases the volume of RFIs, and reduces available capacity. Third, GMP timing operates as a governance constraint rather than a coordination variable. Once GMP is established, behavior shifts from collaboration to cost protection, regardless of the quality of prior coordination. Fourth, the highest-impact lever lies in the middle governance layer, defined by three conditions: clear compensation for early engineering work, formalized supplier decision authority, and relational continuity across project portfolios. This study contributes to procurement governance and stakeholder coordination literature while providing foundational insights relevant to transaction cost economics in construction procurement. Methodologically, the study offers a replicable mixed-methods framework for examining procurement as a dynamic behavioral system. In practice, the simulation tool enables procurement managers to identify which governance parameters limit performance before coordination failures become visible, allowing targeted intervention at the root cause rather than a reactive response. More broadly, engaging supplier expertise early through structured coordination and supportive governance leads to more innovative outcomes and stronger long-term stakeholder relationships, and the Integrated Coordination Framework is designed to enable this opportunity.

works.title: Activist Learning under Constraint: Stratified Struggles and Resistance of Indonesian Student Activists
works.venue: Open Access Victoria University of Wellington | Te Herenga Waka (Figshare)
works.abstract: This thesis examines how Indonesian higher education student activists learn and develop critical consciousness within fields shaped by structural inequality. In Indonesia, student activism has long played a central role in shaping national politics, yet its pedagogical dimensions remain under-researched. Amid shrinking civic spaces, increased surveillance, and the marketisation of the university, questions of how student activists come to understand, critique, and act upon injustice have taken on renewed urgency. While student movements are often celebrated for their resistance, less is known about the everyday learning processes that sustain this resistance and the constraints activists face as they attempt to politicise their own educational experience. This thesis seeks to address this gap by exploring how student activists navigate and contest the stratified terrains of higher education student activism in Indonesia, and how their access to resources, be it economic, cultural, and social, shapes their activist learning. Grounded in the critical traditions of Pierre Bourdieu and Paulo Freire, the study brings together Bourdieu’s theory of capital, field, and habitus with Freire’s focus on conscientisation and praxis. Bourdieu’s concepts allow for a structural reading of the unequal conditions that shape participants’ learning within both academic and activist fields, while Freire offers a lens through which to analyse how students critically reflect on and resist these conditions through situated action. Together, these frameworks illuminate how activist learning emerges not in idealised spaces of autonomy but through the negotiation of constraint and the creative mobilisation of their limited capital. This thesis extends research on activist learning and political subjectivity in Indonesia by foregrounding how student activists learn within their activism. It plays close attention to the complexities of conscientisation within informal settings and under conditions of scarcity. In doing so, it offers a grounded analysis of how critical consciousness develops unevenly and collectively within stratified terrains of possibility and exclusion. The research draws on ethnographic fieldwork conducted over 6 months with eleven (n=11) student activists aged 20 to 25 involved in various student movements in Yogyakarta, Indonesia. The methodology combined participant observation, semi-structured interviews, auto photo-elicitation, and nongkrong or hanging out. Participants were selected across a range of higher education institutions (HEIs) from higher-resourced A-accredited and lower-resourced B-accredited HEIs, for an exploration of how institutional and personal differences shaped the availability of resources, opportunities for political engagement, and the forms of learning participants were able to access. By attending to both the structural contours of learning and the relational practices through which knowledge circulates, the study centres student activists’ own reflections, struggles, and agency. Findings showed that student activists entered activist spaces on unequal footing, with their activist learning shaped by disparities in institutional resources, economic means, and linguistic capital. Participants from A-accredited universities accessed well-stocked libraries and critical discourses, while others faced infrastructural scarcity and exclusion. Beyond formal education, participants described learning primarily through activism, via workshops, reading circles, protests, and everyday organising. These spaces became sites of collective inquiry and dialogue, where socio-political understanding developed through both action and reflection. Yet participation in these spaces was also shaped by the same inequalities that structured their formal educational experiences. Many responded through engaging mutual aid or the redistribution of resources by sharing books and food or organising peer-led study spaces. While these strategies were vital, for some the burden of sustaining critical learning under constraint led to exhaustion, disillusionment, and burnout, thus revealing the uneven labour required to stay engaged. Despite these challenges, participants’ critical reflections sharpened their awareness of higher education’s ideological role, exposing its complicity in neoliberal and authoritarian agendas. This awareness prompted some to challenge and critically reimagine HEIs as sites of socio-political transformation. This study concludes that student activism in Indonesia functioned as a relational, communal, praxis-driven pedagogy in which participants developed critical consciousness and to define themselves as activists through their mutual aid practices. Their political understanding was acquired through situated action, collective struggle, and critical reflection grounded in lived experience, both within their activist spaces and in their higher education institutions. This learning, rooted in social relationships and everyday practice, cultivated a disposition oriented toward reflexivity, critique, and communal transformation. Extending Crossley’s (2003) concept of ‘radical habitus’, this thesis argue that these processes give rise to a ‘communal radical habitus.’ Yet as this process unfolded unevenly, far from levelling the field, inequalities continued to shape who could participate, sustain engagement, and deepen their learning, further reproducing the very exclusions the movement aimed to dismantle.

works.title: The Lost Combinator
works.abstract: Let me begin by thanking the Association for Computational Linguistics and its Executive Committee for conferring on me the great honor of their Lifetime Achievement Award for 2018, which of course I share with all the wonderful students and colleagues that have made many essential contributions to this work over many years.At the heart of the work that I have been pursuing over my research lifetime so far, whether in parsing and sentence processing, spoken language understanding, semantics, or even in musical understanding by machine, there lies a theory of natural language grammar that brings parsing, compositional semantics, statistical modeling, and logical inference into the closest possible relation. This theory of grammar is combinatory, in the sense that its operations are type-dependent and restricted to strictly string-adjacent phonologically or graphologically-realized inputs, and categorial, in the sense that those operands pair a syntactic type with a type-transparent semantic representation or logical form.I’d like to use this opportunity to briefly address three questions that revolve around the theory of grammar, both combinatory and otherwise. The first question concerns the way that Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) was developed with a number of colleagues, over a number of stages and in slightly different forms. The second is an essentially evolutionary question of why natural language grammar should take a combinatory form. The third question is that of what the future holds for CCG and other structural theories of grammar in computational linguistics and NLP in the age of deep learning.I have called this talk “The Lost Combinator” in homage to the Victorian era poem “The Lost Chord,” in the hope of suggesting that the theoretical development of CCG has always been empirical, rather than axiomatic, in search of the simplest explanation of the facts of language, rather than for confirmation of linguistic received opinion, however intuitively salient.In the late 1960s (when I was a psychology undergraduate at the University of Sussex under Stuart Sutherland, and then started as a graduate student in artificial intelligence at Edinburgh under Christopher Longuet-Higgins), a broad community of theoretical linguists, psychologists, and computational linguists saw themselves as all working on the same problem, under the definition provided by the “transformational” theory of grammar proposed by Chomsky (1957, 1965), using theories of psycholinguistic processing, language acquisition, and language evolution proposed by Lashley (1951), Miller, Galanter, and Pribram (1960), Miller (1967), and Lenneberg (1967), theories of natural language semantics proposed by Carnap (1956), Montague (1970), and Lewis (1970), and computational models of parsing such as those proposed by Thorne, Bratley, and Dewar (1968) and Woods (1970). (I myself was so convinced that this program would succeed that I believed it was time to apply the same methods to other cognitive faculties, taking as my research project for Ph.D. their application to the interpretation of music by machine, following the lead of Max Clowes [1971] in machine vision.)Almost immediately, this consensus fell apart. First, Chomsky himself was among the first (1965) to recognize that transformational rules, though descriptively revealing, were so expressive as to have little explanatory force, and required many apparently arbitrary constraints (Ross 1967). Second, psychologists realized that psycholinguistic measures of processing difficulty of sentences bore almost no relation to their transformational derivational complexity (Marslen-Wilson 1973; Fodor, Bever, and Garrett 1974). Finally, computational linguists attempting to implement transformational grammars as parsers realized that they were spending all their time implementing even more constraints on rules, in order to limit search arising from overgeneration (Friedman 1971; Gross 1978). (Meanwhile, I realized that the problem had not in fact been solved, and returned to natural language processing, thanks to a postdoc at Sussex with Philip Johnson-Laird.)This disillusion wasn’t just a case of internal academic squabbling. There were also a couple of influential reports commissioned by the U.S. and UK governments that ended funding for machine translation (MT) and artificial intelligence (AI) (Pierce et al. 1966; Lighthill 1973). As a result of the second of these reports, which determined that AI was never going to work, PhDs in artificial intelligence like my classmate Geoff Hinton and myself spent ten years or so after graduation in psychology departments (in my case, at the Universities of Sussex and Warwick), until yet another report said AI was working after all and that Britain and the U.S. were falling behind Japan in this vital area. As a result, I could get hired again in computer science, first briefly back at Edinburgh, and then at the University of Pennsylvania (I learned a lesson from this odyssey that I have tried to remember whenever I have been appointed to a committee to report on anything, which is that while reports very rarely do any good, they can very easily do a great deal of harm.)Meanwhile, as a result of these conflicts, the scientific study of language fragmented. The linguists swiftly abjured any responsibility for their grammars (“Competence”) bearing any relation to processing (“Performance”). Because the psychologists could hardly abandon Performance, they in turn became agnostic about grammar, retreating to context-free surface grammar (which they tended to refer to as “parsing strategies”), or a touchingly optimistic belief in its emergence from neural models. Meanwhile, the computational linguists (whose machines were growing exponentially in size and speed from the 16K byte core of the machine that supported the whole group when I started my graduate studies, on to levels that would soon permit parsing the entire contents of the then embrionic Web) similarly found that very little of what the linguists and psychologists cared about was usable at scale, and that none of it significantly improved overall performance over very much simpler context-free or even finite-state methods that the linguists had shown to be incomplete. The reason of course was Zipf’s law, which means that the events with respect to which the low-level methods are incomplete are off in the long tail.It also became apparent to a few computationalists working on speech, MT, and information retrieval that the real problem was not grammar but ambiguity and its resolution by world-knowledge, and that the solution lay in probabilistic models (Bar-Hillel 1960/1964; Spärck Jones 1964/1986; Wilks 1975; Jelinek and Lafferty 1991) (although it was not immediately apparent how to combine statistical models with grammar-based systems without making obviously false independence assumptions).Nevertheless, as any red-blooded psychologist had always insisted, the divorce between competence and performance that everyone else had accepted did not make any sense. The grammar and the processor had to have evolved in lock-step, as a package deal, for what could be the evolutionary selective advantage of a grammar that you cannot process, or a parser without a grammar?It seemed equally obvious that surface syntax and the underlying semantic or conceptual representation must also be closely related, since the only reasonable basis for child language acquisition that has ever been on offer is that the child attaches language-specific grammar to a universal conceptual relation or “language of mind” (Miller 1967; Bowerman 1973; Wexler and Culicover 1980). It seemed to follow that radically new theories of grammar were needed.Theoretical linguists agree that the central problem for the theory of grammar is discontinuity or non-adjacent dependency between predicates and their arguments:Chomsky described discontinuity in terms of movement, which was known to be formally very unconstrained. By contrast, the ATN parser used in the LUNAR project (Woods, Kaplan, and Nash-Webber 1972) reduced all discontinuity to local operations on registers (Thorne, Bratley, and Dewar 1968; Bobrow and Fraser 1969; Woods 1970).In particular, unbounded wh-dependencies like the above were handled by: (a) putting a pointer into a * or HOLD register as soon as the “which” was encountered without regard to where it would end up; and (b) retrieving the pointer from HOLD when the verb needing an object “had” was encountered without regard to where it had started out. (It also included an ingenious mechanism for coordination called SYSCONJ, which one finds even now being reinvented on an almost yearly basis—cf. Woods [2010].) A * register was also used for wh-constructions within a systemic grammar framework by Winograd (1972, pages 52–53) in his inspiring conversational program SHRDLU.However, it was unclear how to generalize the HOLD register to handle the multiple long-range dependencies, including crossing dependencies, that are found in many other languages. In particular, if the HOLD register were assumed to be a stack, then the ATN becomes a two-stack machine (since we are already implicitly using one stack as a PDA to parse the context-free core grammar).On the computational side at least, the reaction to this impass took two distinct forms. Both reactions took the form of trying to reduce the two major operators of the transformation theory, substitution of immediate constituents, or what is nowadays called “Merge,” and “Move,” or displacement of non-immediate constituents, to one. On the one hand, Lexical Functional Grammar (Bresnan and Kaplan 1982) and Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar (Pollard and Sag 1994) followed Kay (1979) in making unification the basis of movement and merger. Because unification can pass information across unbounded structures, this can be thought of as reducing Merge to Move.On the other hand, Generalized Phrase Structure Grammar (Gazdar 1981), Tree Adjoining Grammar (TAG; Joshi and Levy 1982), and Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG, Ades and Steedman, 1982) sought to reduce Move to various forms of local merger. In particular, the latter authors suggested that the same stack could be used to capture both long-range dependency and recursion in CCG.1Natural language grammar exhibits discontinuity because semantically language is an applicative system. Applicative systems (such as programming languages) support the twin notions of: (a) Application of a function/concept to an argument/entity; and (b) Abstraction, or the definition of a new function/concept in terms of existing ones.Language is in that sense inherently computational. It seems to follow that linguistics is (or should be) inherently computational as well. (Of course, it does not follow that computationalists have nothing to learn from linguistics.)There are two ways of modeling abstraction in applicative systems: Taking abstraction itself as a primitive operation (λ-calculus, LISP):(2)a.fatherEsau⇒Isaacb.grandfather=λx.father(fatherx)c.grandfatherEsau⇒Abrahamor Defining abstraction in terms of a collection of operators on strictly adjacent terms aka Combinators, such as function composition (Combinatory Calculus, MIRANDA).(3)b′.grandfather=BfatherfatherThe latter does the work of the λ-calculus without using any variables.Despite the resemblance of the “traces” (or copies) and “operators” (or complementizer positions) of the transformational theory to the λ-operators and variables of applicative systems of the first kind, natural language actually seems to be a system of the second, combinatory kind. works.title: Educating the Regenerative Leader: Reimagining Learning Ecosystems for a Conscious Civilization
works.abstract: The accelerating convergence of ecological degradation, technological disruption, socio-political fragmentation, and moral uncertainty has exposed a structural inadequacy in contemporary leadership paradigms, and in this foundational reorientation, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) positions regenerative leadership not merely as a managerial innovation but as a civilizational necessity grounded in ethical reflexivity, systemic literacy, and ontological awareness. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) argues that education systems across the globe have historically been designed to produce extractive efficiency rather than regenerative consciousness, privileging productivity over planetary stewardship and competition over collaborative flourishing. Through a rigorous interdisciplinary synthesis that bridges systems theory, ecological economics, moral philosophy, digital transformation studies, and humanistic management, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) articulates a new epistemic architecture in which leadership education becomes the central lever for reshaping institutional metabolism and societal imagination. In advancing this thesis, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) introduces the concept of the “learning ecosystem” as a living, adaptive, co-evolutionary network of actors, technologies, values, and environments that collectively cultivate regenerative agency. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) emphasizes that the crisis of leadership is not primarily a crisis of competence, but a crisis of consciousness, in which instrumental rationality has outpaced moral imagination. By reframing leadership development as an ecological process rather than a transactional curriculum, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) situates education within the broader biospheric context, recognizing that institutions are nested within social systems, which are in turn nested within planetary boundaries. This nested systems approach underpins a new methodological commitment: moving from siloed knowledge production toward integrative, transdisciplinary praxis capable of generating long-term regenerative value. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) further contends that a conscious civilization cannot emerge from unconscious pedagogy, and therefore calls for a radical redesign of governance structures, assessment metrics, and leadership competencies within universities, corporations, and public institutions. Rather than measuring success solely through growth indicators, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) proposes regenerative performance metrics that evaluate resilience, relational equity, ecological restoration, and ethical coherence. The educational transformation envisioned by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) integrates digital platforms, community engagement, and experiential immersion into a coherent developmental arc that cultivates reflective practitioners capable of navigating complexity without collapsing into reductionism. This work situates itself within global debates on sustainability transitions, post-growth economics, and conscious capitalism, yet distinguishes itself through its emphasis on pedagogical infrastructure as the primary catalytic mechanism for systemic renewal. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) advances a conceptual novelty by merging regenerative design principles with leadership identity formation, thereby expanding the discourse beyond operational sustainability toward ontological transformation. The regenerative leader, in the framework articulated by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), is not defined by hierarchical authority but by relational accountability, adaptive intelligence, and a commitment to intergenerational justice. In presenting this book to an international scholarly and practitioner audience, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) invites a re-examination of foundational assumptions regarding knowledge, power, and progress. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) asserts that the future of civilization depends not solely on technological breakthroughs but on the cultivation of leaders who can harmonize innovation with wisdom, efficiency with empathy, and ambition with responsibility. This opening reflection establishes the normative and analytical framework through which the subsequent chapters elaborate a comprehensive blueprint for educating regenerative leaders capable of stewarding a conscious civilization. This book emerges from a deep intellectual and moral concern regarding the trajectory of contemporary civilization, and in articulating this concern Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) affirms that leadership education stands at a decisive crossroads between perpetuating extractive paradigms and cultivating regenerative futures. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) writes from the conviction that the crises confronting humanity climate destabilization, technological acceleration without ethical grounding, widening inequality, cultural polarization, and institutional distrust are not isolated phenomena but systemic manifestations of a fragmented worldview embedded within our learning infrastructures. In this sense, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) approaches this work not merely as an academic contribution but as a civilizational intervention grounded in scholarly rigor, moral responsibility, and a humanistic commitment to intergenerational stewardship. The intellectual journey that informs this volume reflects years of interdisciplinary dialogue, research, and praxis, through which Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) has sought to bridge management science, sustainability transitions, digital transformation studies, ethical philosophy, and systems thinking into a coherent regenerative framework. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) contends that the fragmentation of knowledge has paralleled the fragmentation of ecological and social systems, and therefore the reconstruction of leadership must begin with epistemological integration. This preface sets the tone for a work that challenges dominant assumptions about growth, competition, and performance by inviting readers to reconsider the ontological foundations upon which leadership identity is formed. At the heart of this book lies the concept of regenerative leadership, articulated by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) as a form of authority rooted not in control or extraction but in relational accountability and ecological reciprocity. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) introduces conceptual novelty by situating leadership within nested systems individual, institutional, societal, and planetary thereby reframing leaders as stewards of systemic vitality rather than architects of short-term advantage. In doing so, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) advances a humanistic authority that recognizes the dignity of persons, the integrity of ecosystems, and the ethical weight of decision-making across time horizons. The educational systems that currently shape future leaders were largely designed during industrial modernity, and Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) argues that their structural logic reflects the priorities of efficiency, standardization, and measurable output rather than resilience, empathy, and regenerative value. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) suggests that such systems inadvertently cultivate instrumental rationality while marginalizing moral imagination and systemic awareness. This book, therefore, is an invitation to redesign learning ecosystems as living, adaptive networks capable of nurturing reflective practitioners who can navigate complexity without sacrificing conscience. In articulating the notion of a “conscious civilization,” Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) proposes a societal horizon in which economic activity, technological innovation, and governance structures are aligned with ecological regeneration and social equity. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) positions this horizon not as utopian speculation but as an emergent necessity, grounded in empirical evidence from sustainability science and organizational transformation research. The conceptual architecture presented here advances beyond conventional sustainability discourse by emphasizing identity transformation as the core driver of systemic change. Throughout this work, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) adopts a methodological pluralism that integrates normative theory, qualitative case synthesis, systems mapping, and design-based research. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) believes that transformative scholarship must transcend disciplinary silos while maintaining analytical precision and empirical credibility. In alignment with international academic standards, this volume aspires to contribute to peer-reviewed discourse by offering indexable constructs, operational definitions, and actionable frameworks that can be evaluated, replicated, and refined within diverse institutional contexts. A central premise of this preface is that leadership education cannot remain detached from the ecological realities of the Anthropocene, and Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) therefore integrates planetary boundaries thinking into the normative foundations of curriculum design. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) emphasizes that students must not only acquire managerial competencies but also cultivate ecological literacy and moral courage. Such competencies, as conceptualized by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), include systems cognition, anticipatory governance, emotional intelligence, ethical reasoning, and collaborative innovation. The humanistic authority advanced in this book is not hierarchical dominance but moral credibility derived from coherence between values and action, and Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) underscores that regenerative leaders must embody the principles they advocate. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) recognizes that credibility in an era of institutional distrust requires transparency, humility, and dialogical engagement. Consequently, the learning ecosystems proposed herein prioritize reflective dialogue, community immersion, and experiential engagement as pathways toward embodied understanding. Digital transformation occupies a critical space within this

works.title: Scelo: A Private, Auditable Desktop Workbench for AI-Assisted Actuarial Analysis
works.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
works.abstract: Scelo is a downloadable, offline-first desktop workbench for actuaries who want AI-assisted analysis without sending client data to a cloud. This working paper documents the released v0.1.0 build: its design philosophy, system architecture, feature set, decision-support agent swarm, an Unreal Engine 5 catastrophe simulator, the AI provider layer, and the source-available licence. Modern actuarial work has inherited two frictions from the move to AI-assisted analysis. The first is custody: copying client mortality tables, claims triangles, or policy files into a hosted chat assistant exports regulated data to a third party. The second is opacity: a hosted model returns a number with no reproducible trail from the raw input to the figure that lands in a board pack. Scelo is built to remove both. It runs entirely on the actuary's own machine, bundles a Python and R runtime with the actuarial stack, and scopes AI co-pilots to each stage of the work so that assistance never requires sending data to a cloud. The soft → tools → hard pipeline Scelo organises every analysis as a one-way pipeline. Soft data (raw, fuzzy, uncommitted inputs) is focused by a tools layer of statistical and actuarial models into hard data (board-pack-ready numbers: defensible, reproducible, traceable). The pipeline is one-way by construction: soft data → tools → hard data Soft never writes to hard directly, hard never reads from soft, and the tools layer is the only path between them. Auditability is therefore a structural property rather than a discipline the analyst has to remember: if a number is hard, there is, by construction, a tool that produced it and a soft input it consumed. The product's own analogy: temperature is soft, a thermometer is the tool, 24 °C is hard. Architecture and features Two applications, one boundary. An Electron desktop shell (apps/scelo-ide) wraps a React renderer (apps/web). They meet at a single typed window.scelo surface, the only path the renderer has to the operating system. Bundled runtimes. A portable Python and R runtime ships with the actuarial stack (lifelib, chainladder, climada, statsmodels; ChainLadder, lifecontingencies, forecast, mgcv). A full workbench. Monaco editor, integrated terminal, git, ripgrep search, language servers for Python and R, data-aware viewers (CSV, Markdown, Jupyter), and a per-workspace AI panel. Chat-driven data cleaning with an explicit, reviewable plan, and a small formula language for deriving and transforming columns. A multi-engine model bench spanning reserving, mortality, pricing, climate, capital, pensions, life, and forecasting, which delegates to the canonical packages actuaries already trust rather than reimplementing them, and can export an entire pipeline as runnable Python, R, or C++. Bring-your-own-model AI. The default is a local language model; optional cloud providers are never on by default, and their keys live in the operating-system keychain. Decision-support swarm Scelo can convene a swarm of role-playing professional agents (for example, a finance lead, an investor, an accountant, an actuary, a psychologist, and a lawyer) to pressure-test a decision. The agents report; the actuary decides. The swarm shares a survival projection in which community wealth is treated multiplicatively across material, temporal, and relational capital: W = M × T × R The basis of the lab's nanoeconomics work. Recommended interventions can be applied and re-simulated, then propagated through a population simulation to macro outcomes such as workdays lost, output drag, excess mortality, and insurer claims. Scelo Atlas: world-scale catastrophe simulation A companion product line built on Unreal Engine 5 turns catastrophe modelling into something an actuary can both compute and see. A pure mathematics layer (parametric cyclone wind field, flood inundation, ground-motion attenuation) and a financial engine drive a multi-threaded Monte Carlo event-loss model over an exposure portfolio. It produces the standard catastrophe outputs: an exceedance-probability view, the average annual loss AAL = E[Lyear], a tail measure TVaR99%, and return-period losses read off at the corresponding annual probabilities (1% for the 1-in-100, 0.4% for the 1-in-250). Licensing Scelo ships under the Scelo IDE Source-Available Licence v1.1. Using the software is free, including for commercial use. A per-product royalty applies only once a product built with Scelo succeeds: the first ZAR 1,000,000 of a product's lifetime gross revenue is royalty-free, and a flat 3% applies to the excess. For a product with lifetime gross revenue G (in rand), the royalty owed over the life of that product is: R(G) = 0.03 × max(0, G − 1,000,000) So a product earning ZAR 2.5 M over its life owes 0.03 × 1,500,000 = ZAR 45,000, and a product that never clears the first million owes nothing. An unconditional carve-out keeps nanoeconomics-for-poverty work free without any revenue limit. Status This paper describes a real but early release: v0.1.0, pre-1.0. Public signed binaries await code-signing certificates, the Unreal Engine catastrophe simulator ships as an inspection scaffold not yet compiled against an engine install, and the hosted product at scelo.ai is still a placeholder. What is already true is the part that matters most to the profession it is built for: the data stays put, and the thinking stays in the open.

works.title: The Great God Brown
works.abstract: Seven years after the 1926 premiere of his “mask drama” The Great God Brown, Eugene O'Neill proudly recalled that the play had been “accepted and appreciated by both critics and public,” its presentational eccentricities notwithstanding (“Memoranda on Masks”). The Eugene O'Neill Foundation's production at the Museum of San Ramon Valley replicated this achievement in miniature. The latest entry in a series of staged readings, the play ran for three sold-out performances, each, I am told, enthusiastically received. Saturday night's audience was clearly familiar with O'Neill's work, no doubt aided by the Foundation's long-standing commitment to integrating Danville's most famous former resident into the cultural life of the community. Eavesdropping during the intermission and chatting post-performance assured me that attendees found the production enjoyable as well as challenging. Despite Brown's reputation for being recondite, one conversant remarked, this production “made sense.” On a makeshift stage flanked by a sampling of the museum's printed, painted, and taxidermic curiosities, The Great God Brown was “accepted and appreciated” once again, masks and all.The production succeeded in part because director Eric Fraisher Hayes, dramaturg William Davies King, and the Equity-heavy cast represented the play as a broad meditation on intimacy. In O'Neill's proximate Welded, two characters try to restore a romantic/erotic bond that time has obviously sundered. The characters in The Great God Brown are more numerous and the relational possibilities more genial to O'Neill's imagination. At the play's center is the dyad of the Apollonian Billy Brown and the Dionysian Dion Anthony, here played with impressive complementarity by Aaron Wilton and Willem Long, respectively. Dion dies near the end of act 2, his masked face ravaged by excess. Billy inherits Dion's mask, in effect becoming him, as Wilton reminds us by his spot-on imitations of the barking laughs and “goatish capers” that had characterized Long's turn. At play's end, Brown too dies, having been mistaken for the man he had become—that is, his own alleged murderer. The being-merger that Welded idealizes becomes in this production a sequence of imitations that simultaneously reference and resist intimacy. The Great God Brown is the more mature of these plays and the better one as well.Hayes recognizes the paradoxical complexity of the Billy/Dion relationship, the constituent characters of which are both antithetical and inseparable. Instead of stopping here, however, he uses Billy/Dion as a fluid point of contrast to the play's two circumambient relationships: Dion and the prostitute Cybel (Gwen Loeb), and Dion and Billy-as-Dion's wife, Margaret (Heather Gordon). Less skillfully handled, these relationships risk being adjunctive to a male/male melding that O'Neill accouters pretentiously in Nietzschean garb. Hayes has nudged O'Neill's play toward its own betterment, here as elsewhere. The foregrounding of these pairings allows Gordon and Loeb to manifest range, depth, and subtlety of a sort on which O'Neill does not insist in Margaret and arguably does not demand of Cybel, whom he seems at times to rescue from “whore with a heart of gold” status simply by adding “earth mother” to her job description.Gordon leavens Margaret's definitional maternalism with a wearily exasperated (and very 2019) recognition of the demands of making one's way in a world of man-children. By representing the teenaged Margaret's sexual response to Dion as seemly and as anxiously optimistic (see also Ah, Wilderness!), she makes kid-stuff canoodling a yearning promise of mature joy. This vow, for so it is, will be broken by Dion's self-hatred as surely as by Margaret's horror of Dion's unmasked face. The masks themselves—created by Bonnie DeChant, who also plays Billy's mother—facilitate the coalescence of these ill-fated strands: the masked Dion shares with the unmasked Margaret the evident pleasures of coition but struggles with the arguably more intimate enterprise of kissing, due of course to the prophylaxes, now his, now hers, now theirs. When Dion asks Margaret, “can Margaret still love Dion Anthony?,” Gordon added a pause to the “forced smile” for which O'Neill calls before dully signaling her assent. There's no “of course” here: confronted with two incomplete candidates for matrimony, Margaret had cast her lot with the child who had dazzled and impregnated her but whose childishness would ultimately become burdensome. Gordon captures the commonness and cost of Margaret's decision, thereby accenting the irony behind her do-over “marriage” to the militantly adult Billy, masked as Dion. Margaret initially conveys a purring satisfaction with her simulacral new bedmate, but Billy, by “becoming” Dion, can only replicate Dion's failure as a mature intimate. We never doubt this Margaret's love for Billy, but the extra measure of reticence that Gordon brings to the role helps us understand why her love finds its fullest expression after both Dion and Dion/Billy have died.In their work on Cybel, Hayes and company again decline to take the mother/whore bait that O'Neill dangles. Cybel is the only character who can endure the sensitivity of the unmasked Dion. O'Neill means Dion and Cybel to be friends, allied by a transcendence of desire more comfortably normative than that manifest in, for example, the Nina Leeds/Charles Marsden pairing in Strange Interlude. But O'Neill created a stage prostitute nonetheless, and Cybel's initial encounter with Dion practically dares an incautious actor or director to make her hardboiled in the manner of the “goils” of The Iceman Cometh. Prostitute meets wastrel in act 1 with a quasi-material concern for his well-being; then, momentarily misled by his donning of a “terribly ravaged” mask, she defaults to “whore” mode. Loeb relaxes these polarities by performing “whore” with a bootily bumping and grinding bit of shtick funnier still for following Cybel's twitting of Dion for preferring “ham fats” to conversation. But Loeb's Cybel soon becomes Dion's fellow aspirant to an unhammy intimacy. While the sureness of Loeb's movements and the skill with which she modulates vocal timbre, pitch, and intensity facilitated this transformation, the remarkable limpidity of her eyes completed it: no one in this ensemble unmasked more fully than she. Hayes put Loeb and Long close together and leaning toward each other their second scene, during which they play solitaire and enjoy relazed conversation. Loeb is talking about the performativity of her job, lamenting the ugly coexistence of a real “solitaire” and a phony coalescence. Long does his best to follow, but his sudden masking telegraphs confusion about her subtler vacillations between worldliness and need. This texturing makes their intimacy more credible—Cybel's attachment is a process, not a reflex—if less consistent with O'Neill's design. Here one is grateful for a director and an actor who respond to hints and potentialities rather than by squeezing too hard on the fragile bladder of intention.The rest of the cast acquitted itself ably. Noteworthy are two groupings that add brio and illustrate, wittily here if snobbishly in the script, the duller modes of interchangeability that O'Neill allowed those unblessed by verve. Valerie Weak, who doubles as Dion's mother, joins DeChant and Loeb in Dion's reedy trio of sons and in the committee that visits Billy to discuss his design for a new building. The committee-men's muffled huffing and puffing, and the shuffling of their feet, fared well with the audience. Tim Holt Jones and John Blytt, introduced as Billy's and Dion's fathers, respectively, returned as the mature Billy's Tweedledee and Tweedledum draftsman, nattering on about their boss with caustic restraint and commendable comic synchronicity.Hayes saved his boldest move for last. Recognizing (as dramaturg King told me) the repetitions in O'Neill's epilogue but mindful of the risks of ending the play with an easy if winning “dumb cop” joke (“Well, what's his name?” “Man!” “How d'yuh spell it?”), Hayes repositioned Margaret's requiem for Dion at play's end: “I will feel you stirring in your sleep, forever under my heart….” We now believe Gordon's professions of eternal intimacy as surely as we had believed her exasperation two acts earlier. A fellow patron declared the speech worthy of Mary Tyrone; I found its delivery worthy of Jessica Lange. His red-rimmed eyes were not unique in the room, nor were his earlier laughs and other indicators of approval. Maybe great theatre is a game of solitaire indulged in the genial company of players, variously construed, sometimes masked and sometimes not. Regardless, this was a magnificent production, satisfying in its own right and, incidentally, as a follow-up to the Hayes/O'Neill Foundation Hughie (2018), another successful exercise in enlightened hint-following.
