works.title: Commentary on: The lived experience of the stroke survivor–caregiver dyads during the transitional care from hospital to home with teletraining and telesupport educational program: a phenomenological study
works.abstract: This invited commentary refers to ‘The lived experience of the stroke survivor–caregiver dyads during the transitional care from hospital to home with teletraining and telesupport educational program: a phenomenological study’, by E. Lombardi et al. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurjcn/zvaf203 Stroke remains one of the leading causes of disability and dependency worldwide. The transition from hospital to home is a critical phase for both survivors and caregivers, characterized by anxiety, uncertainty, and unmet psychosocial needs. The article by Lombardi et al. explores this transitional experience through the lens of teletraining and telesupport led by nurse navigators.1 The study’s dyadic approach—addressing both the stroke survivor and caregiver—represents an important advancement in cardiovascular and neurorehabilitation nursing. Although dyadic perspectives are increasingly recognized as essential to comprehensive post-stroke care, they remain underexplored in qualitative research. The authors report findings from 14 survivor–caregiver dyads interviewed 1 month after discharge, identifying two main themes: the impact of transitional care on dyads and the fulfilment of dyadic needs through telehealth support. This commentary evaluates the scholarly and clinical contribution of the work, its methodological strengths, and the refinements that could enhance its scientific and practical impact in cardiovascular nursing. Lombardi et al. provide valuable insights into a nurse-led telehealth intervention that integrates predischarge teletraining with post-discharge telesupport. This aligns with contemporary priorities in European cardiovascular nursing—optimizing self-management, continuity of care, and caregiver engagement through digital means.1,2 By applying a dyadic perspective, the study supports emerging literature that highlights the interdependence of patient and caregiver emotional and behavioural adaptation in chronic and cardiovascular conditions.3 Crucially, the research extends the role of telehealth into transitional education, beyond rehabilitation outcomes, emphasizing how nurse navigators bridge hospital and community through tailored guidance. The findings indicate that teletraining improves preparedness and self-efficacy, while telesupport enhances confidence and psychosocial stability during the early home transition. The study demonstrates methodological integrity through the application of Cohen’s hermeneutic phenomenological framework and adherence to SRQR reporting standards. The use of reflective bracketing, investigator triangulation, and dual coding contributes to analytic credibility. Reflexive journaling reinforces transparency and researcher self-awareness, consistent with current expectations for qualitative rigour in cardiovascular nursing.4 The study’s novelty lies in three key contributions: (1) dyadic exploration of telehealth; (2) integration of teletraining and telesupport; and (3) operationalisation of nurse-navigator roles. These elements advance the discourse on digital nursing interventions and reinforce the central role of nurses in ensuring continuity of care across settings.5,6 Despite its strengths, certain methodological refinements would improve the paper’s applicability and clarity. First, the small, convenience-based sample (14 dyads) limits generalisability. Future studies should purposefully include participants with diverse socioeconomic and technological profiles to address potential inequities in digital access and literacy. Second, the study would benefit from a clearer description of standard discharge and follow-up care procedures in participating hospitals, allowing readers to evaluate the incremental benefits of teletraining and telesupport. Third, the discussion should more explicitly address disparities in access to devices, internet, and digital literacy, especially among older adults or low-income populations. Evidence shows that digital inequity remains a significant challenge in cardiovascular care.7 Finally, reflexivity on researchers’ clinical roles and more illustrative participant quotations would enhance thematic transparency. Clinically, this study provides actionable lessons for cardiovascular nurses. Integrating teletraining and telesupport supports dyadic adaptation by enhancing preparedness, reducing anxiety, and fostering trust through the nurse-navigator role. The model reinforces relationship-centred care and the value of structured, technology-assisted follow-up. Developing a logic model or implementation checklist could support replication. Research priorities include longitudinal mixed-methods studies to assess sustained dyadic outcomes, comparative evaluations for cost-effectiveness, and broader inclusion of diverse populations to inform equitable care design. Lombardi et al.’s phenomenological study makes a significant contribution to understanding transitional care in stroke and cardiovascular nursing. It highlights the power of nurse-led telehealth to enhance continuity, relational support, and dyadic well-being during recovery. With minor revisions to improve contextual clarity, reflexivity, and equity considerations, this manuscript deserves publication in the European Journal of Cardiovascular Nursing as a model for integrating telehealth and nurse navigation in post-stroke care. Agussalim Agussalim (PhD (Conceptualization [lead]; Data curation [lead]; Formal analysis [lead]; Funding acquisition [lead]; Investigation [lead]; Methodology [lead]; Supervision [lead]; Validation [lead]; Visualization [lead])), and Citrawati Citrawati (Resources [lead]; Writing—original draft [lead]; Writing—review & editing [lead]) There is no funding related to this study. This commentary does not contain new data.

works.title: Livestock futures: worldviews, values, and the framing of sustainability pathways
works.abstract: The livestock sector both drives and faces complex sustainability challenges associated with the production and consumption of animal-sourced foods, highlighting the need for system-wide transformation. Despite mounting evidence of impacts, political inertia and conflicting interpretations of sustainability have polarised debate and fragmented action, constraining how future pathways are imagined and pursued. This thesis examines how diverse perspectives shape understandings of sustainable livestock futures, linking research on worldviews, values and framing to show how future pathways are constructed, legitimised and contested. The first study explores how environmental worldviews, values and demographics shape perspectives on the future of the livestock sector. Using mixed methods, it combines survey and interview data from 307 livestock representatives. Results reveal statistically significant variation in preferred sustainability pathways. Respondents with higher pro-environmental, ecocentric and relational worldviews and values favour behaviour-oriented solutions, while those with lower pro-environmental and higher techno-centric orientations prefer technological innovations to improve efficiency and maintain current consumption patterns. Results also highlight the need to recognise cultural and geographic nuance, as well as the gap between preferred and expected futures. This study advances understanding of how perspectives on livestock futures are formed, supporting the development of more holistic and pluralistic approaches to sustainable livestock futures. The second study analyses academic discourse on sustainable livestock futures using topic modelling and framing analysis to identify thematic trends and regional distributions in global research. This approach offers a replicable way to navigate complex and contested debates. The analysis shows that literature remains dominated by techno-scientific and economic framings focused on emissions reduction, environmental management, productivity and efficiency. Such framings narrow interpretations of sustainability, often neglecting equity, justice and demand-side considerations. The study also highlights the strong influence of the US, UK and China, as well as certain funding bodies and journals that reinforce dominant narratives. Alternative framings and regionally tailored approaches remain underexplored and underfunded, revealing a structural imbalance in research priorities. The study calls for more inclusive and systemic approaches to better reflect the complexity of livestock transitions. The third study focuses on the UK livestock sector, which faces a distinctive mix of socio-economic, political and environmental challenges. Addressing these complexities requires tools that help explore future pathways and understand the trade-offs they involve. The study develops the UK Livestock Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (UK-Livestock-SSPs) through an iterative, co-design process adapting the SSP framework to UK livestock contexts. Engaging actors from industry, policy, academia and civil society, the study produces five pathways supported by narratives, visual summaries and semi-quantitative trends that capture sector-specific dynamics. These pathways highlight the governance, societal and production drivers underpinning the range of plausible futures, uncertainties and trade-offs facing the sector. Visual and interactive methods enhanced engagement and reflection on values and priorities. The outputs provide a flexible framework for exploring alternative futures, with potential to inform future policy and research and to support integration into modelling frameworks to assess vulnerabilities and resilience strategies. The fourth study examines how collective action frames and framing processes shape the construction, contestation and negotiation of meaning within two participatory co-design workshops for the UK-Livestock-SSPs, drawing on observational notes and post-workshop reflections. The results show that participants expressed a wide range of diagnostic and prognostic frames across social, economic, political and sustainability concerns, along with motivational frames linked to responsibility, pride, justice, collective agency and economic survival. The study also presents examples of frame amplification, contestation, alignment and reframing, highlighting both emerging shared priorities and tensions in visions of change. Overall, the study demonstrates the value of examining framing processes in participatory scenario co-design, showing how awareness of these interactional dynamics can deepen understanding of collective meaning-making and reveal how participation can both open up and constrain which futures gain legitimacy. These studies provide an integrated understanding of how worldviews, values and framing shape perceptions of, and pathways towards, sustainable livestock futures. By moving across scales from individual perspectives and global academic discourses to sectoral scenario co-design and interactional framing dynamics, the thesis offers empirical evidence that livestock futures are inherently contested and value-laden, and that dominant framings can narrow the perceived problem-solution space. The thesis advances conceptual and methodological innovation by integrating worldviews, values, framing and futures thinking within a mixed-methods design, showing how sustainability problems and pathways are negotiated in practice. Overall, the research highlights the importance of holistic and pluralistic, framing‑aware approaches, with participatory, values‑led, and imaginative futures‑oriented methods helping to surface assumptions and widen the range of pathways considered.

works.title: Improving access to psilocybin-assisted therapy: barriers, challenges, and recommendations
works.abstract: Psilocybin-assisted therapy (PAT) is an emerging intervention that combines the administration of psilocybin with structured psychological support to address profound psychological, emotional, and existential distress. Central to this model is the recognition that many forms of suffering-particularly at end of life-are relational in nature and require relational forms of healing. It is our belief that the relational wounds that keep us from connection can really only be healed in relationship with other humans (Tsang et al., 2023b). This emphasis on relational healing lies at the core of PAT, a treatment model designed to address profound psychological distress through both pharmacological and human-centered care.Located in Nanaimo, British Columbia, Roots to Thrive is currently the only multidisciplinary non-profit healthcare practice in Canada legally offering group PAT. The program primarily serves individuals facing terminal illness, many of whom seek relief from the psychological symptoms that often accompany end-of-life diagnoses. Anxiety, depression, unresolved trauma, and existential distress can be as consequential as physical symptoms, significantly impacting treatment adherence, quality of life, and overall well-being (O'Malley et al., 2021). Among terminally ill patients, psychological distress is associated with decreased life satisfaction, withdrawal from meaningful relationships, increased suicidality, and even earlier death (Griffiths et al., 2016).Despite strong evidence supporting PAT's effectiveness, demand for this transformative therapy far exceeds accessibility. Canada's SAP is a regulatory mechanism that allows healthcare practitioners to request access to drugs that are not otherwise approved for sale when conventional treatments have failed, are unsuitable, or are unavailable. Under the SAP, psilocybin may be authorized on a case-by-case basis for patients with serious or life-threatening conditions, provided there is a clear medical rationale and appropriate clinical oversight.Between 2022 and late 2024, there were 471 total SAP applications submitted to access psilocybin or MDMA for therapeutic use in Canada. Of these, only about 318 were approved.Many individuals die before ever receiving relief. This advocacy piece highlights existing barriers and challenges for patients.The PAT program offered through Roots to Thrive consists of eight to ten small-group therapy sessions. One of these sessions includes the administration of psilocybin via oral route of administration (Dames et al., 2025). The remaining sessions focus on preparation, integration, and relational support delivered through a community-of-practice (CoP) model. In this body of work, a CoP is conceptualized as a structured, collaborative clinical model in which practitioners engaged in psychedelic-and ketamine-assisted therapies participate in ongoing collective learning, reflective practice, and shared clinical responsibility. This model is particularly well suited to novel and highly regulated therapeutic contexts, where clinical complexity and ethical considerations necessitate collective expertise and accountability. Although we do offer individual PAT, the group structure intentionally situates the psychedelic experience within a broader therapeutic and communal framework recognizing the group as part of the healing process rather than treating it as a standalone intervention.The program is facilitated by a multidisciplinary team that may include registered psychotherapists, nurses, physicians, and Indigenous Knowledge Keepers. All providers are trained through their respective colleges and also through specific psychedelic assisted therapy training programs in Canada (Dames et al., 2024). Central to the model are unconditional positive regard, emotional safety, and community-based healing. These relational elements are not ancillary; they are foundational to the therapeutic outcomes reported by participants.From a clinical standpoint, PAT has demonstrated remarkable efficacy and safety.Research shows that PAT produces rapid and sustained antidepressant effects among terminally ill individuals experiencing mood or anxiety disorders (Davis et al., 2020;Davis et al., 2021;Griffiths et al., 2016). Approximately 80% of end-stage cancer patients who receive PAT experience sustained clinical symptom improvement-outcomes that stand in stark contrast to conventional antidepressant treatments, which often perform little better than placebo in this population (Griffiths et al., 2016;Ostuzzi et al., 2015).Concerns about safety are frequently raised in policy discussions; however, psilocybin has a well-established safety profile. The Registry of Toxic Effects of Chemical Substances (RTECS) has assigned psilocybin a more favorable safety profile than aspirin (Griffiths et al., 2006). Importantly, PAT is not intended to replace antidepressants or psychotherapy outright.Instead, psilocybin is used as a catalyst to enhance therapeutic effectiveness for individuals who have not experienced relief through other interventions.Despite growing evidence and patient demand, access to PAT remains profoundly restricted. For individuals with a terminal diagnosis, the process of obtaining legal access is lengthy and burdensome. Patients must secure a referral from a physician or nurse practitioner, complete extensive medical intake assessments, apply to Health Canada's SAP, attend multiple education and integration sessions, and then wait for placement in a clinical trial or approved treatment cohort. For patients whose physical or cognitive capacity declines as their illness progresses, these delays can be devastating. As a result, the Roots to Thrive team spends countless hours advocating for expedited access on behalf of patients whose time is rapidly diminishing.Patients also reported significant emotional and logistical barriers. Many-particularly women-expressed fear of judgment when discussing PAT with their physicians. Others cited anxiety about long wait times, transportation challenges, financial strain, and the difficulty of coordinating PAT alongside complex treatment regimens for terminal illness.Geography further compounds these challenges. Because Health Canada has approved only a small number of PAT providers, most patients must either travel to Nanaimo for the full eight-to-ten-week program or attempt to coordinate care remotely with their primary provider physically present. For many, this is simply not feasible. As one patient, Thomas Hartle, explains, "I have to put chemotherapy on pause just to go out there. So I'm compromising my health, and I'm emptying my bank account." For individuals with limited mobility or those requiring assistance from a caregiver, travel is often impossible. Systemic inequities also disproportionately affect Black, Indigenous, and People of Colour (BIPOC). Data from the OurCare National Survey indicate that individuals who selfidentify as racialized are less likely to have a family doctor or nurse practitioner, limiting their ability to even initiate the SAP process (Kiran, 2022). Dr. Gail Peekeekoot, Medicine Administration Nursing Lead and Facilitator at Roots to Thrive, emphasizes that cultural traditions integral to psychedelic healing are often lost within the current medicalized framework. For Indigenous patients without access to legal providers who share their language, values, or cultural worldview, she explains, "We lose ceremony, we lose the sacred."Conventional palliative care teams-already stretched thin-often lack the resources to adequately address the psychological and existential distress experienced at end of life (O'Malley et al., 2021). Ironically, these are precisely the areas where PAT has shown the most promise. Despite growing clinical evidence and patient demand, access to PAT in Canada remains tightly restricted due to its classification as a Schedule III substance under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act. Legal access is primarily mediated through Health Canada's SAP, a pathway designed for exceptional circumstances but increasingly relied upon for routine compassionate use in palliative contexts (Government of Canada, 2020).Good healthcare should not be political. Currently, only physicians or nurse practitioners may apply to the SAP on a patient's behalf. The SAP application is an extensive eight-page document requiring clinicians to identify an approved manufacturer, justify psilocybin use with comprehensive clinical evidence, document all previous failed treatments, oversee clinical trial participation if applicable, remain physically present during the entire drug session, and submit detailed post-treatment reports (Notice to Stakeholders, 2022;2023). These requirements are unrealistic for most primary care providers and fail to recognize the expertise of non-physician practitioners already trained in PAT delivery. This step moves the governance and use of psilocybin from a medical decision to a parliamentary decision.In response to the volume of SAP applications submitted by Roots to Thrive, Health Canada requested in Fall 2022 that the organization transition entirely to a clinical trial framework. However, we argue that clinical trials are ill-suited to meet the urgent needs of patients who are terminally ill. Prioritizing expensive clinical trials researching new aspects of PAT should not be a barrier to treatment illnesses with sufficient evidence to already be known to benefit from PAT.In the meantime, many individuals who sought treatment have either died or continue to wait in distress for what they consider their last hope for relief. As world-renowned mycologist Paul Stamets notes, such regulatory delays raise serious ethical concerns, describing the approach as "not only academically naive, but immoral." While subjective, this critique reflects a broader ethical unease shared by clinicians working with dying patients.For the Roots to Thrive team, advocating for access to PAT has come at a significant emotional cost. Thousands of hours of unpaid clinician labor have been dedicated to navigating regulatory barriers, often only to receive delays or denials after patients have already passed away. "These people are dying. They are in distress," says Dr. Dames. "What if it was your mother or your child, or your life? Why wouldn't you want the best for them like this?" Physicians, nurses, facilitators, and Knowledge Keepers described profound moral and ethical distress as they watched patients deteriorate while awaiting approval. "We won't have treated anyone [with PAT] for an entire year because we've been trying to figure out how a nonprofit does a clinical trial in order to give people care while they're dying," one provider shared.Patients echoed this distress. Thomas waited 511 days for Health Canada to deny his reapplication for continued PAT access, noting, "I could get access to the MAID system in 73 hours." Reflecting on regulatory priorities, he added, "If you were looking at where Health Canada is placing their emphasis, it's 'end your life, rather than look for a better quality of life with the time you have left.'" These experiences directly contradict Health Canada's own SAP Guidance Document, which states that most requests are processed within one working day and that personalized support is provided for end-of-life cases-services none of the surveyed providers reported receiving (Special Access Program for Drugs, 2020).As access remains restricted, some patients turn to unregulated underground providers.Many of these practitioners lack adequate training, insurance, or oversight. Dr. Peekeekoot adds that stigma and legal barriers push individuals to self-administer psychedelic mushrooms in isolation, simply "hoping for the best" to ease their suffering.Where Do We Go From Here?As psychedelic-assisted therapies move closer to mainstream clinical acceptance, attention must shift from questions of efficacy to questions of access, equity, and implementation. Without regulatory reform, the public health benefits of PAT will remain inaccessible to those most likely to benefit. Although Health Canada has made incremental progress toward acknowledging PAT's role in palliative care, substantial reform is still required.In addition to existing efforts, the following steps could meaningfully reduce barriers to care:1. Establish a streamlined referral pathway allowing primary care providers to refer directly to approved and accredited PAT providers.2. Implement a unique dedicated SAP fast-track for end-of-life patients with guaranteed review timelines.3. Develop a formal provincial billing framework for PAT.4. Expand practitioner education on psychedelic-assisted therapies within medical and nursing curricula.5. Introduce public insurance coverage (e.g., medical services plan) for PAT in palliative and treatment-resistant contexts.6. Reform legislative frameworks to reflect current evidence and reduce stigma associated with psychedelic medicines.7. Mandate integration and family-inclusive support as standard components of PAT.8. Partner with non-profit organizations to deliver community-based models of care. 9. Support Indigenous-led psychedelic healing pathways grounded in cultural safety and sovereignty.10. Fund implementation research to establish standardized dosing, safety, and delivery guidelines.As Dr. Dames emphasizes, "We're all one medical team. We're all tired and really just trying to help the same people." For Thomas, the impact of PAT was profound. Reflecting on his experience, he shares, "It's the difference between actively living and actively dying. I wish other people would be able to experience that."

works.title: Cultural Narrative Destination Branding Theory
works.abstract: In an era defined by hyper-connectivity, algorithmic mediation, and global mobility, destinations compete not only for tourists but for meaning. Branding has evolved beyond logos, slogans, and visual identities; it has become a complex semiotic process through which places negotiate their position within global imagination. Yet, amid this intensifying competition, a fundamental question persists: who constructs the story of a destination, and on whose authority is that story legitimized? Cultural Narrative Destination Branding Theory (CNDBT) emerges as a critical response to this question. Developed through sustained and longitudinal research initiated in 2017 by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), this theoretical framework seeks to reposition destination branding within a culturally grounded and community-authored paradigm. Rather than perceiving branding as a purely managerial or promotional instrument, CNDBT conceptualizes it as a narrative architecture rooted in collective memory, symbolic identity, and socio-cultural continuity. Since 2017, YER’s research trajectory has engaged diverse tourism contexts, employing qualitative depth inquiry, participatory observation, stakeholder interviews, and interpretive policy analysis. Across these engagements, a recurring phenomenon became apparent: while destinations invest heavily in branding strategies, many struggle with representational coherence. Visual campaigns may achieve aesthetic appeal and international visibility, yet they sometimes lack cultural resonance within the communities they portray. This discrepancy reveals a structural tension between externally constructed brand images and internally lived identities. The central proposition of Cultural Narrative Destination Branding Theory is that destinations are not commodities to be packaged but living narratives to be articulated. Branding, within this framework, is understood as a dialogical process through which communities interpret and project their cultural identity. The theory argues that cultural narratives comprising myths, rituals, heritage practices, local histories, and collective aspirations constitute foundational branding capital. These narratives are not merely decorative storytelling devices; they are epistemic resources that confer authenticity, legitimacy, and differentiation. The novelty of CNDBT lies in its integration of cultural narrative analysis with destination branding governance. While existing literature has extensively examined brand equity, consumer perception, and marketing communication effectiveness, fewer studies have systematically embedded narrative sovereignty within branding architecture. CNDBT advances this discourse by asserting that sustainable brand strength derives from culturally endorsed narratives rather than externally imposed imagery. YER’s longitudinal research since 2017 demonstrates that destinations grounded in coherent cultural storytelling exhibit stronger relational credibility among visitors. When branding aligns with lived experience, communities develop ownership of tourism development, and visitors encounter narratives that resonate beyond superficial consumption. Conversely, when branding abstracts culture into marketable clichés, it risks eroding authenticity and weakening community trust. Cultural Narrative Destination Branding Theory therefore introduces a humanistic recalibration of branding practice. It positions communities as narrative custodians and emphasizes participatory co-creation as strategic imperative. Branding becomes an interpretive collaboration rather than unilateral projection. This shift redefines competitiveness: destinations differentiate themselves not merely through scenic attributes or infrastructure but through culturally anchored narratives that cannot be replicated elsewhere. The timing of this theoretical articulation is significant. Global tourism is increasingly shaped by digital storytelling ecosystems, user-generated content, and influencer-driven visibility. Within such environments, narratives circulate rapidly, often detached from contextual nuance. CNDBT argues that digital acceleration heightens the necessity of narrative coherence. Communities must actively participate in shaping digital representations to preserve cultural integrity. By synthesizing insights from branding theory, cultural sociology, and participatory governance studies, Cultural Narrative Destination Branding Theory contributes a structurally integrated framework for sustainable destination development. It aligns strategic branding innovation with ethical responsibility and cultural continuity. This opening invites scholars, policymakers, and practitioners to reconsider the foundations of destination branding. Since 2017, Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER) has pursued this research with the conviction that branding is not simply about attracting visitors; it is about articulating identity with dignity. In embracing cultural narrative as strategic capital, destinations can transcend commodification and cultivate enduring relational legitimacy within the global tourism landscape. The evolution of destination branding in the twenty-first century has unfolded within a landscape shaped by digital acceleration, intensifying global competition, and increasingly sophisticated marketing technologies. Destinations across continents invest substantial resources in constructing distinctive identities, aiming to secure visibility within crowded international markets. Branding strategies are designed through analytical segmentation, consumer psychology modeling, and digital performance metrics. Logos are refined, slogans are optimized, and multimedia campaigns are orchestrated with precision. Yet beneath this strategic sophistication lies a fundamental inquiry that continues to demand deeper scholarly attention: whose story is being told when a destination is branded? And more importantly, who possesses the authority to narrate it? Cultural Narrative Destination Branding Theory (CNDBT), developed through sustained research initiated in 2017 by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad (YER), emerges as a comprehensive response to this question. This book does not merely propose a refinement of branding techniques; it introduces a structural recalibration of how destination identity is conceptualized, governed, and communicated. The foundation of CNDBT rests upon a simple yet transformative premise: destinations are not commodities awaiting aesthetic packaging. They are living cultural narratives shaped by collective memory, symbolic systems, rituals, aspirations, and intergenerational continuity. Branding, therefore, must move beyond graphic design and promotional messaging toward narrative architecture grounded in humanistic authority. The intellectual genesis of this theory did not arise from abstract speculation but from longitudinal engagement with tourism communities beginning in 2017. Over several years, YER conducted iterative qualitative investigations across diverse destinations, employing ethnographic immersion, participatory observation, stakeholder interviews, focus group dialogues, and interpretive policy analysis. Early observations revealed a recurring disjunction between externally crafted branding narratives and internally experienced cultural realities. Destinations often showcased visually compelling campaigns designed by professional consultants, yet community members expressed ambivalence or even detachment from these representations. In certain contexts, cultural symbols were stylized to align with global aesthetic trends; in others, historical narratives were simplified to enhance marketability. While such branding strategies occasionally generated short-term visibility, they did not consistently cultivate long-term relational legitimacy. Communities sometimes perceived themselves as objects of branding rather than subjects of storytelling. This tension illuminated a theoretical gap within destination branding scholarship: the insufficient integration of narrative sovereignty into branding governance structures. Through sustained dialogue with community leaders, youth representatives, artisans, policymakers, and tourism entrepreneurs, YER’s research identified a critical insight. Authentic branding cannot be imposed; it must be co-authored. The durability of a destination brand depends not solely on external perception but on internal recognition. This realization became the cornerstone of Cultural Narrative Destination Branding Theory. The principal theoretical innovation of CNDBT lies in its articulation of humanistic authority. Humanistic authority recognizes communities as epistemic agents who possess legitimate interpretive power over their own cultural representation. In conventional branding paradigms, authority is often centralized within marketing institutions or external consultants. Strategic decisions are guided by consumer research, market analytics, and competitive benchmarking. While such tools remain valuable, they risk marginalizing community voice if not balanced with participatory structures. Humanistic authority reframes this dynamic. It posits that narrative legitimacy derives from community endorsement. Branding decisions must therefore be embedded within governance mechanisms that facilitate inclusive dialogue and collaborative interpretation. This concept operates across three interdependent dimensions: 1. Narrative Legitimacy – Communities retain the primary right to define the symbolic meanings associated with their cultural identity. 2. Participatory Governance – Branding processes institutionalize co-creation mechanisms that integrate local voices into strategic planning. 3. Ethical Accountability – Representations are evaluated not only for market effectiveness but for cultural integrity and social dignity. works.title: Retention Strategies for Millennials in the Indian Startup Ecosystem: A Strategic Framework
works.abstract: Abstract The Indian startup ecosystem has witnessed unprecedented growth, positioning India as one of the world's largest and most vibrant hubs for entrepreneurial ventures. However, this rapid expansion has brought the challenge of talent retention to the forefront of organizational strategy. Millennials, who now constitute the primary demographic of the Indian workforce, possess distinct expectations regarding professional development, work-life integration, and organizational values that diverge significantly from traditional employment models. When these expectations remain unmet, Indian startups experience high turnover rates, resulting in substantial financial loss, erosion of intellectual capital, and hampered innovation cycles. This study synthesizes empirical research to examine the complex determinants of millennial retention and proposes a strategic framework—centered on Personalized Employee Experience (PEX)—to foster long-term loyalty, cultural alignment, and organizational health within the unique, high-velocity Indian market. This expanded version further explores the role of data-driven HR analytics, the nuances of the evolving psychological contract, the socio-cultural pressures unique to the Indian urban landscape, and the strategic importance of building an "employer brand" that resonates with the modern, purpose-driven workforce. Keywords:Millennials, Indian Startups, Employee Retention, Talent Management, Organizational Culture, Job Satisfaction, PEX, Psychological Contract, HR Analytics, Workforce Diversity, Gig-Economy, Employer Branding 1. Introduction: The High-Stakes Talent Landscape The Indian startup landscape is defined by its high-pressure, resource-constrained, and hyper-competitive nature. In major tech corridors like Bengaluru, Gurugram, Hyderabad, and Pune, the "war for talent" is intense, with established multinational corporations (MNCs) and well-funded unicorns vying for the same pool of skilled professionals. For a startup, the cost of losing a key employee involves not just the immediate replacement expense—often estimated at 1.5 to 2 times the annual salary of the departing individual—but also the loss of institutional memory, the disruption of team morale, and the stalling of critical project momentum. Millennials in India are unique in their desire for autonomy, impact, and purposeful work. Unlike previous generations that may have prioritized long-term job security and steady, predictable progression, the millennial cohort is often motivated by rapid skill acquisition, the ability to contribute to a larger mission, and the flexibility to manage personal lives alongside professional growth. As startups operate in environments of extreme uncertainty and frequent pivots, aligning these intrinsic motivators with the startup’s volatile growth trajectory is the ultimate challenge for founders and HR leaders. Furthermore, the post-pandemic shifts in professional expectations have accelerated the demand for "human-centric" workplaces. The "psychological contract"—the set of unwritten, mutual expectations between an employee and their employer—has become the invisible adhesive holding these high-stakes organizations together. The objective of this paper is to unpack these dynamics and provide an actionable framework for modern founders. 2. Factors Influencing Millennial Retention The retention of millennial talent in India relies on a delicate balance of tangible rewards and intangible cultural drivers. Table 1: Factors Influencing Millennial Retention Factor Description Impact on Retention Career Development Access to mentorship, rapid promotion cycles, and upskilling opportunities. High: Reduces stagnation and builds long-term commitment. Work-Life Balance Flexibility in work hours, remote options, and outcome-based performance. High: Essential for preventing burnout in high-pressure environments. Work Environment Supportive peer networks, psychological safety, and flat hierarchies. Medium: Influences daily job satisfaction and cultural alignment. Compensation Competitive base pay, performance bonuses, and ESOPs (Stock Options). High: Essential for talent acquisition, though secondary to growth in the long run. Purpose Aligning the company’s vision with social or personal values. Medium: Drives deeper engagement and discretionary effort. The Evolving Psychological Contract Beyond tangible benefits, the "psychological contract" is a powerful driver of retention. Millennials view their employment as a partnership. When a startup promises a culture of innovation but enforces rigid, legacy-style reporting structures, the resulting dissonance leads to swift disengagement. Retention, therefore, depends on the transparent communication of expectations from Day 1. Every missed promotion promise or failure to provide promised autonomy acts as a significant withdrawal from the "trust bank," leading to "quiet quitting" or resignation. The Role of Compensation and Wealth Creation In the Indian context, while initial base salary is critical for survival, long-term retention is increasingly driven by the "wealth creation" narrative. Startups that effectively educate employees on the potential value of their equity—treating them as co-owners—create a sense of long-term alignment that cash-heavy MNCs often struggle to replicate. 3. Strategic Retention Framework: The Personalized Employee Experience (PEX) To thrive, Indian startups must pivot toward a Personalized Employee Experience (PEX). This model moves away from "one-size-fits-all" HR policies. Fig.1: Strategic Retention Framework: The Personalized Employee Experience (PEX) Implementation of PEX Individualized Growth Maps: Startups should implement bi-annual career mapping. This collaborative exercise ensures that the employee sees a clear, tangible path for personal advancement within the organization, rather than feeling they must leave to secure the next step in their career. Flexible Work Ecosystems: In the Indian urban context, where infrastructure challenges like heavy traffic often contribute to exhaustion, PEX-driven startups prioritize output—measured by quality and milestones reached—over the physical duration spent at a desk. Leadership Feedback Loops: Traditional hierarchies often create a high "power distance." Startups must establish informal, frequent, and safe channels for bottom-up communication, such as "Skip-level" meetings and anonymous pulse surveys. 4. The Role of HR Analytics in Retention Modern retention strategy is increasingly data-driven. Startups must leverage HR analytics to move from reactive to predictive retention management. Churn Prediction Modeling: Analyzing attendance patterns, engagement scores, and performance metrics to identify employees at risk. Sentiment Analysis: Using AI-driven surveys to track the "mood" of the organization in real-time. The "Stay" Interview: Proactively asking high-potential employees what keeps them engaged, rather than waiting for an exit interview to discover the issues. 5. Challenges in the Indian Context Startups frequently struggle with the "instability trap" and the "global talent marketplace." Indian millennials benchmark their benefits against MNCs. Additionally, the cultural tendency towards parental approval for stable careers creates friction for those choosing the riskier startup path. Startups must build an "employer brand" that resonates with the individual’s social circle, highlighting the long-term potential of equity and the unique skill set acquired through entrepreneurial ventures. 6. Recommendations for Startup Leaders Adopt Transformational Leadership: Shift from being "managers" to "leaders." Integrate Sustainability and Ethics: Implementing Green Human Resource Management (GHRM). Formalize Feedback Mechanisms: Move toward structured, yet low-bureaucracy, feedback cycles. Build Community: Treat the workplace as a community through knowledge-sharing and peer-mentoring. Leverage Data for Retention: Treat retention metrics with the same rigor as product-market fit metrics. Focus on Holistic Wellbeing: Offer access to mental health resources, acknowledging that burnout is a significant risk in the "always-on" startup culture. Conclusion The retention of millennial talent in India is a strategic business imperative. By shifting the focus from transactional employment to a relational, personalized experience, founders can build organizations that are not only high-performing but also resilient. The future belongs to organizations that treat talent as their most valuable product. References Ghani, B., et al. (2022).
