works.title: From Levels to Mechanisms: How Stigma and Racism Produce PrEP Non-Adoption Among Black Immigrants in High-Income Countries — A Best-Fit Framework Synthesis
works.abstract: 1. Background and rationale 1.1 The problem Black immigrants and migrants of African and Caribbean origin living in high-income countries (HICs) experience a disproportionate burden of HIV relative to the general population, even as the absolute number of new infections in these countries declines. HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a highly effective biomedical prevention tool, yet its adoption among Black immigrant and diaspora communities remains low and inequitable across the prevention cascade, from awareness and willingness through access, uptake, and persistence. Closing this gap is central to HIV equity goals in Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and continental Europe, where these populations are growing and are frequently underserved by prevention services that were not designed with their experiences in mind. The reasons for low PrEP adoption in this population are not reducible to access or information. A recurring set of psychosocial barriers, namely stigma, shame, social isolation, discrimination, and low risk perception, appears across the qualitative literature. These barriers are typically reported as a list of discrete obstacles rather than analyzed as an interacting system, which limits the ability of the field to explain why barriers persist and how they might be addressed in sequence. 1.2 The state of the evidence and the conceptual gap Research on PrEP among Black and immigrant populations in high-income countries is dominated by the socio-ecological model and related multilevel frameworks, which sort determinants by location (i.e., individual, interpersonal, institutional, community, and policy). This level-based mapping is valuable and necessary. It establishes the breadth of the evidence base, identifies where intervention targets sit, and makes visible the structural determinants that individual-focused accounts obscure. It is not designed, however, to explain the mechanisms that link determinants to one another, or the directional and self-reinforcing relationships among them. A review that records stigma at the community level and low risk perception at the individual level establishes that both are present; it does not establish whether, or by what process, the first produces the second. Two conceptual consequences follow. First, the affective dimension of these barriers (shame) and the enacted and structural dimensions of racism (discrimination) are theorized thinly relative to the descriptive attention they receive. Whether they are also reported thinly in the primary qualitative literature is an open empirical question that this synthesis will test rather than assume. A low yield on either construct could reflect a genuine gap in the evidence base, or it could reflect the difficulty of separating shame from stigma, and anticipated from enacted discrimination, within participant accounts in which these are narrated as one interwoven experience. The synthesis is designed to distinguish these two possibilities and reports the distinction as a finding (Sections 3.8 and 3.9). Second, low risk perception is routinely treated as an information deficit that can be corrected through education. If it is instead, at least in part, a defended cognition, that is, a motivated distancing from a category understood to be stigmatized, discredited, or racialized, then educational intervention alone will not shift it, and the dominant intervention logic in the field is misspecified at the level of mechanism rather than at the level of delivery. This synthesis therefore departs from the level-based tradition by treating the constructs as an interlocking psychosocial process that operates within, and is produced by, structural conditions. The aim is mechanistic and relational rather than locational: to explain how the constructs generate and reinforce one another, and how they converge to suppress PrEP adoption across the prevention cascade. 1.3 A priori conceptual framework The synthesis is guided by an a priori conceptual model (Figure 1, reproduced separately and deposited with the registration) that specifies two co-constitutive generative roots rather than one. Racism (structural, institutional, and interpersonal, and in high-income settings inseparable from migration governance) and intersectional HIV and PrEP stigma are treated as mutually reinforcing rather than hierarchically ordered. This is a deliberate departure from models that position discrimination as a downstream, enacted expression of stigma. Structural racism and immigration regimes are prior to, and operate independently of, PrEP-specific stigma. They determine who is eligible for reimbursed PrEP, whose risk is recognised in clinical guidelines and funding criteria, to whom PrEP is offered in routine care, and which populations appear in prevention messaging and in trials. To subsume them under stigma would be to render racism as a psychological process experienced by individuals rather than as a structural condition that produces differential exposure. This protocol does not adopt that position. Three registers are specified from these two roots: • An affective register (shame): the internalization of stigma as moral self-threat, bound up with respectability, religious framings of sexuality, and gendered expectations of sexual conduct. • A relational register (social isolation): concealment, anticipated exclusion, and withdrawal from the family, faith, partner, and diaspora networks that might otherwise normalize PrEP. • A cognitive register (low risk perception): understood in part as defensive distancing from a stigmatized category, and not solely as the absence of information. Discrimination is retained as a construct in the coding frame, but as a root-level condition with registers of its own: anticipated discrimination and mistrust, enacted interpersonal discrimination, institutional discrimination including racialized medical mistrust, and structural or legal exclusion. These registers are coded separately so that the synthesis can distinguish racism that is experienced from racism that is built into service design and eligibility criteria. The registers converge on non-adoption across the PrEP cascade. Non-adoption in turn sustains community-level stigma and confirms the structural presumption that PrEP is "not for" this population, closing a self-perpetuating cycle. The model is therefore explicitly circular, and the synthesis will test whether the evidence supports the return path as well as the forward pathways. The framework draws on stigma theory (Link and Phelan), the enacted, anticipated, and internalized distinction of the HIV Stigma Framework (Earnshaw and Chaudoir), minority stress theory (Meyer), intersectionality and intersectional stigma scholarship (Crenshaw; Bowleg; Turan and colleagues), scholarship on structural racism and health (Bailey and colleagues), and the literature on PrEP-specific stigma (Calabrese and Underhill; Hartmann and colleagues). Status of the model. This model supplies the deductive coding frame for the synthesis. It is treated as provisional. Best-fit framework synthesis is designed to test, extend, and revise an a priori framework against the evidence rather than to confirm it. The team commits in advance to reporting the revised model in full, even where it departs from, qualifies, or contradicts the model registered here, and to reporting which a priori constructs the evidence failed to support. 1.4 Rationale for best-fit framework synthesis Best-fit framework synthesis (Carroll and colleagues) is well suited to a field that already possesses candidate constructs but lacks an integrative, mechanism-level account. It begins from an a priori framework, codes study findings against it deductively, and then uses inductive thematic analysis to capture and theorize what the framework does not accommodate, yielding a revised framework as its principal output. This makes the method directly compatible with the twin aims of the review, which are to characterize how each construct operates and to articulate the relationships among them. It is also the reason that a further descriptive review would not answer the question. A second mapping exercise would re-describe determinants that are already documented, whereas framework synthesis subjects an explicit account of process to disconfirmation and produces a model that can be tested, applied to intervention sequencing, and rejected. The requirement of the method to report framework failure, that is, content that the a priori model cannot accommodate, is what protects the synthesis from confirming its own starting assumptions. 1.5 Relationship to prior work by the review team The lead author of the present synthesis (TN) was lead author of a prior review of barriers and facilitators to PrEP adoption among Black immigrants in high-income countries, which mapped determinants across socio-ecological levels using scoping review methodology (Nyoni and colleagues, under review). That earlier review is the immediate antecedent of this work. Its relationship to the present synthesis is declared here in full so that the distinction between the two is a matter of record rather than of subsequent inference. Overlap in personnel. Three members of the present review team (TN, DF, and DHS) are authors of the earlier review. Two members (CS and BHH) are not, and were not involved in its design, conduct, or interpretation. To limit the risk that the present synthesis simply reproduces the interpretive commitments of the earlier work, CS and BHH are assigned as the adjudicating reviewers for all decisions that bear on whether the a priori framework fails against the evidence, namely the promotion of inductive themes, the specification of the revised model, and the CERQual coherence judgements. The a priori conceptual framework was specified before the present review team was constituted (Section 3.12). Overlap in corpus. The corpus for the pres

works.title: Dancing Toward Freedom
works.venue: GLQ A Journal of Lesbian and Gay Studies
works.abstract: Kwaito, a hybrid genre of music formalized in South Africa that draws on marabi, kwela, and mbaqanga as well as more explicitly international genres of house, hip hop, and R&B, emerged from practices of remixing that became popular in the 1980s and took the national and at times international stage in the 1990s. While kwaito is often derided as an apolitical, consumerist genre, embraced by a generation seeking to escape the traumatic histories of struggle for freedom in South Africa, it importantly took shape coterminously with the political uprisings that brought about the fall of the white supremacist apartheid project and the turmoil of establishing and contesting a post-apartheid reality. In Kwaito Bodies: Remastering Space and Subjectivity in Post-Apartheid South Africa, Xavier Livermon mines these very politics and shows how they offer resources for realizing liberation beyond neoliberal and capitalist inclusion currently shaping post-apartheid South Africa.Livermon makes an important contribution to existing studies of kwaito by paying particular attention to embodiment and how the form elicits certain kinds of performances from certain kinds of bodies, what he names “kwaito bodies.” Performance's indeterminacy and multivalence allow Livermon to take stock of kwaito's political implications far beyond analysis of form or genre, to understand how the hybrid cultural production of/by kwaito exceeds spatial divides (from apartheid segregation to national borders to Afrodiasporic circulations), identity categories, and contemporary and historical political economic formations. In attending to a range of performances from dance duo Tofo Tofo's appearance in Beyoncé’s “Run the World (Girls)” music video to the hypermasculine tsotsi (thug) figure, from the licentious “dangerous woman” diva to his own dancing body at various parties and festivals, Livermon addresses a scope of contradictory, shifting, and misrecognized political tactics that articulate radical self- and world-making possibilities.The first half of Kwaito Bodies establishes the text's foundational frames of analysis, namely “remastery,” “Afrodiasporic Space,” and critical consumptive practices. In the introduction, Livermon considers the musical terminology of “remaster,” refining a piece of music through distilling existing elements, not adding new elements or rearranging those elements. In his theoretical configuration, remastery is used to index how the post-apartheid transition smooths out and replicates existing colonial, neoliberal, and heteropatriarchal logics of what freedom looks like and who can participate in, shape, or lay claim to such freedoms. In this way, remastery contributes a sound studies framework to critiques of the multiple afterlives of colonial and racial capitalist formations. Livermon connects these debates to the neoliberal capitalist roots of South Africa's post-apartheid transition and its consequential struggles to realize class and gender equity specifically. Livermon then uses the syllabic form of “re-mastery,” as in to fashion a new master, to chart the ways kwaito performances remake notions of freedom, centering Black femme, queer, and poor practices of seizing liberation within the confines of continued oppression.Chapters 1 and 2 extend Livermon's contributions to Black feminist and queer of color theorizations of racialized gender and sexuality by tracing how kwaito traffics in Afrodiasporic Space, rethinking the formation of the national body through transnational Black queer and femme subjectivities and performances. Kwaito, with its notoriously hybrid influences, accentuates Afrodiasporic Space, which brings together two bodies of diaspora studies: that which centers African experiences as always already synchronous products of transnational migrations, encounters, and circulations and Avtar Brah's notion of “Diaspora Space,” which thinks of diaspora as a relational space not only of those who have been displaced, but between the displaced and those “who are constructed and represented as indigenous” (30). Livermon reads Beyoncé’s “Run the World (Girls),” the South African group Boom Shaka's controversially sexualized performance of the national anthem, and his own travels through multiple night clubs and neighborhoods in Johannesburg to show how kwaito embodies an Afrodiasporic understanding of space that rewrites the nation, imagining other spatial formations of freedom that exceed national borders and histories of forced displacement within and beyond South Africa and the African continent.In chapter 3, Livermon homes in on the dismissal of kwaito as a culture of apolitical materialism, complicating reductive analyses of consumption as mere capitalist capitulation, by noting how consumption can be a practice of self-making, particularly for those who have been violently excluded from such practices. Livermon focuses on excessive self-comportments at kwaito festivals as well as the performance of izikhothane (those who show off) battles, in which groups of young Black men spar using the latest dance moves and boastful freestyles accompanied by the display and destruction of expensive commodities. Livermon connects izikhothane to histories of performative excess in Black South African communities and to performances of “ghetto fabulosity” across Afrodiasporic Space as a marker of critical practices of Black consumption. Ultimately, kwaito's culture of excess and consumption present opportunities for youth to remaster their subjectivity to one critically engaged with the proliferation of a capitalist market in the parameters of what their freedom can and is supposed to look like.Chapters 4–6 consider gendered and classed performances of kwaito, articulating a remastery of freedom away from the persistence of heteropatriarchy within post-apartheid liberation. Chapter 4 approaches kwaito icon Lebo Mathosa, who crafts a persona that Livermon calls the “dangerous woman”—a disidentification with both the hypersexualization of Black women and the “cult of femininity” (126). Mathosa's indeterminate performances also allow her to be taken up queerly by kwaito bodies performing to her music on the dance floor, in drag personifications, and Mathosa's own “shapeshifting” sexuality. Chapter 5 centers another kwaito celebrity, Mandoza, whose performance of the “focused thug” rescripts national and diasporic narratives of the tsotsi (thug) used to condemn and coerce Black masculinities into productive and heteropatriarchal relationships with capital through the Black bourgeoisie. Mandoza's contradictory and mobile masculinities likewise open up strategies for queer masculinities beyond a gay/straight binary in townships.Chapter 6 looks at the expansive career of the popular duo Mafikizolo as well as quotidian performances of Youth Day parties that memorialize the 1976 Soweto student uprising—a key turning point in the struggle against apartheid. Livermon looks at how kwaito's promiscuous citationality pushes boundaries that allow Mafikizolo to blur multiple gender performances, temporalities, and traditions in their music videos, thus queering romanticized notions of the past. Likewise, present-day revelers at Youth Day parties queer the memory of that day by shifting conventional post-apartheid memorial practices from an emphasis on Black death, struggle, and oppression to practices of joy, celebration, and excess. In queering the nation's mobilizations of the past to at times conservative ends, these case studies reveal how kwaito has facilitated not only the remastery of space and subjectivity, but the remastery of the tempo of history.Each of these case studies, threaded through Livermon's own Black queer dancing body, ground the assertion that kwaito has not only been influential in shaping future visions of freedom within South Africa, but has done so in a way that “empowers the centrality of the erotic, of women's bodies, of transnational imaginaries in the construction of the post-apartheid polity” (153), remastering affiliations with the state to imagine and enact more complex and nuanced choreographies toward liberation.

works.title: Can social robots improve the hospital experience of children?
works.abstract: Child hospitalization constitutes a critical event that frequently disrupts the daily lives of children and their families (Chang et al., 2023). Beyond the biomedical dimension, hospital admission processes generate ruptures in routines, social bonds, and play experiences, which can increase the psychological and educational vulnerability of pediatric patients. This situation is linked to a broader challenge: how to ensure that assistive technologies also respond to the emotional needs that arise in hospital environments (González-González et al., 2021).In this context, social robots have emerged as a visible and rapidly developing branch of assistive technology in pediatric settings. These systems are understood as physically embodied interactive technologies designed to engage users through social behaviors such as communication, emotional expression, or relational interaction, distinguishing them from purely digital applications or passive entertainment devices (Park and Whang, 2022). In recent years, advances in social robotics and supportive technological environments have enabled the incorporation of tools that, without replacing healthcare personnel, complement care through interventions aimed at improving the hospital experience. As these technologies expand across clinical and research contexts, questions remain regarding their scope, intended use, and evaluation. Should they be conceived only as devices for entertainment or distraction, or can they be consolidated as instruments that strengthen children's emotional resilience and expand the care capacity of the hospital system?As in other areas of disability and rehabilitation research, where the importance of combining objective and subjective measures to capture patients' lived experience is debated (Moradi and Møller-Skau, 2025), the field of assistive technology in pediatric hospitalization faces the need to transcend the strictly technical paradigm. Rather than focusing exclusively on hardware performance or design characteristics, it becomes important to consider how these tools are positioned within clinical routines, how their effects are framed and assessed, and how they contribute to broader inclusion and well-being goals promoted by organizations such as the WHO.This article seeks to contribute to that debate with a critical reflection grounded in recent literature and studies applied in hospital contexts. It aims to assess the methods used, identify strengths and weaknesses of current hypotheses, and open a constructive discussion on the relevance of social robots as assistive technology within the healthcare framework.It is difficult to continue discussing the role of social robots in pediatrics as if they were merely "technological novelties." Growing evidence indicates that these systems can support the clinical and emotional needs of hospitalized children when integrated into existing care pathways. Playful interaction with robots such as CoderBot (an interactive robot platform) (Castiglioni et al., 2022), PLEO (a dinosaur-like robotic companion) (Moerman and Jansens, 2021), aibo (a pet-like social robot) (Tanaka et al., 2022) or projects such as the Baby Goldrake humanoid robot does not replace medical treatments. Rather, it can expand the hospital system's capacity to deliver more comprehensive care by addressing psychological well-being alongside physical health. This shift in framing is important, as it positions social robots as complementary assistive supports embedded within supportive care practices rather than as incidental distractions or autonomous therapeutic solutions.Within this perspective, a social robot may be considered a structured clinical tool when its use is linked to an explicit therapeutic objective, implemented through a brief and reproducible protocol within the care pathway, and supervised by healthcare personnel. Its value lies in facilitating engagement and emotional regulation in coordination with clinical routines, rather than functioning as an independent therapeutic agent. Evaluation through relevant outcomes such as anxiety, distress, or cooperation helps situate these interventions within rehabilitation-oriented care while maintaining appropriate safety and privacy safeguards (Stanojevic et al., 2023).Evidence from controlled settings further supports this view. In Turkey, a randomized trial with 84 children undergoing ambulatory surgery demonstrated that the presence of an interactive robot reduced anxiety prior to postoperative mobilization and increased parental satisfaction with the care provided (Topçu et al., 2023). From the perspective of clinical practice, this finding is particularly valuable because it links the emotional dimension to functional recovery, a central objective of enhanced recovery protocols following surgery. It is not simply a matter of the child being calmer, but of reducing anxiety in a way that enables more efficient recovery, with direct benefits for hospital stay duration and patient cooperation. In this sense, the clinical relevance of social robots emerges most clearly when emotional support is aligned with concrete care processes and observable engagement.Even among populations with greater psychological vulnerability, such as children with social anxiety, evidence suggests that interaction with robots fosters prosocial behaviors and openness to contact, positioning these devices as relational mediators with still underexplored potential (Kitt et al., 2021). The robot should not be seen as a substitute for human interaction, but as a facilitator that opens communication channels where anxiety or fear might otherwise close them. These findings are promising, although broader validation across diverse clinical contexts remains necessary.Moreover, social robotics can be embedded into hospital routines without the need for complex infrastructure or disproportionate investment, functioning as an extension of therapeutic play already recognized in pediatrics (Pourteimour and Kazemi, 2021). Yaren was introduced as an open-source humanoid torso, accessible and anthropometrically close to the proportions of a child. Its design is not a minor technical detail, as it offers a solution that does not depend on proprietary and costly platforms and can be implemented particularly in low-and middle-income countries (Sánchez-Orozco et al., 2025). These examples illustrate why the field is moving toward clinically oriented uses, while also underscoring that feasibility and scalability will shape real-world adoption in pediatric hospitals.The value of social robots lies not only in the child's direct experience but also in what they represent for those who accompany their process. From the perspective of families, the usefulness of these technologies is measured both in the relief they bring to the child and in the reassurance they provide to parents (Jin and Choi, 2022). As noted by (Dosso et al., 2023), the possibility of the robot becoming a "safe space" to express feelings or practice coping techniques gives caregivers the sense of having an additional ally, rather than just a temporary distraction. In this sense, parental acceptance is not a minor detail but a decisive criterion for ensuring that the use of robots can be sustained over time within the hospital environment. This acceptance reflects how families interpret supportive technologies in moments of uncertainty, and it may shape the child's participation, adherence to mobilization or therapy-related tasks, and sustained coping beyond the acute hospital encounter (Butchart et al., 2021).A similar perspective emerges from healthcare professionals. (Hudson et al., 2023) show that physicians and nurses recognize the value of robots with adaptive intelligence to accompany invasive procedures but emphasize that these should act as complements, never as replacements. In pediatric settings, this complementarity depends on clear safeguards that protect children and families while ensuring that robots can be integrated without disrupting clinical routines. Robots are more likely to be welcomed when they reinforce, rather than compete with, the caregiver's role by offering relief during critical moments and easing part of the emotional burden carried by families and healthcare teams (Soljacic et al., 2024). At the same time, concerns remain about reduced human interaction and data sensitivity in an already delicate care context (Nishat et al., 2023). These issues should not be treated as static barriers, but as practical determinants that shape how social robots can be designed and deployed to respect human boundaries and strengthen the bond between the child, caregivers, and the clinical team.Social robots should be discussed in pediatric hospitalization not only as an innovation in patient experience, but as a potential contributor to rehabilitation-relevant care. Advances in this area suggest that their most consistent contribution lies in reducing anxiety, stress, and distress, rather than directly relieving pain (Littler et al., 2021). This finding calls for a reconsideration of the initial hypotheses: robots should not be regarded as "technological analgesics," but as tools of emotional and pedagogical support that complement medical and psychosocial interventions (Kitt et al., 2021). This distinction is clinically meaningful because improvements in functional outcomes appear to be mediated through emotional regulation, engagement, and increased willingness to participate, rather than through direct therapeutic action. By supporting emotional readiness and reducing avoidance behaviors, these systems may facilitate cooperation, participation in mobilization, and adherence to therapy-related activities, particularly in perioperative and inpatient contexts (Topçu et al., 2023).An important strength is the high acceptability reported by children and families, who perceive robots as companions, playmates, and mediators of communication. In practice, this acceptability has implications beyond satisfaction: caregiver reassurance and engagement can shape adherence to care routines and sustain coping behaviors throughout hospitalization, influencing the continuity of supportive and rehabilitative care.At the same time, the evidence base is not yet mature enough to justify one-size-fits-all clinical protocols. Recent reviews point to heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes, which complicate interpretation and reduce transferability across clinical contexts (Kabacińska et al., 2021;Pan et al., 2024). Technological variability also remains substantial, with a predominance of humanoid robots such as NAO, while more accessible formats have received less systematic evaluation (Rossi et al., 2022). Rather than undermining the field, these limitations clarify what is needed next: reproducible interventions, clearer descriptions of interaction components, and outcomes that reflect both emotional regulation and rehabilitation-oriented engagement.To help bridge the gap between promising findings and practical implementation, we propose the CARE-R framework as a structured approach to guide clinically meaningful use of social robots in pediatric hospitalization (Figure 1). This approach supports decision-making that aligns the intended clinical purpose, context-sensitive interaction design, rehabilitation-relevant outcomes, and implementation safeguards. It also highlights the value of brief, feasible protocols and outcome selection that prioritizes emotional and educational indicators while reserving pain as a secondary endpoint when appropriate (Triantafyllidis et al., 2023). Importantly, sustainable adoption in pediatric hospitals depends on governance conditions, including consent and assent, privacy-by-design, infection control, staff training, and workflow integration. (Hudson et al., 2023;Nishat et al., 2023). This includes clear consent and child assent processes, as well as privacy-by-design practices, particularly when robots interact with children during vulnerable moments of care. Infection control routines, staff training, and workflow integration are equally critical, as they determine whether these systems can be deployed without introducing new risks, increasing workload, or disrupting time-sensitive clinical procedures. Equity must also be considered, since the clinical value of social robots will remain limited if implementation relies on proprietary platforms, specialized personnel, or resources unavailable in public and resource-constrained pediatric units.Beyond their current limitations, social robots align with the vision of assistive technologies as instruments to "leave no one behind." When deployed with scientific grounding and equity in mind, they can contribute to a more inclusive form of universal health coverage, where the emotional and educational well-being of hospitalized children is recognized as a legitimate healthcare goal. Thus, the answer seems clear. Yes, social robots can improve the hospital experience of children, provided they are implemented responsibly and supported by evidence.

works.title: How to Shift Your Attention
works.abstract: Willis Jenkins's “Migrations of the Sacred” is about how to notice, understand, value, and grieve the diminishment of animals whose numbers are dwindling. Specifically, Jenkins attends to Red Knot and their kin. Red Knot are small birds that fly a great distance. They are about the size of a robin, and most of them travel 19,000 miles every year, from one end of the Earth to the other, from Tierra del Fuego in Argentina to the Hudson Bay in the Arctic. Red Knot are declining in huge numbers, “dwindling, diminishing” in Jenkins's haunting idiom, headed toward extinction.How, Jenkins asks, might true apprehension of Red Knot loss affect the framing and practice of climate equity initiatives in the world the Red Knot is leaving? This question arises directly from Jenkins's experience. Jenkins has been involved in two simultaneous research projects, both focused on effects of climate change, both on Virginia's Eastern Shore. Nonetheless, these two projects are life worlds apart from one another. The first focuses on the diminishment of the Red Knot. The second, a “Coastal Futures Hub,” responds to community-driven concerns in this low-lying area on the Atlantic Ocean, in a place where people are experiencing increasing salt-water incursion, failing septic fields, and road flooding, all of which often reproduce longstanding social inequalities. Where these inequities are affecting people's lives and livelihoods, Red Knot are not—generally—a key priority. The world of Red Knot biology and the world of climate equity, both on Virginia's Eastern Shore, are often not in conversation with one another.Sometimes Red Knot flourishing and human coastal futures may even seem to be in tension, as pressing survival concerns for human communities present obvious priorities for folks living on the coast, some of whom don't even know they share their home with Red Knot. In this way, Jenkins's involvement in these two projects presents him with a laboratory of what I consider among the most interesting concerns in contemporary environmental ethics: what do we make of values that we hold dear when they seem to be in tension with one another? With so many ongoing troubles, how do we direct our focus without leaving something vital out?While Jenkins appreciates a wide array of values in this scene, he is also clear about what he wants to get into the picture. He is struck by the absence of Red Knot from the vision of justice in the “Coastal Futures Hub,” and he wants to know: how would values need to transform for people living on Virginia's Eastern Shore to see these two worlds—the Red Knot flyway and human vulnerabilities to changing climate conditions—as belonging to one another? And then, what would that world look like and to whom?In responding to “Migrations of the Sacred,” I will focus on two things—the first an observation about Jenkins's questions, and the second a meditation on what Jenkins's proposal looks like from my classroom. First, I describe one of Jenkins's key questions, which is how humans come to see themselves as caught up in sacred networks of kinship with other creatures living in their communities. Second, I respond to Jenkins's proposal that environmentally focused research in religious studies might build practices of attention that contribute to small, pragmatic shifts in the appreciation of sacred value among our communities. Ultimately, I will suggest that building these kinds of experiences is complicated and difficult, but also deeply related to pedagogical questions about what education is for, whether it is possible, and how we might go about doing it. If teachers are going to build these kinds of experiences for our students, we probably need to learn to create them for ourselves as well.How do humans value Red Knot as part of our world? In popular discourse, human concerns with other species’ diminishment are often oriented by the threat of extinction, which is to say the end of the species and its ability to make its home on Earth. But Jenkins describes how the concept of extinction—with its focus on individuated species and individual organisms—fails to capture the disvalue in Red Knot diminishment and dwindling. “How to name the loss in that diminishing, the disvalue in a migration's dwindling?” Jenkins is wondering what metaphors of connectedness can represent the loss of a lifeway. As Red Knot numbers decrease, we lose not only the Red Knot themselves, but the entire network of relations that support that fabulous migration. This includes the other species with which the Red Knot have been enmeshed in kin networks longer than any human history (with horseshoe crabs, snails, mussels) and even the climactic conditions that enabled those networks to sustain themselves. “Part of the challenge for ethics is to repair conceptual language that obscures the relations involved in extinctions.” When we consider Red Knot apart from their kin, Jenkins seems to say, we fail to mourn what is lost. When we do not mourn the communities undone by the extinction of one species, because we are missing concepts for the relations at stake, this is an ethical failure for which the scientific method so far lacks a language.Because of course Red Knot are not the only creatures in Virginia who are impacted by a changing climate. They are caught up—as all of us are—in webs of relations, a whole world of give and take that has gone on for millennia. Through this, they have accrued world wisdom that many humans barely fathom. Sometimes these webs are called “ecosystems,” but Jenkins's essay reminds us that such an idiom may undervalue what Red Knots and the lifeways they share with their kin are communicating. Through their massive annual migration, they know where to return, year after year, to keep their “appointments with sand-dwelling mollusks” and other species. And they continue to keep these appointments, or they keep trying to, even as their numbers dwindle from hundreds of thousands to tens of thousands.1In this essay, Jenkins is taking up an effort to imagine, as he writes, “ways otherwise, what might happen.”2 He is searching for how humans might transform ourselves to value the Red Knot and their kin. As examples, he observes places where humans have become susceptible in new ways to dwindling migrations—to Monarch Butterfly, to Chum Salmon, to Bowhead Whale, to Black-necked Crane.3 In relation to these species, new traditions have developed around the migration as it diminishes. When this happens, those migrations are not, he argues, merely providing “cultural ecosystem services” by transforming the human cultures made newly susceptible to their presence. The phrase—“cultural ecosystem services”—undersells the phenomenon it aims to describe. Something significantly more profound is happening. There is a form of “religious valuing in which a being or relation has status due to its power to change the beholder's imperfect moral regard.”4 The claim is grander than we might at first notice. Jenkins suggests that rather than simply contributing to cultural values, these animals have moral significance. They aren't merely part of our lives in ways we usually fail to recognize—they can make us better people by teaching us to do justice.This idea, that there is moral value in the relations between beings, is often presented as a recent intervention in sustainability literature under the category of “relational values.”5 While Jenkins is allied with the importance of relational practice, he thinks there are a couple of important problems with the framing of relational values as new-found in the sustainability literature. Presenting relational values as a recent discovery “1) deprives itself of available genealogies of relational value in ethics and 2) obscures the kind of moral regard evident in the expectation of some communities that their values should be transformed by multispecies relation.” By presenting “relational values” as an innovation in an academic literature, this rhetoric ignores assets it could otherwise retrieve, and it misrepresents already underrepresented communities.Communities who take it that multispecies relations are a moral matter have always existed, Jenkins reminds us. In Indigenous cultures, yes, and in dissenting movements from a supposed European Enlightenment consensus, and among contemporary, everyday people on Virginia's Eastern Shore, people Jenkins meets through his work on these interdisciplinary projects. In communities like that, “people may recognize that their present norms are not fully those they want to reproduce and, especially when thinking about the future, may identify values by which they hope their communities will be reshaped.”6 The hope that we might be able to improve our moral lives is far more widespread than academics sometimes make it seem. Some people are looking out for how they might meet their obligations better. Humans are often people who want to be transformed.Jenkins's question is how sacred values come into being for us, how humans might come to appreciate the Red Knot and their lifeway as the sacred things they are. Jenkins suggests this would require transformation. And yet he describes how it's increasingly easy to find examples of people hoping to be transformed into deeper relationship with Red Knot and hoping to transform others. In one example that Jenkins cites, the author Phillip Hoose wrote a large format book illustrated with many photographs, focused on a famously long-lived Red Knot known as Moonbird. (The name refers to the incredible distances this individual has flown over the course of its life—migrations combining to equal the distance from the Earth to its Moon and part of the way back.) This book, entitled Moonbird: A Year on the Wind with the Great Survivor B95, traces the annual migration of Red Knot, focusing specifically on one individual (B95) who lived at least 20 years.7 The book is written by an author who clearly cherishes the birds, and it is written for people (specifically children) who want to learn to appreciate the Red Knot migration. In its descriptions of the places that Red Knot stop on their route, the book repeatedly appeals to the category of the sacred. In at least three instances, Hoose marks the places that Red Knot stop on their migration as sacred: “sacred stepping-stone places” (56), “a sacred slice of the Earth” (76), “the sacred places . . . had sustained this amazing aviator” (104–105). In each case, Hoose suggests that the migration's stopping places are sacred sites, without ever thematizing what such an attribution means exactly. While Jenkins does not spend much time analyzing this particular source, Hoose himself may be doing something like what Jenkins is interested in understanding.For Jenkins, drawing on the sociologist Hans Joas, conceptions of the sacred move, and they ought to—when conceptions of the sacred shift, we see a value transformation of the kind increasingly studied by sustainability researchers. Thus, religious studies is particularly situated to understand such value transformation, as the study of religion often focuses on the continuities, transformations, and possibilities of intellectual, spiritual, and moral traditions with deep histories. This means it has particular strengths for just the thing these sustainability researchers are interested in.Jenkins is not focused on the ways that the rhetoric of the sacred in children's books might contribute to value transformation.8 Instead, he offers a practical focus on specific practices of attention that people do every day. He focuses on shifting what we look at in the small ways we can and letting those relational engagements in a particular place transform us. He is on Virginia's Eastern Shore, with the Red Knot, among climate inequities and people who care about them, and with a whole lot of Christians. In this context, Jenkins does not aim to alter anyone's ontological commitments about the relationship of the divine to the world, as a wave of scholarship across the environmental humanities does, but he does think values can be transformed in more practical and open-ended ways.
