works.title: Beyond policing AI: reflections on teaching, assessment, and pedagogy in social science education
works.abstract: AI has permeated almost every aspect of our lives. What began as a limited experimental tool has rapidly evolved into a powerful technology, seamlessly woven into our daily routines. Its expansion is not only swift but also reshapes our reality, raising profound questions about the role of the human, the nature of originality, and the boundaries of creativity (Hassan & Kumar, 2024).In academia, AI has become integral to the landscape of research and teaching, shaping much of academic practice. It is present in scientific writing, in the daily workflow, in supporting student assessment, and even in managing routine administrative tasks. Students, for their part, increasingly rely on it for learning, planning assignments, and meeting academic requirements.Recent findings consistently show that AI is becoming an embedded component of students' higher education learning. The 2025 HEPI Student Generative AI Survey reveals a sharp rise in adoption: nearly all students now use AI in some form, compared with only 66% in 2024. Most rely on AI to clarify concepts, summarize articles, and generate research ideas, and around 18% reported incorporating AI-generated text directly into their assignments. Students frequently note that AI saves them time and improves their work. At the same time, many fear of being accused of academic misconduct and are concerned that AI may produce inaccurate or biased results. Women report higher levels of concern, whereas men, as well as students from higher socioeconomic backgrounds and those studying STEM subjects, express greater enthusiasm with the use of AI in academia (Freeman, 2025). Similar findings have emerged in additional studies (Mazaheriyan & Nourbakhsh, 2025;Ravšeljet al., 2025;Vieriu, & Petrea, 2025), reinforcing the understanding that AI is a widespread global phenomenon actively reshaping both the learning experience and the pedagogical landscape Alongside the rapid increase in students' use of AI, a range of dilemmas has emerged within the academic sphere. Beyond issues of academic integrity, such as uncredited use of AIgenerated outputs or the blurring of boundaries between legitimate assistance and fully AIproduced work, concerns have also been raised about potential harm to core learning skills, including critical thinking, creativity, and even the ability to read and write independently.Additional dilemmas, such as exposure to inaccurate or biased information, widening gender and socioeconomic gaps, and how to assess student work, further underscore the complexity this new technology introduces (Lowe, 2024).As a new faculty member, I am sometimes struck by the intensity of the dilemmas and the extent to which the discourse around AI has come to dominate academic conversations. I have received a steady stream of emails from the university: guidelines on acceptable uses of AI, formal requirements for courses, and best practice statements on academic integrity that faculty are expected to embed in their syllabi. Many of these documents lack clarity, some of their recommendations are difficult to implement in practice, and most are subject to frequent revisions. Interviews with higher education leaders across the globe express the same preoccupation with students' use of AI and level of oversight required.My experience is also shaped by everyday conversations with colleagues, many of whom describe a persistent sense of uncertainty regarding the assessment of student work. Some have shifted from written assignments to closed-book exams in an effort to maintain academic integrity, whether as an individual choice or as part of a broader departmental or institutional approach. Others fear that AI may erode foundational skills such as critical and analytical skills and the ability to formulate coherent arguments.Unlike the prevailing anxieties voiced by institutions and colleagues, however, I do not feel threatened by it -certainly not within the social sciences. Rather, I see AI as a productive challenge: an opportunity to rethink the very nature of teaching and to revisit the foundational goals of student training. From my perspective, the current debate primarily exposes what we have neglected long before the advent of AI-a clear articulation of what our teaching is meant to accomplish. The central question is not how to police the use of AI, but whether we expect students merely to memorize content and produce written assignments or aim to foster deeper competencies. There appears to be a broad consensus that higher education aims to develop skills rather than merely transmit knowledge. If so, AI cannot threaten the core of social science education, as it is fundamentally incapable of replacing the acquisition and honing of skills grounded in human interaction, dialogue, and collective learning spaces, such as critical thinking, reflexivity, and leadership.Informed by this understanding, I find myself questioning how I can teach social science courses to groups of 120 students. Even when these are introductory or research method classes, teaching at such a scale fundamentally undermines the stated goal of skill development, AI or no AI. It is difficult-if not impossible-to cultivate critical thinking, thoughtful discussion, and analytical practice in mass classrooms where opportunities for meaningful interaction are limited.The ongoing debate surrounding student assessment in the age of AI further highlights the gap between our educational aims and prevailing practices. As we have seen, one of the prominent concerns in that age is with assessment. But are the exam or assignment grade the true product of the learning process? Can they genuinely reflect the capacities of those being trained to become social science professionals? Does the fear of compromised "authenticity" in student work not obscure a deeper question about the very purpose of assessment?The current preoccupation with the credibility of submitted assignments and test revives the perennial question: Who is responsible for academic integrity? At times, universities appear eager to assume total responsibility by setting rules and monitoring compliance, yet even the most stringent measures prove largely unworkable. Many institutions have come to recognize that preventing the use of AI is infeasible, opting instead for permitting its use under specified conditions and requiring formal declarations. However, such policies are rarely enforceable and do little to address the core issue, so that responsibility for AI use-and for academic integrity-ultimately remains with the students. I believe the solution lies in a decisive shift toward very small learning groups. Such a move is not intended merely to prevent AI from undermining the quality or integrity of education, but first and foremost to ensure that we are genuinely cultivating the skills we expect social science students to develop. A systematic transition to small-group teachingincluding in introductory and research methods courses-would enable the use of a wide range of pedagogical practices that foster deep learning: open dialogical spaces in which every voice can be heard, collaborative teamwork, the analysis of complex social situations, case-based learning, peer teaching practices, and individual and collective reflective exercises. Within small groups, learning processes can be built around dialogue, shared inquiry, and the coconstruction of meaning, rather than the passive consumption of information. A classic meta-analysis has demonstrated that small-group learning produces superior outcomes in higher education, both in academic achievement and in the development of cognitive and social skills (Springer et al., 1999). Moreover, small-group learning constitutes a central component of highimpact educational practices, which aim to promote meaningful learning, deep skill development, and personal and social responsibility as students engage with complex societal issues (Kuh, 2008).The shift to small also requires a transformation in modes of instruction, including preparing instructors to teach in ways that allow students to lead portions of the class, present insights, pose questions, and practice skills in real time. In such settings, learning becomes genuinely interactive-not as a technological simulation, but as a human process that unfolds within the classroom. In this context, as a faculty member, I am often encouraged to integrate "engagement-enhancing" technological tools, such as Wooclap and similar platforms, to maximize student participation and speak in a language familiar to them. Yet in my experience, these tools tend to create only a brief departure from an otherwise unidirectional lecture. They do not replace authentic interaction, they do not deepen learning, and at times even produce a sense of paternalism-as if the instructor's role were to "entertain" or "occupy" students rather than to lead a meaningful pedagogical process. Our responsibility is not to amuse our students but to create a space that enables the practice and development of skills; the students' responsibility, in turn, is to participate actively in the learning process.Within this context, I find it essential to place interdisciplinary thinking at the center of small-group teaching-not only at the level of course content, but also in terms of the group composition and the structure of instruction. One can imagine models in which a small group is composed of students from different social science departments, and the course is co-taught by two instructors from distinct disciplines who actively model interdisciplinary dialogue: points of disagreement, areas of overlap, and moments of complementarity. Such models represent not merely pedagogical but a reflection of the professional reality in which social science graduates ultimately operate, where fields are rarely isolated, and meaningful work is almost always carried out through sustained interdisciplinary collaboration.For example, I would like to see a course such as Developmental Psychology for Social Work taught jointly to students of social work, education, psychology, and sociology. This form of learning enables students to examine how the same theoretical knowledge is applied across different professional contexts: how developmental psychology informs the field practice of a social worker, the pedagogical perspective of an educator, the clinical framing of a psychologist, or the societal analysis of a sociologist.While such models already exist in some universities, they are often treated as exceptions, requiring special approvals, dedicated resources, and deviations from standard curricula. I argue for a reversed logic: interdisciplinary small-group teaching should become the norm. If we are truly committed to preparing graduates to engage with complex social realities, we must intentionally design interdisciplinary learning frameworks not as marginal elective offerings, but as an integral component of the core training. Small groups are not only a foundation for deeper interaction, but also a way to move beyond the limitations of traditional assessment practices. Particularly in large courses, exams and written assignments fail to reveal the full potential of many students. Having studied social sciences in a second language -often as the only minority student in the classroom -I frequently struggled to express my abilities. In mass lectures, I rarely spoke, and for many years, I felt a gap between my true skills and their evaluation.In small-group settings, by contrast, marginalized students can be seen, heard, and fully exercise their abilities, while instructors are better able to identify skills that do not easily surface through conventional assessment. Small groups make it possible to see everyone, not only the confident, dominant, and fluent students. They allow instructors to offer close guidance, recognize potential, offer support, and actively work to reduce gaps. In this sense, rather than allowing AI to deepen existing inequalities, small-group learning creates a space that strengthens equity. This perspective resonates with critical pedagogical traditions in higher education, which emphasize visibility, voice, and relational engagement as essential not only for meaningful learning, but also for fostering a more inclusive and just academic environment for marginalized students (hooks, 2014).Small-group learning also enables richer and more flexible forms of assessment: longitudinal evaluation, assessment of participation, scaffolded writing processes, close mentoring, and greater attention to effort and learning processes rather than to final products. These forms of evaluation also alleviate concerns about plagiarism or inappropriate uses of AI.Indeed, AI can be intentionally integrated into the learning process-not as a substitute for learning, but as a point of departure. Students can bring AI-generated texts into the classroom, and analyze, critique, and rebuild them. Through this process, they learn not only disciplinary content, but also how AI operates within social systems, reproduces power relations, and transforms modes of knowledge production-questions that lie at the very heart of the social

works.title: How Far Does the Diverse Economies Approach Take Us?
works.abstract: Julie and Katherine Gibson-Graham and Kelly Dombroski (eds), The Handbook of Diverse Economies. Cheltenham and Northampton, MA: Edward Elgar, 2020. 546 pp. Hardback £ 199.80. There is a long-standing tradition of thought on human-centred and communitarian economies. It connects to a search for utopias (no lands) and udetopias (neverlands) which has accelerated with the advent of capitalism and the obsession with capital accumulation that gave the latter system its name. Intellectuals like Charles Fourier, Silvio Gesell, François Marie, Karl Marx, Robert Owen and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon were pioneers in developing social, economic and political alternatives to capitalism. They engaged with the original 16th century collectivist and utopian socialism of Sir Thomas More, which, as French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu (1998: 125) observed, was ‘often discredited, dismissed and ridiculed in the name of economic realism’. Drawing on this tradition, the scholarly couple Katherine Gibson and Julie Graham added the diverse economies (DE) approach three decades ago.1 Since then, it has developed into a fully-fledged research programme among scholars and a vision of social transformation among activists. The latest arrival in their scientific production The Handbook of Diverse Economies, is edited by J.K. Gibson-Graham and Kelly Dombroski, and the subject of this critical review. Through capturing and valorizing the variety of economic, social and political spaces that currently proliferate in the interstices of the capitalist system, the diverse economies approach has gained considerable traction. These spaces, DE authors and followers would emphasize, are not an exercise of the imagination occurring in the no lands and neverlands of utopianism, but tangible and true sources of global hope. They are existing spaces which evade capitalism or shape resistance to it, and mobilize collectives. Underlining that building alternatives to capitalism is feasible as it is ongoing, The Handbook of Diverse Economies adds cases, findings and reflections, and invites analysis of the way scholars understand and write about economic alternatives. However, as in previous works (see Gibson-Graham, 1996, 2008), engagement with academics outside feminist, post-structural and post-development circles remains pending in this last book. While this new volume refines the contrast with neoliberal politics and the ‘crushing uniformity of mainstream circuits of value’ (Fuller et al., 2016: xxiv), it does not meet the need to engage with other ways of theorizing alternatives to overcome the relatively marginal position of diverse economies within the dominant capitalist system. Some of the older critiques of the DE approach are explicitly addressed, but the general lack of receptiveness to criticism limits the influence of the research programme beyond the circles of supporters and partisan advocates of a post-capitalist future. This essay begins by introducing the notion of alterity and the trajectory of utopianism, and how the diverse economies approach is situated within this tradition. It subsequently presents a critique of previous research, which is followed by a review of the new book (hereafter referred to as the handbook) and its contribution to this body of scholarly work. The essay delves into the details of what has and what has not been covered by this new addition, and its relevance to the field of development studies. A key achievement of the diverse economies framework is that it has rekindled the debate on the notions of alternatives and alterity (Fickey, 2011; Lee et al., 2004). It is not a new debate, considering that the intellectual production of alternatives to capitalism has inspired humankind since the origins of capitalism itself. In line with this, contending conceptions invariably reject surplus extraction based on private property and its resulting waged employment, but they differ in their interpretation and focus of the meaning of alternative. Gritzas and Kavoulakos (2016) have clustered scholarly work on alternatives to capitalism in two broad groups. The ‘utopians’ favoured the organization of a cooperative or community economy; Proudhon was among them, and to some extent, Polanyi and Gesell later followed. The sceptic camp, of which Marx and Engels are representatives, were particularly dismissive of utopian projects and their lack of ‘scientific’ reflection; they were convinced that such utopian initiatives were bound to fail (Engels, 1968). Marx and Engels reasoned that individuals cannot change society from below because they do not have the resources to afford a life outside a waged relationship. As workers do not own or control the means of production, they are not able to access the resources needed to afford food, accommodation and meet other basic needs for survival. According to Marx and Engels, forming small networks or communities does not improve utopians’ chances of success in the long run either, because a life outside capitalism requires resources that must come from somewhere. Furthermore, if such a withdrawal from capitalism becomes the life choice of significant numbers of workers, the state would intervene to prevent a mass opt-out from the capitalist economy (North, 2016). Subsequent orthodox Marxist scholars similarly discarded the potential of such initiatives as naïve and instead promoted full-scale radical social change that would terminate the hegemony of capitalism when the system had reached its productivity boundary. Recently, scholars have contested the sterile nature of alternative projects and suggest that in current times, the claim that utopian initiatives from below have no potential needs to be researched empirically (Gómez, 2018; North, 1999, 2016; Pacione, 1997). The scepticism of the Marxist strand eventually dominated the intellectual debate that challenged capitalism during the 20th century, consigning smaller utopian initiatives to the intellectual margins (Fuller et al., 2016). The confrontation between socialism and capitalism resulted in the regulation of capitalist economies which in some countries led to the emergence of welfare states that redistributed economic benefits, further pushing utopian economic and political experiments to the margins (Gritzas and Kavoulakos, 2016). With the decline of radical political economy and the rise of neoliberalism in the late 1980s, the scope for alternative thinking was lost in no lands and neverlands. Ironically, this intensified the search among academics who were not deterred by the apparent implications of small-scale practices (Holloway, 2010). There was a dire need among scholars to find alternative economic and political practices that would bring hope against the background of hegemonic neoliberal capitalism. The search finally made progress towards the mid-1990s, when the retreat of the welfare state was being contested, new social movements such as the Zapatistas in Mexico emerged and anti-globalization protests gained momentum. In 1996, the feminist economic geographers Katherine Gibson and Julie Graham published The End of Capitalism (As We Knew it): A Feminist Critique of Political Economy (Gibson-Graham, 1996). A decade later, they collected their ideas in A Postcapitalist Politics (Gibson-Graham, 2006). The End of Capitalism was a provocative, fresh and ground-breaking attempt to capture the efforts of various communities around the world that were building different spaces of economic and political interaction. The qualification of ‘different spaces’ applies to a varied set of non-capitalist projects as well as alternatives that directly oppose capitalism. The key analytical instrument of the DE approach is a comprehensive canvas based on grounded and weak theory. The framework presents a broad inventory of empirical practices related to enterprises, labour, transactions, property and finance to construct three loose categories or domains of economic activity: non-capitalist, capitalist and alternative to capitalist (see Table 1). In subsequent publications identifying with the approach, more examples have been added. In this way, the DE approach collected studies on a multitude of different practices around the world that facilitate the material survival of communities and the reproduction of their cultural life. The publications led to a group of scholar-activists forming the Community Economies Research Network (CERN), which engages in research, reflection and practical activities around the world.2 At the time of writing,3 The End of Capitalism (Gibson-Graham, 1996) has been cited 5,350 times and Google Scholar lists 10,500 hits for the keyword ‘diverse economies’, which shows how the concept has gained in popularity in some academic and activist circles. ALTERNATIVE PAID Self-employed Reciprocal labour In-kind Work for welfare ALTERNATIVE MARKET Fair trade Alternative Currencies Underground market Barter ALTERNATIVE PRIVATE State-managed assets Customary (clan) land Community land trusts Indigenous knowledge (Intellectual Property ALTERNATIVE CAPITALIST State owned Environmentally responsible Socially responsible Non-profit ALTERNATIVE MARKET Cooperative Banks Credit unions Community-based financial institutions Micro-finance UNPAID Housework Volunteer Self-provisioning Slave labour NON-MARKET Household sharing Gift giving Hunting, fishing, gathering Theft, piracy, poaching OPEN ACCESS Atmosphere International Waters Open-source IP Outer Space NON-CAPITALIST Worker cooperatives Sole proprietorships Community enterprise Feudal Slave NON-MARKET Sweat equity Family lending Donations Interest-free loans Intellectually, the DE approach positions itself between the utopians and the Marxists. Gibson-Graham (1996, 2006) define capitalism in relation to five pillars as shown in Table 1: waged labour, exploitative enterprises, private property, market exchange and interest-based finances. They contend that there are too many experiments that do not follow these five characteristics and they criticize the structuralist Marxist approaches for being ‘capitalocentric’, meaning that they ignore the immense variety of practices in the non-capitalist categories. They further argue that Marxist approaches assess capitalism with an essentialist, monolithic discourse that clouds ‘other’ economic practices that are not based either on wage labour or on exploitation. Marxist work, they claim, describes capitalism with ‘totalising concepts and machine-like metaphors’ (Jonas, 2016: 6) to express its domination over non-capitalist spaces. As these practices go unnoticed and are treated as unworthy of consideration, the Marxist narrative would endorse the belief that non-capitalist projects are too small, marginal and irrelevant to achieve any systemic transformation. According to Gibson-Graham (1996), keeping non-capitalist projects hidden or invisible makes them appear irrelevant and powerless, thereby silencing existing diversity and further preventing the imagining of non-capitalist futures. The capacity to see diversity is thus impaired and part of the DE project is precisely to construct another dictionary to discuss and analyse alterity. The point of departure of the approach, that non-capitalist economic systems have remained invisible, calls for further discussion. Radical political economy scholars have examined these different economies within capitalism but based on the assumptions that they are subordinate subsystems of the capitalist economy, which sustains them to secure its own survival, and that they lack autonomy as alternative economic projects (Jonas, 2016). For example, radical development geographer Milton Santos (1977) posited the theory of spatial dialectics with two interconnected economic circuits. Santos reasoned that the urban economy is composed of the ‘upper circuit’ populated by capital-intensive modern industries while the ‘lower circuit’ groups the labour-intensive smaller enterprises exposed to price bargaining. In Santos’s account, the two circuits struggle for control over the urban territory, with the upper circuit normally dominating the lower one and relegating it to the margins. Similar, or at least compatible, theories of two-sector economic structures in which one is superior to the other were salient in radical political economy and structural economic theory (e.g. Fuchs, 1974; Hirschman, 1958; Lewis, 1954). Other authors (e.g. Elson, 2007, 2017) argue that capitalism depends for its reproduction on the unpaid work of the domestic economy to sustain the political and economic spheres, which in turn generate the resources that sustain the capitalist economy. These parallel readings of the relation between capitalist and non-capitalist economies situate the latter in a relationship of subordination. Gibson-Graham criticize this a priori value judgement; at the risk of overgeneralization, they argue that Marxist accounts fail to see the potential of such alternatives and, rather than regarding them as equals, they are treated as subordinates. In contrast, the diverse economies approach emphasizes horizontality and spatial differentiation with co-existence, although not without tensions. Gibson-Graham critiqued the assumed superior–inferior relationship and proposed an escape out of capitalocentrism by means of a systematic analysis of diversity and alterity. That is, they aim at ‘creating a discourse of economic difference as a contribution to a politics of economic innovation’ (Gibson-Graham, 2005a: 6). Their approach emphasizes diversity and combinations across the five pillars of capitalism (see Table 1) and the prospect that current heterogeneity is only the beginning of future systemic transformation. They substitute a conception of a single overarching global capitalist economy with a diverse economy (Jonas, 2016). They seek to reveal that the economy is heterogeneous and that it includes other mechanisms of exchange, organization of production, types of property and rewards for labour and finance (Healy, 2009, 2011). As a research programme, the DE approach focuses on identifying and recording the great variety of economic activities around the globe. It is oriented towards describing a post-capitalist economy in which ‘other’ projects are registered and revalued. While Gibson and Graham took explicit distance from Marxism, they also distanced themselves from utopianism. The diverse economies approach aims at identifying the myriad of economic practices already implemented as complements or as alternatives to the capitalist economy. The idea is to show them as autonomous spaces, and not as inferior or subordinated projects that may occur in neverlands. As a result, the academic project is also a legitimizing force for innovative activists who have already conceived and implemented alternative economic practices and who see their efforts reflected in scholarly theorization. They equally encourage acting, and especially invite academics to try action research. The focus of the DE approach is on the possibilities of the struggle and not on the probability of success (Gibson-Graham, 2008: 615). The idea of diversity suggests an innate positive connotation or a certain aura of progressiveness that needs to be examined. As argued by Samers (2005), some non-capitalist economic practices are equally or more exploitative than capitalist practices, such as modern slavery and various forms of unpaid work. According to a recent database, over 30 per cent of the world economy is produced informally, although the proportion has been shrinking substantially in the last two decades, up to the pandemic (Medina and Schneider, 2019). This figure of 30 per cent hides an enormous diversity in itself; the informal economy is an amalgam of economic relations and practices under a single name that includes informal workers paid in cash, semi-informal workers that are not completely remunerated through the formal banking channels, and others that work without any pay (Gómez et al., 2020; Williams, 2011; Williams and Windebank, 1998). In some corners of informality, agents have organized marketplaces, associations, self-help initiatives, and other ways of structuring their economic life that fit nicely in the ‘other-than-capitalist’ box of the diverse economies framework. However, in other corners of the informal economy, there is nothing progressive about it and the notion of diversity veils myriad forms of exploitation and misery. The diverse economies framework does not acknowledge the contrasting diversity of other-than-capitalist enterprises. In keeping with the heterogeneity of the informal economy, there is a minority of well-paid digital workers that have little in common with the great number of unprotected apps-based workers (Meagher, 2019) and low-income ‘working poor’ (Fisker, 2022; Williams and Round, 2008). Similarly, the ‘community’ behind the community economy is often rife with power asymmetries and inequalities (Bayat, 1997). Cooperatives and self-managed worker businesses rarely provide a decent living to the unemployed that create them (Suryanata et al., 2021). Collective action requires trust which generally is absent in the informal economy or economies, so it remains unorganized and populated by crowds of destitute workers struggling to survive. By critiquing capitalist practices, all other practices appear deserving of promotion, whereas alterity is not necessarily superior. works.title: The Ethical Crossroads: Balancing Autonomy and Safety in Sedation Practices for Psychiatric Agitation in Critical Care
works.abstract: Introduction The intensive care unit (ICU) represents a uniquely challenging environment for patients with pre-existing psychiatric conditions or those who develop agitation secondary to critical illness. Agitation in the ICU—defined as excessive motor or verbal activity that interferes with patient care, patient or staff safety, or medical therapies—presents significant clinical and ethical challenges.[1] While sedation remains a cornerstone of managing severe agitation in the ICU, ethical tensions arise when balancing the immediate need for safety with long-term concerns about the autonomy, dignity, and iatrogenic harm.[2] For clarity in this viewpoint, we define “psychiatric agitation” as agitation primarily stemming from underlying psychiatric conditions (including delirium, pre-existing mental health disorders, substance withdrawal, or acute psychosis), as distinct from agitation primarily caused by physiological factors such as pain or hypoxemia. This distinction is important as management approaches and ethical considerations may differ, although we acknowledge the frequent overlap between psychiatric and physiological drivers of agitation in critically ill patients. Recent advances in critical care medicine have highlighted the adverse consequences of excessive sedation, including prolonged mechanical ventilation, increased delirium, longer ICU stays, and higher mortality.[3] Simultaneously, literature on psychiatric disorders has increasingly emphasized the importance of trauma-informed approaches, patient autonomy, and the potential harms of coercive interventions.[4] These parallel developments have created a complex ethical landscape for clinicians managing psychiatric agitation in critically ill patients. This viewpoint examines ethical dilemmas in sedation practices for psychiatric agitation in ICU settings, addressing the research question: How can clinicians navigate competing ethical principles when managing agitation of psychiatric origin in critically ill patients? We analyze current evidence, identify key ethical tensions, and propose a structured approach to clinical decision-making that respects both autonomy and safety imperatives. Current evidence: Critical analysis Pharmacological interventions: Efficacy and safety profiles Three key findings emerge from recent studies on the pharmacological management of agitation in ICU settings: Dexmedetomidine shows advantages over benzodiazepines but with important limitations. A 2023 Cochrane review by Martinez-Salazar et al.[5] examined 28 RCTs comparing different sedative agents for agitation in critically ill adults. While dexmedetomidine was associated with a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation and ICU stay compared to benzodiazepines, the review identified significant methodological limitations including heterogeneous outcome measures and exclusion of patients with pre-existing psychiatric conditions.[6] Antipsychotics show limited effectiveness for delirium-associated agitation. Girard et al.[7] conducted a landmark RCT comparing the efficacy of administering haloperidol, ziprasidone, and placebo for delirium in mechanically ventilated adults, finding no significant difference in the number of days alive without delirium or coma. This contradicts widespread clinical practice and raises important questions about the evidence-practice gap. Limited data exist on optimal approaches for patients with pre-existing psychiatric conditions. Ostuzzi et al.[8] identified only 12 studies addressing maintenance psychiatric medications during critical illness, with methodological quality rated as low to moderate. This evidence gap creates significant clinical uncertainty when managing one of the most vulnerable patient populations. Non-pharmacological approaches: Promise and barriers The ABCDEF bundle represents the strongest evidence for non-pharmacological prevention of agitation, with implementation barriers limiting effectiveness in real-world settings. This multicomponent approach (assess, prevent, and manage pain; both spontaneous awakening and breathing trials; choice of analgesia and sedation; delirium assessment, prevention, and management; early mobility and exercise; family engagement and empowerment) demonstrated a 35% relative reduction in delirium incidence across 15,000 patients.[9] However, implementation studies identify persistent barriers including staffing constraints, knowledge gaps, and institutional resistance.[10] Implementation science research reveals that effective strategies exist but face significant adoption challenges. A 2024 cluster-randomized trial by Patel et al.[11] found that despite proven benefits, less than 50% of eligible patients received the full ABCDEF bundle, with adherence declining for patients with behavioral disturbances. This implementation gap represents a significant ethical concern as evidence-based practices remain underutilized for the patients who might benefit most. Special populations: Evidence gaps and disparities Research consistently demonstrates worse outcomes for vulnerable populations but offers limited guidance on mitigation strategies. Studies examining ICU outcomes for patients with schizophrenia,[12] substance use disorders,[13] and dementia[14] consistently demonstrate higher rates of physical restraint use, increased sedation levels, longer ICU stays, and higher mortality compared to matched controls. However, interventional studies for these populations are notably absent from the literature. Racial and socioeconomic disparities in sedation practices represent a significant ethical concern with limited intervention research. Johnson et al.[15] documented that Black and Hispanic patients received higher doses of benzodiazepines and were more likely to be physically restrained than White patients, even after controlling for severity of agitation. Despite these documented disparities, we identified no published intervention studies specifically addressing this issue. Key ethical tensions: A framework for analysis Autonomy vs. safety: Case-based analysis The central ethical dilemma in managing psychiatric agitation can be illustrated through the following case: A 68-year-old man with schizophrenia develops hyperactive delirium following coronary artery bypass surgery. He repeatedly attempts to remove his endotracheal tube, stating that “the government put it there to poison me.” The patient lacks decision-making capacity but has previously expressed wishes to avoid psychiatric medications due to previous negative experiences. This scenario highlights the fundamental tension between respecting the patient’s previously expressed wishes (autonomy) and preventing potentially life-threatening self-extubation (safety). The concept of “relational autonomy” may offer guidance, recognizing that autonomy exists within social relationships and contexts rather than in isolation.[16] This perspective acknowledges that critical illness itself may temporarily compromise autonomous decision-making while still honoring the patient’s values and prior choices. Berger et al.[17] proposed a staged approach to agitation management that maximizes opportunities for autonomous choice. Their framework begins with non-pharmacological de-escalation, progresses to patient-controlled pharmacological options, and reserves involuntary sedation for situations where all other approaches have failed and significant harm is imminent. This approach balances respect for autonomy with recognition of safety imperatives. Beneficence and non-maleficence: Weighing complex tradeoffs Evidence increasingly recognizes harms from both over-sedation and under-treatment, creating genuine ethical dilemmas with no risk-free options. Recent research has highlighted previously underappreciated harms of sedation, including increased delirium, prolonged mechanical ventilation, post-ICU cognitive impairment, and post-traumatic stress.[18] A 2023 prospective cohort study by Williams et al.[19] found that 64% of patients reported traumatic memories of receiving sedation for agitation in the ICU, even when acknowledging the intervention’s necessity. Proportionality offers the most ethically sound approach to balancing beneficence and non-maleficence.[20] Dalmau et al.[21] articulated this principle, arguing that the degree of autonomy restriction should be proportional to the severity of the risk, with the least restrictive effective intervention always preferred. This approach respects individual dignity while acknowledging legitimate safety concerns. Justice considerations: Resource allocation and equity Justice in ICU sedation practices encompasses three dimensions: resource allocation, equitable treatment, and addressing systemic biases. Deeply sedated patients typically require more intensive monitoring, nursing care, and longer ICU stays, raising questions about resource allocation in resource-limited environments.[22] The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted resource allocation challenges when multiple patients required intensive care simultaneously, forcing explicit consideration of justice principles that might otherwise remain implicit in clinical decision-making.[23] Documented disparities in sedation practices reveal potential implicit biases affecting clinical decision-making. The previously mentioned study by Johnson et al.[15] raises serious concerns about how patient characteristics may influence sedation decisions independent of clinical factors. Addressing these disparities requires both individual awareness of potential biases and systemic approaches to ensuring equitable care. Proposed ethical framework for clinical practice Based on our analysis of current evidence and ethical principles, we propose the following structured approach to managing psychiatric agitation in the ICU. Proactive prevention Implement evidence-based delirium prevention strategies universally, with intensified approaches for high-risk patients. The ABCDEF bundle should be standard practice for all ICU patients, with additional preventive measures for those with pre-existing psychiatric conditions, cognitive impairment, or substance use disorders.[9] Prevention aligns with non-maleficence by avoiding the need for more restrictive interventions.[24,25] Structured assessment and tiered intervention Utilize a structured, staged approach that exhausts less restrictive options before progressing to more coercive interventions:[26-28] Tier 1: Environmental modifications and non-pharmacological approaches (reorientation, family presence, and noise reduction) Tier 2: Patient-controlled pharmacological options (as-needed oral medications when possible) Tier 3: Provider-initiated pharmacological interventions (targeted at underlying causes) Tier 4: Involuntary sedation (reserved for imminent safety threats when other approaches have failed) This tiered approach aligns with both respect for autonomy and the principle of proportionality.[17] Interdisciplinary collaboration Involve psychiatric consultation early for patients with known psychiatric conditions or when standard approaches prove ineffective.[29] A 2023 study by Rodriguez et al.[30] demonstrated that implementation of a psychiatric consultation-liaison service in the ICU was associated with reduced benzodiazepine use, decreased physical restraint application, and shorter ICU length of stay for patients with psychiatric comorbidities. Transparency and regular reassessment We clearly document ethical reasoning and implement protocols for regular sedation interruption and reassessment. Transparency supports accountability and reflective practices,[22] while regular reassessment prevents continuation of sedation beyond the minimal necessary duration.[28] Limitations and future directions Our analysis identified significant evidence gaps that limit definitive guidance in several areas: Limited long-term outcome data for different sedation strategies Inadequate evidence for managing patients with pre-existing psychiatric conditions Few intervention studies addressing identified disparities in care Limited patient-centered metrics of successful treatment Future research should address these gaps while incorporating ethical considerations into study design and outcome measures. Specifically, we recommend the following: Studies comparing sedation strategies that include long-term cognitive and psychological outcomes Research specifically inclusive of patients with pre-existing psychiatric conditions Implementation studies of interventions to reduce disparities in sedation practices Development and validation of patient-centered outcome measures Conclusion Management of psychiatric agitation in the ICU exemplifies the complex ethical challenges inherent in critical care medicine. Evidence increasingly supports approaches that prioritize proactive prevention, targeted interventions, minimal effective sedation, and interdisciplinary collaboration. These approaches align with respect for autonomy while acknowledging the duty to prevent harm in vulnerable patients. The framework proposed in this viewpoint offers a structured approach to navigating competing ethical principles, emphasizing proportionality, transparency, and regular reassessment. By combining evidence-based practices with individualized patient-centered care, clinicians can navigate the ethical crossroads of psychiatric agitation management in critical care settings while respecting both autonomy and safety imperatives. Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the writing process No generative artificial intelligence tools or software were used in writing this work. Author contributions SS: conceptualization, drafting, critical care ethical perspectives, and integration of sedation practices. HD: contribution of psychiatric and ethical frameworks, analysis of autonomy, and legal considerations. All authors have reviewed and approved the final version of the manuscript. Data availability statement The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author, SS, upon reasonable request. Ethical policy and institutional review board statement This is a commentary based on literature and clinical practice. It does not involve any human or animal research or patient-identifiable data. All ethical principles and international guidelines for publication ethics have been followed. Financial support and sponsorship Nil. Conflict of interest There are no conflict of interest.

works.title: The Status of the Social Fact
works.abstract: What does it mean to do interpretive social science research in today's changed reality? How can anthropological investigations of the social institutions; the cognitive, psychological, and philosophical processes; and the physiological phenomena that have long concerned us be brought to bear upon a world in which there is simultaneously limited consensus regarding what constitutes facts and seemingly little impetus to observe and recognize each other's truths? Philosophers have long grappled with the difference between fact and truth. Fact is said to be something that is arrived at through objective observation of concrete realities; this, of course, does not mean facts can't change (we now acknowledge that the world is not flat), but it is also the case that we are not always in agreement about how these ontological changes happen. Truth, on the other hand, is arrived at through perspective and experience. Truth is not merely individual but is also collective, and therefore it is contextualized within a set of identifiable historical and social relations. What seems critical about this difference is that the basis for fact tends to be seeing. We are able to know the world because we visually apprehend it, a regime of knowledge that became epistemologically hegemonic during the Enlightenment era and the colonial exploration and exploitation that both produced and was produced by it. Truth, on the other hand, depends on a different way of knowing, on affect, which necessitates attention to context—historical and otherwise—and to the forms of intersubjectivity through which we identify it. Truth unequivocally relies upon interpretation, which is our business, where fact wants to resist it. It is true that anthropologists have made great advances by challenging facts. Sometimes, we have done this by laying bare the modernist assumptions that undergirded them and sometimes by drawing attention to societies in which the facts don't hold true (often “non-Western,” itself a laden term, as Michel-Rolph Trouillot [1991] taught us so long ago). A few examples of these assumptions: All people make decisions by weighing options and rationally maximizing their gain, families are organized through male descent lines, people of African descent have smaller brains but better musical facility, capitalism distributes wealth more equally than other economic arrangements, the direction of all evolutionary change is toward improvement. Durkheim defined social facts as the norms and structures that exercise social control over individuals. In the world of social facts, society (in the guise of social institutions like kinship, language, and political organization, or of value systems like racism and misogyny) exerts force, constrains possibilities, molds, shapes, and influences—often without our explicit realization. The point of a science of society, for Durkheim, was therefore not to study individuals, but to identify these social facts, and to understand something about how they operate. We are no longer all the kind of positivists Durkheim might have imagined in the early twentieth century, of course. Nevertheless, our ability to identify and challenge dominant worldviews framed as fact has been the result of our constant examination of our interpretive apparatuses. In other words, we have been willing to create knowledge inductively rather than by applying existing theoretical frames or methodological structures to material we collect “in the field” or in the lab. We are, one might argue, the most creative of the social sciences, following the lead of our data. Although this creativity has certainly generated facts, it has also helped to move us toward a deeper understanding of the truths of others (and ourselves). This brings me to our place in the university, and where we stand in relation to our allied fields, including biology, history, sociology, cultural studies, linguistics, Africana studies, gender studies (the list goes on). This is something tackled by Richard Handler in his opening gambit for the new “Anthropology in the Classroom” section on our website (www.americananthropologist.org). The essay encourages us to think about how the insights of anthropology can be situated more squarely within the educational careers of students and in relation to our own research trajectories. It also challenges us to ask how we penetrate the new climate of uncertainty by simultaneously emphasizing the interpretive dimensions of our science and the reality of having deconstructed a number of truths currently being pushed as fact. In his essays responding to the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, Slavoj Zizek (2002) argued that whereas the nineteenth century was characterized by a proliferation of interest in the prophetic, and the twentieth century elicited a subsequent “passion for the Real,” the early twenty-first century should be seen to privilege the virtual. Here, virtualization leads us to “begin to experience ‘real reality’ itself as a virtual entity” (11), one in which the affective dimensions of truth are not rendered through relational experience but instead through the virtual reliving of that experience, often over and over again. For psychologists, this would indicate a kind of trauma, and it could result in various forms of paralysis. But I am more optimistic. Before we declare truth as dead (see the Time magazine cover for April 3, 2017), let us remember the strength of inductive, interpretive analysis and the creativity of our approach. The essays in this issue certainly do this. We begin with a trio of essays that together, and from different intradisciplinary vantage points, offer new directions for thinking about migration and its effects. In “Temporal Patterns of Mexican Migrant Genetic Ancestry,” Cris Hughes et al. mobilize biological and ethnographic methods to think about the forensic identification process for migrant deaths on the US–Mexico border. They document a bias, through forensic genetic markers, in DNA-based identification of migrant remains, a bias that accompanies a demographic shift in patterns of migrant origin from predominantly northern to central and southern Mexico, home to the majority of Mexico's indigenous population. Based on genetic markers of Native and European ancestry, they argue that migrants with a greater proportion of European ancestry are more likely to be identified forensically than migrants with primarily indigenous ancestry. This leads them to assert that the structural vulnerabilities faced by indigenous Mexicans not only attend to life but also haunt death and that any attempt to improve forensic identification protocols requires a more robust consideration of social and historical context. Iván Sandoval-Cervantes's “Uncertain Futures” urges us to see, in unfinished houses, the aspirational trajectories of undocumented migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico. Drawing from both sociocultural anthropological and archaeological approaches to materiality, he asks us to look through the lens of affect to understand something about the kinship norms and familial responsibilities that bind together “home” and “host” as spatial locales, the precarity suffusing both the materiality and practice of building a house, and the quotidian experiences of waiting, preparation, and disappointment. He is interested in how violence and uncertainty become part of the built environment, shedding light on both past and present efforts toward social mobility and familial unification, and on the future potential of these processes (sometimes seemingly endlessly deferred). Hilary Dick's “Una Gabacha Sinvergüenza (A Shameless White-Trash Woman),” asks us to consider the following questions: What kinds of moral lives do people forge in the spaces of migratory circulation? How do people negotiate the competing visions of ethico-moral personhood they encounter? Through the linguistic anthropological lens of interdiscursivity, Dick explores how family members of those who have migrated from Uriangato, Mexico, to the United States enact forms of ethical personhood—forms that, in this case, define “proper Mexicanness” in relation to the racialized, gendered, and classed popular cultural traffic from the United States. Using an encounter about a Britney Spears doll as a foil, she shows also how women negotiate the desires of their children with their own sensibilities of proper womanhood and family life in the interstices between sending and receiving countries, and in relation to her own presence as a white, female, American ethnographer. All three of these essays, in different ways, speak to that which remains, thereby tempering an often-dominant focus in migration studies on mobility. In doing so, they also build upon the transnational perspective that was developed in the 1980s and elaborated in the 1990s (Basch, Glick Schiller, and Szanton Blanc 1994; Glick Schiller, Basch, and Blanc-Szanton 1992; Sutton and Chaney 1985), especially in terms of the assertion that the space of analysis of migration should be the “transnational sociocultural sphere” that develops in its wake. By focusing on what and who is left behind, these essays help us to more clearly see what exactly circulates as people move—forms of structural and symbolic violence, affects and aspirations related to family and mobility, notions of propriety, and the complex material, biological, and sociopolitical production of the social formation of the nation-state. We are asked to analyze the boundaries of citizenship and the boundaries of personhood, and to think anew about the relations that produce these as nonequivalences, a phenomenon that is most obviously visible in today's United States. We also feature two archaeological essays, both of which proved somewhat controversial in the review process, in part because they suggest that we think differently about our methodological approaches and about how we build theory. Grounded in very different contexts, both ask us to imagine anew the relationships between space, temporality, and the forms of social relationships that emerge within this nexus. More traditional practitioners might find these essays too speculative, insufficiently grounded in more conventional forms of data, but I believe the dialogues they have already provoked on methods and on the relationships between data and theoretical interventions are productive ones for the discipline as a whole. Shannon Novak's “Corporeal Congregations and Asynchronous Lives” uses the assemblage of skeletal remains at Spring Street Presbyterian Church in Manhattan (in use from 1820 to 1850) to think through what they might tell us about contemporaneity and noncontemporaneity. She wants us to overcome the “temptations of conflation”—the sometimes unconscious collapsing of diverse individuals, moments, and positions within an assemblage—and instead urges us to engage the complex relationships that might have obtained among people who would not necessarily have experienced themselves as part of the same community. Her broader concern is with how a bioarchaeology of urban landscapes can destabilize assumptions about the “demographic bundles” and processes of categorization she sees as prevalent in bioarchaeological research as well as in anthropology more broadly. By engaging social theory outside anthropology, extensive archival research, and recent work on temporality within archaeology and sociocultural anthropology, she outlines what these burial-ground remains tell us about social life in New York City during the thirty-year period of the cemetery's operation. Dante Angelo's “Histories of a Burnt House” similarly asks us to think through the ways one domicile can tell us something about the various population waves that moved through Arica, Chile, and thus about changes in the region as a whole. He combines historical, archaeological, and ethnographic methods to conduct an archaeology of the contemporary past, bringing the story of the “blue house” alive as a case that can illuminate the materiality of wave after wave of displacement and dispossession, as well as broader processes of gentrification and heritage making. As such, Angelo advocates a view of material structures as always in processes of becoming, and therefore social and dynamic. Our last research article, Daromir Rudnyckyj's “Subjects of Debt,” examines what neoliberalism looks like outside the North Atlantic. By investigating shifts in Islamic finance in Malaysia—specifically, the move from a “debt-based” model that was geared toward integrating the disadvantaged Muslim majority into the national economy through affirmative action mechanisms to an “equity-based” model designed to encourage entrepreneurialism and risk sharing—he explores the dynamics through which neoliberal knowledge and practices are applied toward alternative financial projects. As the equity model is seen as being more tethered to Islamic traditions, Rudnyckyj argues that the shift he has identified produces an Islamic entrepreneurial, risk-calculating subject that is, nevertheless, a refusal of the rationally self-interested Western subject. Here, we see that the development of financial instruments can theoretically include a focus on equality and social justice. We also feature our four Year-in-Review essays, charting trends and emphases across the subfields for 2016. In our World Anthropologies section, we present a dialogue regarding the new South-South relations that have emerged as a result of growing investment, aid, and technology transfer to Africa on the part of China, India, and Brazil. What does it mean to speak of South-South partnerships to describe a relationship that has typically been characterized as imperialist humanitarianism or development when a Western power is involved? Letícia Cesarino is interested in how contemporary conditions differ from earlier manifestations of these “trade and aid” relationships and in what this has to do with anthropology (both the field as a whole and its Brazilian instantiation). She offers an analysis of “culture-talk”—when and where it happens, and who engages in it—as that which has enabled new forms of cooperation within the context of Brazilian engagement with African countries. She argues that the focus on “culture” can reproduce familiar elisions with respect to Afro-Brazilian cultural practice and heritage, even when “culture” is mobilized to serve postcolonial nation building rather than the consolidation of empire. She calls this a “postcolonial kind of Orientalism.” Cesarino's essay, which ultimately calls for more ethnographic scholarship by Brazilian anthropologists in Africa, is followed by four commentaries that question some of her premises. Ultimately, they suggest that we interrogate the ways discursive frames such as North-South and South-South simplify scenarios that are much more complex in terms of the kinds of hierarchies and inequalities they index. In other words, we cannot assume that a South-South cooperation is necessarily less imperialist in spirit and practice than a North-South one, and we must be attentive to the ways these complexities are also intrinsic to the concept of “world anthropologies.” We require, therefore, not only a more robust Brazilian anthropology of Lusophone Africa but also one that is grounded in an understanding of the colonial field in which Portugal, Brazil, and Africa are—unequally—located. Within our Multimodal Anthropologies section, PhD candidate Richard Powis offers a response to Collins, Durington, and Gill's March 2017 invitation regarding multimodality. Powis describes how his own multiplatform work engages social media as a way to engage with colleagues and ethnographic interlocutors about research topics and design.
